statement: When designing a new app or feature area, start from one concrete piece of functionality rather than from the global app shell.
condition: At the beginning of a new product or feature design.

statement: Navigation and page-shell decisions depend on what the product features require, so making those decisions before designing representative features is under-informed.
condition: Before representative features have been designed.

statement: For a selected workflow, first identify the user inputs and actions the interface must support before working on broader layout structure.
condition: When translating a product idea into an initial interface.

statement: Early feature design should defer low-level aesthetic choices such as typefaces, shadows, and icons until the main structure is working.
condition: During the earliest exploration of a feature.

statement: Use deliberately low-fidelity sketching when high-fidelity tools make it hard to ignore visual details.
condition: When the designer is prematurely optimizing details in a browser or design tool.

statement: Refine initial layouts in grayscale before introducing color so hierarchy depends on spacing, contrast, and size first.
condition: When moving from rough sketching into higher-fidelity layout exploration.

statement: Treat sketches and wireframes as disposable decision aids rather than artifacts worth polishing for their own sake.
condition: When low-fidelity work has already answered the design question.

statement: Design and build in short feature cycles instead of trying to specify every feature and edge case before implementation.
condition: When building a product with multiple features or uncertain edge cases.

statement: A usable implementation exposes interaction problems and edge cases that are hard to predict from static mockups alone.
condition: When design decisions involve real user interaction or dynamic states.

statement: Iterate on a working version of the current feature until its major design problems are resolved before moving to the next feature.
condition: When the current feature is implemented enough to use.

statement: Avoid showing functionality in a design unless the team is prepared to build it for the current release.
condition: When designing a feature that has likely future enhancements.
exception: Unless the implied functionality is intentionally out of scope and clearly not presented as available.

statement: Design the smallest useful shippable version of a new feature first, and defer nice-to-have capabilities until after the core version works.
condition: When implementation cost or complexity is uncertain.

statement: An interface should have a deliberate personality that matches the product domain and desired user impression.
condition: When establishing the visual and verbal direction of a product.

statement: Choose typography to support the intended personality of the interface rather than treating fonts as neutral decoration.
condition: When selecting fonts for a product or feature.

statement: Choose colors by how well they fit the desired feel of the product in practice, not by relying mechanically on color psychology.
condition: When selecting a product palette.

statement: Keep corner-rounding choices consistent across an interface because border radius contributes to perceived formality or playfulness.
condition: When defining component shape language.

statement: Select interface copy and tone as part of the product personality, since words can influence perceived professionalism, friendliness, or seriousness as strongly as visual choices.
condition: When writing labels, headings, prompts, and other UI text.

statement: If the desired personality is unclear, study products already used by the target audience for direction while avoiding close imitation of direct competitors.
condition: When there is no strong initial design direction.
exception: Do not borrow so closely from competitors that the product appears derivative.

statement: Constrain recurring design decisions by defining a small set of allowed values instead of choosing from an unlimited range each time.
condition: When decisions repeat across the interface.

statement: Define color scales and type scales up front so later UI decisions reuse a vetted system rather than one-off tweaks.
condition: When a product will need repeated color or font-size choices.

statement: Pick among system values by comparing a likely option with neighboring values and eliminating the ones that clearly do not work.
condition: When choosing a size or similar token from a predefined scale.

statement: Create systems for repeated low-level variables such as font weight, line height, spacing, dimensions, shadows, radii, borders, and opacity as those decisions arise.
condition: When repeated minor styling choices start consuming attention.

statement: Clear visual hierarchy is a primary mechanism for making an interface feel designed and understandable.
condition: When multiple elements compete for user attention.

statement: Emphasize important elements and deliberately de-emphasize secondary and tertiary information to reduce visual noise.
condition: When arranging content with differing importance levels.

statement: Use font weight and color, not font size alone, to communicate hierarchy while preserving readable text sizes.
condition: When primary and secondary content need different emphasis.

statement: Limit routine UI hierarchy to a small set of text colors and font weights instead of adding many subtle variations.
condition: When defining typographic hierarchy for interface text.

statement: Avoid font weights below 400 for small UI text because they reduce legibility; use color or size to de-emphasize instead.
condition: When styling small text in an interface.
exception: Large headings may tolerate lighter weights.

statement: On colored backgrounds, reduce text contrast by choosing a related color with adjusted hue, saturation, and lightness rather than using generic grey text.
condition: When de-emphasizing text on a colored surface.

statement: Avoid lowering white text opacity over images or patterns because the background can show through and make the text look faded or disabled.
condition: When text sits on non-solid or colored backgrounds.

statement: If an important element still fails to stand out, reduce the emphasis of competing elements before adding more visual treatment to the target element.
condition: When further emphasis on the target would make the interface louder.

statement: Use labels for displayed data only when format or context is insufficient to explain the value.
condition: When presenting database-like values or attributes.

statement: Where possible, combine labels and values into natural text so the information can be styled as a single meaningful unit.
condition: When a value needs clarification but a separate label would flatten hierarchy.

statement: When labels are necessary, style labels as supporting content unless users are expected to scan primarily for the labels.
condition: When displaying multiple labeled data values.
exception: On dense specification-style pages, the label may need more emphasis than the value.

statement: Choose HTML elements for semantic meaning and accessibility, then style them according to the needed visual hierarchy rather than browser heading defaults.
condition: When building application interfaces on the web.

statement: Treat many application section titles as supporting labels instead of large document headings when the section content is the real focus.
condition: When the title merely identifies a region whose content is self-explanatory.

statement: Balance visually heavy icons or solid shapes next to text by lowering their contrast.
condition: When an icon or graphic element draws more attention than adjacent content warrants.

statement: Increase weight rather than contrast when a subtle element such as a soft border needs more presence without becoming harsh.
condition: When darkening the element would make the design noisy.

statement: Button styling should communicate an action’s importance in the page hierarchy, not only the semantic category of the action.
condition: When a page offers multiple user actions.

statement: Use prominent solid treatments for true primary actions, quieter treatments for secondary actions, and unobtrusive link-like treatments for tertiary actions.
condition: When assigning visual treatments to page actions.

statement: Do not style a destructive action as the page’s strongest button unless it is the current primary action; reserve the strongest destructive styling for confirmation contexts where the destructive choice is primary.
condition: When a destructive action is available but not the main page action.

statement: Start spacing exploration with more whitespace than seems necessary, then remove space until the whole interface feels balanced.
condition: When a layout feels cramped or visually busy.

statement: Choose compact density deliberately when many items must be visible at once, rather than letting tight spacing be the default.
condition: When the product value depends on seeing substantial information on one screen.

statement: Use a constrained spacing and sizing scale instead of trialing arbitrary pixel values one at a time.
condition: When sizing elements or setting margins and padding.

statement: Build spacing and sizing scales so adjacent options are visually distinct, with roughly a quarter-step difference or more.
condition: When defining reusable size or spacing tokens.

statement: Construct spacing scales from a sensible base value with tighter steps for small sizes and larger jumps for large sizes.
condition: When designing a practical UI spacing system.

statement: A spacing and sizing system improves both workflow speed and subtle visual consistency.
condition: When designers repeatedly choose similar sizes or distances.

statement: Do not stretch content to fill the available screen; give each element or section only the width it needs.
condition: When a large viewport provides more room than the content requires.

statement: Use a smaller or mobile-sized canvas when a large canvas makes it hard to design a naturally narrow interface.
condition: When a responsive interface needs to work well at small widths.

statement: Use columns to occupy available horizontal space without making a form or text region wider than its optimal reading or interaction width.
condition: When narrow content feels unbalanced inside a wide layout.

statement: Allow a layout to use substantial space when the content genuinely needs it; the rule is to avoid obligation, not to force compactness.
condition: When the interface has content or interactions that benefit from a larger area.

statement: Grid systems can simplify layout decisions, but treating the grid as the sole layout authority can harm component fit.
condition: When a design system uses column grids.

statement: Use fixed widths for elements whose contents have an optimal width, and let adjacent regions flex around them.
condition: When a fluid grid would make an element too wide or too narrow.

statement: Avoid percentage-based sizing unless the element is supposed to scale with its container.
condition: When choosing between fixed, max, and fluid dimensions.

statement: Use max-width constraints and shrink elements only when the viewport is smaller than their optimal width.
condition: When a component has a known ideal size such as a card or form.

statement: Do not assume proportional size relationships remain correct across screen sizes.
condition: When designing responsive typography or components.

statement: Large elements should usually shrink more aggressively than already-small elements on smaller screens.
condition: When adapting a large-screen layout to a small screen.

statement: Tune component properties such as padding independently across sizes instead of scaling every property from the font size.
condition: When creating small, medium, and large variants of a component.

statement: When spacing alone communicates grouping, make the space around a group larger than the space within it.
condition: When elements lack borders, backgrounds, or other explicit separators.

statement: Define a type scale to avoid inconsistent font sizes and slow one-off font-size decisions.
condition: When an interface uses repeated text roles.

statement: Use a non-linear type scale with closer options for small text and wider jumps for large display sizes.
condition: When selecting reusable font-size tokens.

statement: Prefer hand-crafted type scales for interface design when modular scales produce fractional values or omit useful intermediate sizes.
condition: When defining UI typography rather than only long-form article typography.

statement: Use px or rem units for type-scale values so nested elements still compute to values in the scale.
condition: When implementing a reusable type scale.

statement: Choose a neutral sans-serif or the system font stack for safe UI typography when the goal is legibility and familiarity.
condition: When a distinctive typeface is not required or font taste is uncertain.

statement: Use the availability of many weights as a heuristic for typeface quality, while recognizing it is not an absolute rule.
condition: When filtering large font libraries.

statement: Avoid condensed typefaces with short x-heights for main UI text because they are typically less legible at small sizes.
condition: When choosing fonts for body or interface text.

statement: Use font popularity and the choices of strong design teams as pragmatic filters for finding high-quality typefaces.
condition: When choosing fonts outside a neutral default.

statement: Set paragraph widths to roughly 45 to 75 characters per line, using about 20 to 35 ems as a practical web range.
condition: When styling readable paragraph text.
exception: Wider lines can work, but they are riskier for readability.

statement: Constrain paragraph text independently from wider images or components in the same content area.
condition: When mixed content needs a wider overall container than the prose itself.

statement: Align mixed-size text on a shared baseline instead of vertically centering it.
condition: When different font sizes appear on the same row.

statement: Increase line-height as line length grows so readers can reliably find the next wrapped line.
condition: When text columns are wide.

statement: Use taller line-height for small text and tighter line-height for large headings.
condition: When setting typography across multiple font sizes.

statement: Use subtle treatments such as heavier weight or darker color for most links when an interface contains many links.
condition: When link styling would otherwise compete with primary actions.

statement: For ancillary links, consider applying color or underline only on hover so they stay discoverable without competing for attention.
condition: When the link is outside the main user path.

statement: Align text according to the reading direction, and avoid centering blocks longer than a few lines.
condition: When setting alignment for paragraph or explanatory text.
exception: Short independent headings or short text blocks can be centered effectively.

statement: Right-align numbers in tables so magnitudes and decimals are easier to compare at a glance.
condition: When a tabular column contains numeric values.

statement: Enable hyphenation when using justified text to avoid distracting word gaps.
condition: When text is justified for a print-like or formal presentation.

statement: Leave letter-spacing alone by default, adjusting it only for specific readability or display reasons.
condition: When styling normal mixed-case text.

statement: Tighten letter-spacing when using a widely spaced text typeface for large headlines, but avoid repurposing headline fonts for small text.
condition: When a font intended for small-size legibility is used at headline scale.

statement: Increase letter-spacing for all-caps text to improve readability.
condition: When styling labels or headings set in all caps.

statement: Use HSL for web color work because hue, saturation, and lightness map to intuitive adjustments and CSS understands the format.
condition: When choosing or tuning colors for web interfaces.

statement: Build UI palettes with greys, primary colors, and accent colors rather than relying on a handful of generic colors.
condition: When defining colors for a real product interface.

statement: Provide roughly eight to ten grey shades, starting from a dark grey rather than pure black and stepping steadily toward white.
condition: When defining neutral colors for text, surfaces, panels, and controls.

statement: Provide multiple lighter and darker shades for each primary color so it can support actions, active states, tinted backgrounds, and dark text.
condition: When a color defines the main product look or primary actions.

statement: Define accent colors and shades for semantic states, highlights, and category distinction, with more accents when the interface must distinguish many similar items.
condition: When status, warning, success, trends, tags, events, or chart series need color coding.

statement: Define fixed palette shades up front instead of generating lightened or darkened variants on demand.
condition: When implementing a reusable color system.

statement: Choose a color scale’s base shade by practical use, such as whether it works as a button background, rather than by a fixed lightness formula.
condition: When starting a primary or accent color scale.

statement: Choose the darkest and lightest shades from expected uses such as text and tinted backgrounds, then fill intermediate shades between them.
condition: When constructing a color shade scale.

statement: Use a systematic shade scale as a starting point, but refine colors by eye once they appear in real UI contexts and avoid adding new shades casually.
condition: When palette values are tested in actual designs.

statement: Increase saturation for very light and very dark shades so HSL lightness changes do not make the palette look washed out.
condition: When generating shades away from middle lightness values.

statement: Rotate hue toward perceptually brighter or darker hues when adjusting apparent brightness without losing as much color intensity.
condition: When lightness changes alone make a shade dull or muddy.

statement: Keep hue rotation modest so a lighter or darker shade still reads as the same color family.
condition: When using hue shifts inside a palette scale.

statement: Saturate greys slightly to create a warm or cool temperature, and increase saturation at the light and dark ends to maintain that temperature.
condition: When defining neutral greys that should have a deliberate feel.

statement: Accessible text contrast requirements can force colored backgrounds behind white text to be darker than the intended visual hierarchy allows.
condition: When normal-sized text is placed on colored surfaces.

statement: Use dark colored text on a light colored background when a dark colored background would make a secondary element too visually dominant.
condition: When color is needed but the element should not capture primary attention.

statement: For colored text on colored backgrounds, rotate the text hue toward a brighter hue to improve contrast without making the text nearly white.
condition: When secondary colored text must remain accessible on a dark colored panel.

statement: Communicate meaning with color plus another cue instead of relying on color alone.
condition: When color indicates status, direction, category, or importance.

statement: Use lightness contrast as well as hue differences to distinguish chart lines or similar colored items for users with color-vision limitations.
condition: When several colored marks encode different data series or categories.

statement: Create interface depth by mimicking how a top-down light source would affect raised and recessed surfaces.
condition: When adding highlights, borders, inset effects, or shadows for depth.

statement: Decide whether an element should feel raised or inset before applying edge highlights and shadows.
condition: When styling controls, wells, inputs, or panels for depth.

statement: Hand-pick highlight colors instead of overlaying transparent white when saturation needs to remain intact.
condition: When creating light edges on colored raised surfaces.

statement: Keep simulated lighting effects subtle so depth improves clarity without making the interface busy or photorealistic.
condition: When using real-world lighting cues in UI styling.

statement: Use shadow size, blur, and offset as an elevation system where larger softer shadows imply elements closer to the user.
condition: When positioning elements on a visual z-axis.

statement: Match shadow elevation to the element’s interaction importance, using lower elevation for routine controls and higher elevation for overlays that need focus.
condition: When styling buttons, dropdowns, dialogs, and similar layers.

statement: Define a small fixed shadow scale instead of inventing a different shadow for every component.
condition: When a product uses shadows in multiple places.

statement: Change shadows during interactions to indicate that an item has lifted, moved forward, or pressed into the page.
condition: When designing drag states, press states, or active controls.

statement: Use separate cast and contact shadows when a single shadow cannot express both broad softness and near-edge definition.
condition: When designing realistic but controllable elevation shadows.

statement: In flat designs, use relative lightness to imply depth: lighter surfaces can feel raised and darker surfaces can feel inset.
condition: When shadows and gradients are intentionally minimized.

statement: Use short vertically offset solid shadows to suggest depth while preserving a flat visual style.
condition: When a card or button needs separation without soft shadow realism.

statement: Overlap elements across containers or background transitions to create a layered sense of depth.
condition: When a composition feels too flat or boxed-in.

statement: Separate overlapping images with a background-matched gap or invisible border so layers do not visually clash.
condition: When images overlap each other.

statement: Use professional photography or high-quality stock photography when photos are part of the design.
condition: When a design depends on photographic assets.

statement: Do not design around placeholder images while assuming low-effort later photos will preserve the design quality.
condition: When final photographic assets are not yet available.

statement: For text over photos, reduce the image’s visual dynamics because inconsistent background contrast is usually the readability problem.
condition: When no single text color remains readable across a background image.

statement: Use dark or light overlays to make photo backgrounds more uniform for light or dark text respectively.
condition: When an image needs a simple global contrast adjustment behind text.

statement: Lower image contrast, adjust brightness, or colorize the image when a background photo needs more controlled contrast or stronger brand alignment.
condition: When a full overlay would alter the image too bluntly.

statement: Use a subtle no-offset text shadow or glow to protect text while preserving more of the image’s original contrast.
condition: When text needs local contrast help on a photo.

statement: Respect assets’ intended display sizes instead of enlarging small icons, shrinking detailed screenshots, or shrinking detailed logos beyond what their detail supports.
condition: When placing icons, screenshots, logos, or favicons.

statement: Place a small icon inside a larger colored shape or container when the layout needs a larger visual element without scaling the icon itself.
condition: When only small-size icons are available for a large-feature treatment.

statement: Control user-uploaded image shape and size with fixed containers and cropping so arbitrary image aspect ratios do not break the layout.
condition: When the interface displays many user-provided images.

statement: Prevent user-uploaded images from blending into similar page backgrounds with a subtle inner shadow or semi-transparent inner border rather than a clashing outer border.
condition: When uploaded image backgrounds can match the surrounding UI.

statement: Add polish by enhancing existing default elements before introducing new decorative elements.
condition: When a design feels plain but the structure is already sound.

statement: Replace ordinary list bullets with meaningful icons when the icons reinforce the list content.
condition: When a list is a visible part of the design and the icon meaning is clear.

statement: Promote testimonial quotation marks or similar existing punctuation into visual elements when they can add character without adding content.
condition: When a quote or testimonial needs more visual presence.

statement: Use custom link treatments such as weight, color, or underline styling to make links feel intentionally designed.
condition: When links are visually important elements in a composition.

statement: Style checkbox and radio selected states with brand colors to make forms feel more polished than browser defaults.
condition: When default form controls look visually disconnected from the product design.

statement: Use colored accent borders as a simple way to add visual flair to otherwise plain UI regions.
condition: When cards, active navigation, alerts, headings, or page edges need distinction.

statement: Decorate selected backgrounds with color, subtle gradients, patterns, or simple illustrations to reduce monotony without changing the underlying layout.
condition: When hierarchy, spacing, and typography are working but the design still feels plain.

statement: Keep gradient hues close together for a smoother background effect.
condition: When using a gradient as a decorative background.

statement: Keep decorative background patterns and illustrations low contrast so they do not interfere with content readability.
condition: When adding background decoration behind text or interface controls.

statement: Treat empty states as priority design work for features that depend on user-generated content.
condition: When a new product area can initially have no user content.

statement: Design empty states with a strong next action and an attention-grabbing visual rather than leaving a blank or purely mechanical screen.
condition: When the user needs to create or import the first item.

statement: Hide supporting controls such as tabs and filters in an empty state when those controls cannot do anything yet.
condition: When no content exists for the controls to operate on.

statement: An empty state is often a user’s first interaction with a new feature, so it should communicate energy and direction rather than neglect.
condition: When launching a new feature or product area.

statement: Use fewer borders by considering subtler separation methods first.
condition: When two elements need distinction.

statement: Use a box shadow instead of a border when it can outline an element more subtly and the element already contrasts with the background.
condition: When a bordered element feels distracting.

statement: Use slight background color differences to separate adjacent regions, and remove borders that duplicate that separation.
condition: When adjacent sections already have distinct surfaces.

statement: Use extra spacing to distinguish groups of elements without adding another visible separator.
condition: When separation can be achieved by distance alone.

statement: Question default component conventions when a more expressive structure would better serve the content.
condition: When a standard component pattern feels limiting or generic.

statement: Structure dropdowns with sections, columns, supporting text, or icons when that helps the menu communicate richer choices.
condition: When a dropdown contains choices that benefit from explanation or grouping.

statement: Combine related table data and introduce hierarchy when separate sortable columns are not needed.
condition: When table values are related and independent sorting is unnecessary.

statement: Use images or color inside table content when they clarify or enrich the data rather than acting as decoration alone.
condition: When visual treatment makes tabular information easier to understand.

statement: Use selectable cards or similarly rich controls for important radio-button choices instead of default stacked labels.
condition: When radio choices are central to the interface.

statement: Study admired designs by identifying decisions the designer made that you would not have considered.
condition: When improving design judgment from examples.

statement: Rebuild polished interfaces from scratch without inspecting implementation details to discover the small choices that make them work.
condition: When practicing UI design skills from existing products.

statement: Design patterns for interfaces endure because they derive from the stable ways people perceive and use software; good patterns work with human senses and psychology rather than against them.

Interface design patterns are durable building blocks for any screen because they are grounded in the recurring tasks people want to do with software: searching, entering data, creating and manipulating objects, managing payments, and exchanging messages and files.
Treat UI component libraries and frameworks as a floor that gets a design to a solid base quickly, not as a ceiling; they should not cap design innovation.
Prefer assembling software from existing, separately operated services (authentication, analytics, hosting, infrastructure) rather than building each capability from scratch.

Specify each design pattern with four parts: what it is (a definition), when to use it (context plus special considerations and exceptions), why to use it (purpose, benefits, and who benefits), and how to implement it effectively.
Good interface design begins with understanding people (who they are, why they use the software, and how they interact with it), not with pictures, layouts, or visuals.
Software is only a means to the user's ends; the more effectively a design satisfies those ends, the more successful and satisfying it is.
Apply the maxim 'you are not the user': do not assume your own preferences, knowledge, or behavior represent the audience's.

Characterize your audience along their overall goals, the task breakdown for those goals, how they think about the domain, the vocabulary they use, their skill level, and their attitudes, and ground design decisions in what they want to do and bring to the interaction.
Treat each use of an application as a conversation between the user and the software: a continuous back-and-forth of requests, commands, and responses that the UI mediates.
Give the user continuous feedback confirming that the system is active and listening, that inputs are being processed, and that they are progressing toward their goal.

Design the software to behave like a considerate conversation partner: understandable, signaling when it is active, making it obvious when it is responding, and offering anticipated next steps or recommendations.
Match the interface's subject vocabulary to the users' level of knowledge; when some users will not know the terms, give them a way to learn the unfamiliar vocabulary.
condition: some users will not know the domain vocabulary

statement: When users are not skilled with computers, avoid sophisticated widgetry and uncommon interface-design conventions.
condition: users are not computer-savvy

statement: When users' interest or motivation is low, do not demand much effort for too little reward.
condition: user interest or motivation is low

statement: Tune how much freedom or openness the interface gives to fit the audience: too little leaves users feeling trapped, too much leaves them paralyzed and unsure what to do next.
Honestly decide whether most of your users will remain perpetual beginners, intermediates, or experts, and design for that reality.
For frequent or expert users, optimize for efficient operation rather than learnability (document- or list-centered, without step-by-step hand-holding).
condition: audience is frequent or expert users

statement: For occasional or one-time users, restrain functionality and explain it along the way with simplified interfaces and wizards, assuming no prior knowledge.
condition: audience is occasional or one-time users

statement: Because most applications serve a mix of newcomers and frequent users, let new users reach a first success quickly while letting intermediates get things done smoothly.

To find users' real goals, keep asking 'why' past the stated request (a five-whys style), because users and clients describe desired features and solutions rather than their underlying needs and problems.
The core value of interface design is solving the right problem (helping the user reach their goal) and then solving it right.
If a transaction can be completed without a given form or step, remove that step so the user reaches their goal with less time and effort.

Do not model users as a single faceless 'The User' with one task-goal; account for softer factors (expectations, gut reactions, preferences, social context, beliefs, values) and for multiple distinct user groups.

Empirical research is the only reliable way to understand users: use qualitative methods such as interviews for expectations, vocabulary, and mental models, and quantitative methods such as surveys for numerical validation.
Study enough individual users to separate personal quirks from the behavior patterns that are generally true of the audience.
Define the audience concretely and honestly; refusing to (for example, claiming 'everyone is a user') leaves the design ungrounded and unfocused.
Direct observation and interviews conducted where users actually work reveal their goals and typical tasks, and can be run either structured or unstructured.
Case studies give deep, detailed views of a few representative users and suit exploring extreme users, longitudinal use over time, or single-site custom software.
Surveys can reach statistically significant numbers of users but only reveal what you ask about, so the questions, recipient selection, and analysis must all be done carefully.
exception: you learn nothing about aspects you do not explicitly ask about

statement: Use personas, fictional proto-persons capturing each group's tasks, goals, and experience levels, to keep design decisions focused on real target audiences.
In UI design, target audiences are defined by their task goals and behaviors, unlike marketing segmentation, which is defined by demographics and psychographics.
Be wary of focus groups: one or two dominant participants can skew your understanding, so do not treat group opinion as representative.
Treat self-reported user data as biased and account for biases such as self-selection, or the data will not reflect the actual target audience.
Even without time for formal methods, informally meeting a few users is better than doing no user discovery at all.
Although individuals differ, people in general behave predictably, so recurring behavioral patterns reliably appear in user observation and can be designed for.
Support safe exploration: let users try something unfamiliar, back out, and try again without stress or dire consequences, because people who can explore safely learn more and feel more positive.
Even mild annoyances (dismissing pop-ups, re-entering erased data, unexpected loud audio) can deter users from exploring voluntarily, so keep exploration cheap and low-cost.
Keep the Back button, and anything that looks like it, behaving predictably; unpredictable Back behavior disorients users and can drive them to abandon the app.

People want immediate results: giving a new user a success experience within the first few seconds increases the odds they keep using the product and boosts their confidence, even if it gets harder later.
If you can predict a new user's likely first action, make that first action stunningly easy and point the way to an obvious starting point.
condition: the user's likely first action is predictable

statement: Do not block a user's first task behind registrations, long instructions, slow-loading screens, or advertisements; deliver value first, before asking for something valuable such as an email address or a sale.

Users do not read an interface methodically; they rapidly scan it, pick the first thing that looks like it might work, and try it even if it is wrong, accepting 'good enough' over 'best' when learning all alternatives would cost time or effort (satisficing).

To support satisficing, provide clear calls to action, make labels short, plainly worded, and scannable so the user's first guess at meaning is correct, and use layout, color, and form (which users parse on sight, faster than reading) to communicate meaning.
Make it easy to move around and back out of a hastily made wrong choice by providing escape hatches, because a complex interface imposes a large cognitive cost that pushes nonexperts to satisfice.
Satisficing explains why users keep using a familiar but less-efficient path rather than learn a better one, because breaking a habit costs energy that a small improvement may not justify.
Expect users to change their goal mid-task; keep choices available and do not lock users into a choice-poor environment with no connections to other functionality unless there is a good reason.
exception: when a deliberately constrained flow such as a wizard or modal panel is justified

statement: Support reentrance: let users start a task, stop in the middle, and return later to pick up where they left off without losing entered data (remember previously typed values, keep dialogs non-modal so they can be set aside, allow multiple concurrent projects).
Do not confront users with too many upfront choices; ask only the minimum needed to proceed and let the rest be deferred to later.
On forms users must complete, clearly distinguish required from optional fields, keep required fields few, and let users move on without answering the optional ones.

Let users return to deferred fields later in obvious places, persist half-finished entries (as with shopping carts), and use good defaults, remembering that prefilled answers still cost the user a glance to verify.

When registration is required at a site offering useful services, users are more likely to register if they can first experience and engage with the site and are asked to register later, sometimes even after completing a purchase.
condition: registration is required at a site that provides useful services

statement: Creation is iterative and incremental: even experts work in fits and starts, moving backward as much as forward through many small changes, rather than in one methodical pass.

Builder-style interfaces must support incremental work: make small pieces easy to build, stay responsive to quick changes and saves, continuously show what the whole thing looks and behaves like, and keep the change-to-feedback cycle as short as possible, because even a half-minute delay breaks concentration and disrupts flow.
With repeated use, frequent actions become reflexive habits that improve efficiency but lay traps when a habituated gesture does not work, or does something destructive, in a new context.

Exploit cross-application consistency (universal shortcuts like Ctrl-S) and enforce consistency within an application; never let a gesture do one action normally but a different action in one special mode, because habituated users will make mistakes.

Do not rely on confirmation dialog boxes to protect against accidental changes; when they appear routinely, clicking OK becomes a habituated reflex and the dialog stops registering, so it is often better not to use them.

Support microbreaks (short downtime, especially on mobile) by making an activity fast and easy to reach: require no complicated setup, load quickly, and retain previous authentication so users do not have to sign in every time.

Engineer pages so that readable, useful content loads first with very little delay, because long load times make users abandon an app (especially during microbreaks), and restore activities to their previous state without asking.
People often relocate objects and controls by remembering where they are, not what they are named, so spatial memory is a strong and effective retrieval cue to design for.

Place recurring controls (such as OK/Cancel buttons and navigation) in predictable, consistent locations; adding items to blank space is safe, but rearranging existing controls disrupts spatial memory, so test with users when unsure.
Keep menu and navigation items in the same place and order across all subpages; dynamically rearranging or compacting menus to be 'helpful' works against habituation and leads to user errors.
The first and last items of a list or menu are noticed and remembered more than middle items, so place items you want noticed at the beginning or end.
People use external artifacts (windows left open, notes, bookmarks, flagged email) as reminders of future tasks, relying on knowledge 'in the world' to aid imperfect memory (prospective memory).

Support prospective memory with flexible, hands-off tools and avoid being 'too smart': do not auto-close idle windows, do not 'helpfully' clean up files or objects the system deems useless, and do not auto-organize or sort things unless the user asks.

Reduce repetitive operations to as few keystrokes or clicks as possible (ideally one per repetition, or a few for all repetitions) using tools such as find-and-replace, recordable macros, scripting, copy-and-paste, shortcuts, and bookmarks.
Use direct observation to discover which repetitive tasks are worth streamlining, because users often will not report them and may not even notice they are doing them.

Ensure no operation requires the mouse so keyboard-only users (from physical limitations, efficiency preference, or assistive technology using the keyboard API) are not shut out of any functionality, using standard techniques such as shortcuts, tab traversal, arrow-key selection, and a default button activated by Return.
Prioritize full keyboard operation for data-entry applications, where entry speed is critical and moving to the mouse for each field is costly, including automatic advance between fields.
condition: the application is data-entry focused where entry speed is critical

statement: People are strongly influenced by peers (social proof): they are far more likely to watch, read, buy, join, share, or comment when they see that someone they know recommended or did it.
Building social capabilities into software (user-generated reviews and comments, shareable social objects, and collaboration features) can increase engagement, virality, community, and growth.
The purpose of information architecture is to create a framework so a product is successfully understood, learned, and used with a minimum of mental strain; the interface should not get in the way.
Good information architecture is invisible: users notice it only when it is bad, and when it is done well they simply have a natural, efficient, and pleasant experience.

Design the app to do what a good customer-service representative would: anticipate needs, organize and describe information from the customer's point of view, present it clearly and simply, use words the customer understands, offer clear next steps, make it obvious where the user is and what is happening, and confirm when a task completed.

Treat information architecture as organizing and labeling the information space (content structures and categories, navigation paths, intuitive multistep workflows, labels and language, and search/browse/filter tools) and, especially for a new product, begin the design here.

Plan the information space before building it (like architectural blueprints before a house): think through the information, workflows, and language and organize them from the user's point of view first, without locking into specific visual-design decisions yet.

Separate information from presentation by designing in three layers: an IA foundation (concepts, labels, relationships, categories), then a functionality and information-delivery layer (screens and tools), then a presentation layer (visual design); each layer shapes what is built on top of it.

Organize content into categories that are Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive (MECE): distinct with no confusing overlap, and complete so there is a place to find or put everything, and able to expand to new data without becoming confusing.

Common ways to organize and categorize content are captured by Wurman's LATCH acronym (Location, Alphabet, Time, Category, Hierarchy) plus Number; alphabetical order is a good default for any list or menu and reverse-chronological order is common for feeds.
In digital systems it is critical for users to know their location in the information space, both overall and on each individual screen.
Use faceted classification (assigning each item multiple qualities, each with a range of values) so users can combine facets to narrow a search across large datasets.
Make frequently used tasks, controls, and commands immediately available without searching or browsing, and hide rarely needed items (such as settings and help) behind navigation.
Chunk a large task or process into a sequence of steps so each step is less demanding on the user (as in a wizard), and always communicate where the user is in the process.

Design for both ends of the skill spectrum: give novices a simplified interface, extra help, or onboarding to improve learning and retention, and give experienced users accelerators such as shortcuts, customization, and keyboard-only operation.

Decide which channels, modes, and devices (desktop, mobile, messaging, voice, and varied screen sizes) the product must work across, because that drives how the information is organized, segmented, and sequenced.

Favor a card as the building block of a mobile-first experience (a small container of information that works alone or arranged in a list or grid on larger screens) and plan how the experience scales down and up.
Design a system of screen types, each with a differentiated function, so users can learn to use each screen reliably even when its content changes with topic or filters.

A single-purpose page primarily does one of four things (Theresa Neil's framework): Overview (show a list or set), Focus (show one single thing), Make (provide tools to create a thing), or Do (facilitate a single task); most apps combine these, but each screen should have one clear organizing principle.

When designing overview (list or grid) screens, decide the dataset size, available space, whether it is flat or hierarchical, the ordering and whether the user can change it, how the user can search/filter/sort, and what per-item information and operations to show and when.

A simple, self-contained task (like a sign-in box) needs little information architecture, but a long, branched, or many-optioned task must be structured, broken into steps with a wizard, or for settings, given open access to many switches the user can change selectively.

The Feature, Search, and Browse pattern combines on the main page a featured item, a search box, and a browsable list of items or categories, because searching and browsing are complementary: some users know what they want and search while others browse open-endedly.

Use featured items with appealing images and headlines to engage arriving users immediately and give them something to read or try without extra work; the feature is the site's front door and defines what the site is about, so choose features carefully.

Place the search box prominently (an upper corner or a top banner) and demarcate it with whitespace or a contrasting background; on small screens it may be collapsed to an icon or 'Search' label as long as it stays easy to see and access.
Help users 'stay found' while browsing categories and subcategories by providing breadcrumbs.
Decide whether search or content and browsing should dominate the screen based on whether the site is content-centric, commerce-centric, or task-centric, and lay out the visual emphasis accordingly.
Document and communicate the organization scheme with tools such as site maps and content outlines.

In the Mobile Direct Access pattern, make the first screen present immediately actionable output without requiring input by having the app assume the likely settings or query (such as location or time) tied to its primary function; this suits an app known for doing one thing well.
condition: the app is used or known for one primary thing

statement: Generate the landing screen from live device data (with the user's permission), primarily location and time, and get the user as close as possible to completing the likely action with a minimum of input, using smart prefilled defaults.

The Streams and Feeds pattern is a continuously updated, scrollable strip of items (usually cards with an image, headline, teaser, and source) suited to content that updates frequently and is checked often, or to gathering asynchronous feedback from multiple collaborators.
List feed items in reverse chronological order with the newest first, updating without waiting for the user to request it, so each visit reliably shows something new.
exception: in collaboration and messaging apps the newest entry conventionally appears at the bottom of the feed

statement: Provide an immediate refresh or update control and let users scroll back to older, unreviewed items in a feed.

For each feed item show What (a title, short teaser, and thumbnail, or the whole thing for micro-updates), Who (author or source, where real names humanize but must be balanced against authoritative outlet names), When (a timestamp using relative times like 'eleven minutes ago' then switching to an absolute date as it ages), and Where (a link to the source).

Give users low-effort response controls (star, thumbs-up, like) placed right next to each feed item to encourage interaction, while still allowing longer replies, and use a 'More' link or drill-down when an item exceeds the list display.
Feed order is frequently determined by algorithms optimizing for engagement, clicks, or interest rather than strict chronology, which enables more personalized, context-responsive experiences.
Images carry a lot of information and are recognized quickly, so a grid of images (with or without descriptions) is a compact, near-universal way to let users select one item from a large collection.

Build a media browser as two principal views the user moves between (a grid or matrix of items and a large single-item view) and drive it with a browsing interface (a search box for the user's own or public items, or simply a scrollable grid) matched to the app's complexity.

Show only a small amount of per-item metadata (such as title or author) to avoid cluttering a media browser, and offer thumbnail-size control, sorting (by date, label, or rating), and filtering (such as showing only starred items).

On selecting an item in a media browser, show it immediately in the single-item view, support keyboard traversal (arrow keys and space bar), and provide previous/next and Back navigation between items.

When the user owns the items, offer move, reorder, and delete with a multiple-selection mechanism (Shift-select, checkboxes, or lasso) plus cut/copy/paste; keep editing features grouped and launch a full editor when in-place editing is too complex.
condition: the user owns the items being browsed

statement: A dashboard is a single, information-dense page showing key data points updated regularly (actionable information, charts, messages, and links to key metrics or workflows), often the login landing screen for business platforms; use it when users benefit from continuously monitoring an incoming flow of information.

Determine what information users actually need and what tasks they must stay on top of, then apply an editor's eye: eliminate confusing or unimportant data, remove or deemphasize information that does not help, and feature the most important information or next steps.

Arrange a dashboard with a good visual hierarchy, keep the main information on one page with little or no scrolling so it is visible at a glance, group related data into titled sections, and use tabs only when users will not need the tab contents side by side.
Provide dashboard details on demand through drill-down (One-Window Drilldown) and datatips that appear when the pointer rolls over a graphic, rather than crowding every detail onto the main page.

Choose information graphics that convey the data best: gauges, dials, pie charts, and 3D bar charts look nice but rarely show comparative information well, whereas simple line and bar charts express data better (especially time-based data), and lists and tables are better when numbers and text matter more than graphics.

Because users read a dashboard at a glance rather than closely, highlight keywords and numbers so they stand out from surrounding text, and consider letting users customize the layout with movable panels and selectable gadgets.

The Canvas Plus Palette pattern pairs a central canvas (a large blank workspace to create or edit an object) with surrounding palettes (grids of tool icons), forming a digital workbench suited to any graphical editor.

Canvas Plus Palette works because it maps naturally from familiar physical objects and leverages visual recognition, since common tool icons (paintbrush, hand, magnifying glass) are reused across applications with the same meaning each time.

Lay out Canvas Plus Palette so the large empty canvas is visible side by side with a palette of iconic buttons (adding text when icons are cryptic) placed to the canvas's left or top, with property panels and swatches to the right or bottom, dividing a large palette into subgroups via module tabs or collapsible panels.
Usability-test the gestures used to create and modify objects on a canvas, because tool behaviors are often not obvious and can be hard to learn.

The Wizard pattern leads users step by step through a task in a prescribed order and fits tasks that are long or complicated, usually novel, done infrequently, where the user wants little fine control and the designer knows the best path better than the user, especially branched or long, tedious tasks.
condition: the task is long or complicated, usually novel, and the designer knows the task better than the user

statement: A wizard requires the user to surrender control, which works when deciding is an unwelcome burden but backfires for expert users, for creative processes, and for users who want to learn, because a wizard hides what each action does and what state it changes.
exception: the user is an expert, is doing creative work, or wants to learn how the software works

statement: A wizard's benefit is divide-and-conquer: splitting a task into chunks, each handled in its own mental space, spares the user from having to figure out the task's overall structure.
Treat the need for a wizard as a signal that the task may be too complicated; if you can reduce it to a short form or a few button clicks, prefer that, since a wizard is also somewhat patronizing.
Split a wizard at decision points so earlier choices dynamically change or skip downstream steps, sparing the user anything irrelevant to the choices they made.
Balance the number and size of wizard steps: a two-step wizard is pointless and a fifteen-step one is tedious, and no single chunk should be overwhelmingly large.

If each wizard step is its own page with Back/Next, let users move back and forth and change earlier choices and consider a selectable overview map of the steps; if steps share one page, use numbered titled sections, responsive enabling, or progressive disclosure, and use good defaults and smart prefills regardless of layout.

A Settings Editor is an easy-to-find, self-contained page or window for changing settings, preferences, or properties, divided into tabs or pages when there are many, and unlike a wizard it must support random access so users can find and edit any property without walking a prescribed sequence.
Group settings into well-labeled categories that make immediate sense to aid findability, using card-sorting exercises with representative users to discover the categories and their names.
Design a settings editor for viewing settings as well as changing them, communicating each setting's current value at a glance.

Place preference editors, account settings, and user profiles where experienced users expect them and have them behave in familiar ways (follow platform conventions and put account links where the username is shown), rather than being overly clever.
Avoid deep settings hierarchies that force many clicks to reach commonly needed properties; put shortcuts to frequently used settings on the top page and add a search box.

Decide whether to apply setting changes immediately or via Save/Cancel by the settings type and established convention (platform settings apply immediately, websites mostly use Save, application settings vary); follow the convention or test with users.

The Alternative Views pattern offers substantially different views of the same information for scenarios a single design cannot serve well, such as printing, viewing data through a different analytical lens, or a structural versus end-user view.

Design specialized alternative views for a few unserved scenarios and present them within the same window, adding or removing some information but keeping the core content essentially the same; for stripped-down output such as printer or screen reader, remove secondary content, shrink or drop images, and cut all but the most basic navigation.

Give alternative views a mode switch on the main interface (it need not be prominent) that is easy to reverse, and preserve all application state across a switch (selections, location in the document, uncommitted changes, undo/redo) because losing it surprises users; remember the user's view choice across sessions.

The Many Workspaces pattern lets users view more than one page, project, file, or context at once (tabs, panels, windows, or placed side by side) and fits when different views or task modes are needed simultaneously, such as comparing items or editing while watching the output.

Support multitasking and side-by-side comparison directly with Many Workspaces (which also supports leaving a window open as a prospective-memory reminder and safe exploration at no cost), choosing tabs, separate windows, panels, or adjustable split windows: split panels for simple content and their own tabs or windows for complex content.
Automatically save the set of open workspaces so they can be restored after the application is closed or crashes.

Treat labels, explanations, and help as a fundamental part of usable software: provide help in multiple forms so it is reachable in different situations, mixing lightweight and heavyweight techniques for users with varying needs.

Start help with inline on-screen copy: meaningful headlines and subheaders, short instructions at particularly tricky spots, clear labels for form elements, and prompts or example inputs to prevent misformatting.
Offer tool tips as brief per-component explanations shown on hover, or revealed by tapping a question-mark icon or link placed next to the component.

A full help system is a complete written user guide (descriptions, glossaries, FAQs, how-tos, and videos), embedded in the app or hosted separately, and is most common for complex desktop applications.
Guided tours or walkthroughs use stepwise pop-ups or pointers (often a lightbox layer on top of the app) triggered by first use, a 'show me how' option, or behavior analytics.
A knowledge base is a growing question-and-answer database, often opened to customers as the first line of self-support and the core of a modern app help system.
An online user community (company-hosted and moderated, or formed on social platforms) is an advanced help technique that builds long-term users who help one another and foster platform growth.
Give every well-designed site or app at least some help (on-screen copy, form prompts, and tool tips are a must) and provide full training and help documentation for complicated applications.

Users need varying levels of support: first-time and infrequent users need different help than frequent users, and even first-timers differ in commitment and learning style (some want a tutorial video, some do not; most find tool tips helpful while a few find them irritating).

Provide help on several levels at once so it reaches everyone, keeping it within easy reach but not constantly in the user's face, and use only techniques familiar to your users, because a hidden collapsible panel goes unseen if users do not open it.

Layer help as a continuum of increasing user effort and detail: on-page headings, instructions, and examples (while keeping total page text low); form prompt text; tool tips; hover tools; collapsible panels; introductory material; a separate help window or manual; live support; and community support.
Remember that rollover tool tips and hover tools work only where the pointer can be tracked (desktop); on mobile, which has no hover concept, they must be reachable by a tap, icon, or menu.
condition: the platform is mobile with no hover concept

statement: Use tool tips for very brief one- or two-line descriptions of features that are not self-evident (critical for icon-only features), add a short hover delay of one or two seconds to remove the irritation of tips popping up constantly, and remember a tip hides whatever is beneath it.

Use introductory material (static screens, guided tours, videos) to orient a new user toward their first steps, but offer a toggle to turn the introduction off (users eventually stop finding it useful) and a way to return to it later.

Tags classify information by attaching descriptive metadata labels, forming a topic-based faceted classification and navigation system that users can search and browse; they can be user-generated, and hashtags (#) link a post to a feed of other posts carrying the same tag, spreading information rapidly.

Enable tagging to leverage users' desire to classify, browse, share, and promote content by topics of interest, letting a homegrown topic-navigation system grow alongside the content as a complement to the formal information architecture.

User tagging both increases usage (users find highly relevant content) and increases investment (users create their own content), and it crowdsources an organic organization scheme that would be too expensive to build yourself, with a user-centered structure emerging over time.

To implement tags, let words be added to content, make search index the tagged content and produce a results screen of everything sharing a tag, and format tags and hashtags as automatic links that run that search when selected.

Base information architecture on the users' vocabulary and mental model of the domain, and design it to be evergreen: able to accept new content and data over time while still organizing everything without confusion.

Navigation is overhead like commuting, so the best navigation is as little as possible: keep tools within reach (especially for intermediate-to-expert users) and keep the distances a user must travel short.

The purpose of navigation is to help users understand the information and task space: what information and tools are available and their scope, how content and functionality are structured, where they are now, where they can go, and where they came from and how to go back.

Signposts help users figure out their immediate surroundings (page and window titles, logos and branding, tabs, selection indicators, plus progress indicators, breadcrumbs, and annotated scroll bars) and help them stay 'found' and plan their next steps.

Support wayfinding with good signage: clear, unambiguous labels that anticipate what users seek, placed where users expect them, so no decision point is left without guidance; verify by walking every major use-case path and signing each decision point, and use strong calls to action on the first pages.

Exploit environmental clues by placing elements where users expect them (an X close control at the upper-right of a modal dialog, a logo at the upper-left of a web page), but remember these clues are culturally determined and newcomers to that culture may not know them.

Some users, especially frequent ones or those in densely built or poorly signed spaces, want a map (a mental picture of the whole space), so provide overview aids, since a progress indicator is itself a form of map.
Give users an Escape Hatch: a navigational trump card that returns them to a familiar page from anywhere in the interface.

Global navigation appears on every main screen (menus, tabs, or sidebars) and is usually placed at the top or left (or both, an inverted-L), rarely on the right because that causes page-size and horizontal-scroll problems; on mobile it is a bottom navigation bar or a hamburger menu.

Put utility navigation (non-content links and tools such as sign-in, help, print, settings, and language) on every main screen, and when visitors are signed-in members place it in the upper-right, often behind the member's avatar, where users look for account, profile, and logout tools.

Associative and inline navigation places links in or near content to present immediately relevant options and tie content together thematically, as with a Related Articles section showing similar-topic or same-author items.

For tag-based navigation, list an article's tags at its end as links to the set of articles sharing each tag; tag clouds work for large sites with fine-grained topics but not for small sites or blogs.
Social integration adds navigation options such as a module of friends' shared activity and a 'trending now' or leaderboard component linking to the most-shared posts.
Navigation must be deliberately designed: decide which options are shown, how they are labeled, and where and when they appear in the interface.

Separate the navigation model from its visual design: first work out the number, sequence, defaults, and depth of navigation options, then decide look and feel, and follow common layout conventions despite the temptation to be different.

Every new page, window, or dialog incurs a cognitive cost: the user must perceive its shape, layout, contents, and exits and work out how to act, and the context switch forces them to refocus, so even a familiar page costs time to reorient.
Keep loading fast because latency costs viewers: a page that loads too slowly or fails is abandoned before users find what they came for, and chronically slow sites are explored less.
Minimize the number of page-to-page jumps and keep the taps or clicks needed to get from point A to point B as small as possible.

Make the site structure as flat as possible with more selections at the top level (broad global navigation), rather than a few top-level items that force users through many category and subcategory menus.

Elevate frequently used actions to the top level of navigation for direct access regardless of where they sit in the structure, and bury infrequently used tools and content behind drilldowns, accordions, or tabs.

Structure the app so the most common tasks (aim for the top 80% of use cases) complete on a single screen without context switches, because forcing a simple or frequent task across multiple subpages and dialogs, especially with dependencies between steps, is one of the most annoying situations for users.

To fit a complex tool on one screen, first simplify and minimize (group and segment, shorten labels, turn words into pictures, use space-saving controls, move instructional copy into tool tips and pop-ups), then use progressive disclosure, module tabs, or an accordion to hide the rest, or combine steps into a wizard.
In the Hub and Spoke model (common on mobile), a home hub lists the major parts of the app; the user goes to a tightly focused spoke, does the job, and returns to the hub to go elsewhere.
In the Fully Connected model, every page links to all others through global navigation (single-level or multilevel), so any page is reachable from any other in a single jump.

In the Multilevel or Tree model, main pages are fully connected but subpages connect only among themselves, so reaching one arbitrary subpage from another takes two or more jumps; converting it to fully connected with drop-down menus, fat menus, or a sitemap footer is preferable.
The Step by Step model leads users through screens in a prescribed sequence with prominent Back/Next links, as in wizards, ecommerce checkout flows, and onboarding questionnaires.

In the Pyramid model, a hub or menu page lists an entire sequence in one place; the user picks any item, jumps to it, and can then step through the others with Back/Next or return to the hub at any time.

Treat some artifacts as single large spaces rather than many small ones (maps, large images or documents, information graphics, time-based media) and, since panning and zooming are navigation, provide controls to pan, zoom in and out, and reset to a known position and state.

Flat navigation suits apps like Canvas Plus Palette editors and spreadsheets, where many tools are reachable at once via menus, toolbars, and palettes: the user always knows where they are but may struggle to find a specific tool among the many.

Navigational models are mix-and-match, and although universal global navigation and short jumps are usually good, a mode with very few navigation options is sometimes better (a full-screen slideshow needs only Back/Next and an Escape Hatch), because full global navigation everywhere costs space, adds clutter and cognitive load, and signals that leaving the page does not matter.

Decide information architecture and navigational models before visual design, and postpone rendering choices (tabs versus menus versus a sidebar tree, or a lightbox versus a modal dialog) until page layout.

Present only a few main entry points so users know where to start, making them task-oriented or audience-directed with clear calls to action, which removes the learning burden for first-time and infrequent users.
condition: the site or app has many first-time or infrequent users

statement: Do not use Clear Entry Points when the app's purpose is obvious to everyone and an extra navigation step would irritate users, as in applications designed for intermediate-to-expert users.
exception: the purpose is clear to all users and an extra step would irritate expert users

statement: Make entry points collectively cover most reasons most users are there, phrase them in language first-timers understand (not app-specific tool names), show them with emphasis proportional to importance as the site's front doors, and keep global and utility navigation smaller and less prominent.

A Menu Page fills the screen with links to content-rich pages (with enough information per link to choose well) and shows no other significant content, serving as a table of contents; use it when users know what the site is about and want to locate a destination quickly and would not want featured content.

On mobile, use a compact one-column Menu Page for apps with many navigation options, keeping labels short, tap targets large, and hierarchies shallow; because menu pages easily become overwhelming, reserve dense ones for seldom-used reference or index screens and align, group, and label for comprehension.

Label menu-page links well with just enough context to decide, adding descriptions, teasers, or thumbnails only where titles alone are insufficient (they cost space), and keep descriptions accurate so users are not frustrated after clicking through.
Express the list's organizational scheme (categories, hierarchy, or date) in a menu page, include a search box, and reconsider whether valuable home-page space could instead hold engaging content.
In the Pyramid pattern, link a sequence of pages with Back/Next and also give each a link up to a parent page that lists all the items, letting users view them in order or out of order.

Adding an Up link to the parent (giving Back, Next, and Up) sharply reduces clicks for users who browse casually or change their mind versus forcing repeated Back presses, and chaining the pages spares users who want to see all of them from repeatedly bouncing back to the parent.

On a Pyramid parent page list all items in order rendered to suit their type, put Back/Next (with a preview of the next item) plus an Up or Cancel link on each item page, and when the order matters link the last page back to the parent (not looping to the first) to signal completion.

A Modal Panel is a screen with no navigation except acknowledging its message, completing its form, or dismissing it, shown on top of the current screen (often as a lightbox that grays out and blocks the rest) for a small, focused task needing the user's full attention.

Use a modal panel to focus on a single action, to handle a quick subtask without losing context, or when the app cannot proceed without user input (a filename on save, a sign-in, or acknowledging an important message).
condition: the task needs full attention or the app cannot proceed without input

statement: When the user merely initiates a minor action that might need input, avoid a modal panel (for example, show a text field below the clicked button and let it hang until the user returns) rather than holding up the whole app until the input is given.

A modal panel cuts off all other navigation so the user must deal with it now and is then returned; it is easy to understand but disruptive and was overused, so reserve it for when channeling attention to a required decision is worth interrupting the workflow.
Place a modal panel where the user's attention lies, prevent the user from bringing up other pages while it is open, and keep it uncluttered to focus attention on the task.

Give a modal panel only a few clearly marked ways out (one to three), as buttons with short verb labels such as 'Save' or 'Don't save' plus a Close or X control at the upper-right, and return the user to the previous page on click.

Use the lightbox effect (dimming the rest of the screen) to highlight a modal panel, making sure it is large enough to find effortlessly, and on websites prefer lightweight overlay techniques over OS-level modal dialogs, which are harder to control and more disruptive.

The Deep Links pattern captures a site or app's state in a URL or link that can be saved or shared, so loading it restores both the location and the state (signed in, a resumed process, or retained input), sparing the user from traversing many steps to get there.

Use deep links when content is specific and interactive (a map location and zoom, a book page, a video clip) that is hard to find or takes many steps to reach, or when the app has many user-settable states such as viewing modes, scales, and data layers.
condition: the content is specific and interactive or has many user-settable states

statement: Implement deep links by tracking the user's position and supporting data (comments, layers, markers) in a URL so reloading restores it, but do not capture settings the user would not want changed (like magnification); URLs are the best format because they are universal, portable, and short.

Put the updated deep-link URL live in the browser's address field as the user changes state, and also offer an explicit 'Link' or 'Embed' feature so users discover how to copy or embed it, since not everyone thinks to look in the address bar.

Provide an Escape Hatch (a well-labeled button or link that returns the user from the current screen to a known place) on screens with limited navigation and whenever a user may be entangled, in an error state, or deep-linked into a page with no context.

A page with no way out feels trapping, so a simple, no-strings escape makes users less likely to feel trapped and less likely to close the whole app, and it supports safe exploration much like an undo feature.

Link an escape hatch to a safe place (a home page, a hub page, or any page with full navigation and something self-explanatory); a clickable site logo at the upper-left and a Cancel button are common forms.
Put escape hatches especially on pages reachable out of context via search results and on dead-end screens such as 404 error pages.

Fat Menus (mega-menus) show a long list of navigation options in drop-down or fly-out menus exposing all the subpages in site sections, making a complex site more discoverable and turning a multilevel site into a fully connected one where any subpage can reach any other.

Fat Menus are a form of progressive disclosure: menu headings give a high-level view while the many subpage links stay hidden until the user opens the menu, so users are not shown everything before they are ready.

Organize each fat menu into titled sections for subcategories (or an alphabetical or time-based sort otherwise), use headers, dividers, whitespace, and horizontal multi-column space, avoid making it so tall it runs off the browser, and style it to fit the site.

Ensure fat menus work with screen readers and other accessibility technology, switching to a static strategy like a Sitemap Footer if they cannot, and on mobile linearize the columns into a single stacked column, preferably as a separate reference navigation screen rather than on every screen.

A Sitemap Footer is a comprehensive, category-organized directory of links in the page footer that gives an at-a-glance view of the site's full scope and, like Fat Menus, turns a multilevel site into a fully connected one, with the advantage that the footer has no vertical space limits.

Use a Sitemap Footer when the site has generous page space, more than a handful of pages but not an outrageous number, and a site map that fits in about half a browser window, and when you prefer a simple static footer to Fat Menus.
condition: the site has generous space and a moderate number of pages

statement: Prefer a Sitemap Footer over Fat Menus for accessibility and simplicity, since it is static, works with screen readers, and needs no fine pointer control, but because casual users may ignore the footer, usability-test and watch click metrics.

Design a footer sitemap to complement the header: make the header task-oriented (answering 'what is this' and 'where do I find X now') and the footer the complete, permanent information architecture, and place it on every page alongside utility navigation and copyright/privacy information.
Place utility navigation for a signed-in user (shopping cart, profile, account settings, help, sign-out) in the upper-right corner for any site or service where users often sign in.
Put sign-in tools where users expect them, because their placement is pure convention: users look to the upper-right, so honoring that convention gives them a successful experience.
