Reserve upper-right space for sign-in tools, place the user's sign-in name (and a small avatar) there first unless already shown elsewhere, and make each tool behave identically on every page.

Cluster sign-in tools (a prominent sign-out, account and profile settings, help, customer service, cart, notifications, collections, and home), keep the area small and quiet like utility navigation, use standard small icons where they exist, and reuse the space for a sign-in box when no one is signed in.
For a mainly linear, page-by-page progression (a narrative, process flow, or wizard), show a map of all the pages in the sequence with a 'you are here' indicator.
condition: the user's path through the pages is mainly linear

statement: A Progress Indicator tells users how far they have come and, more importantly, how far remains, helping them decide whether to continue, estimate how long it will take, and stay oriented, and it doubles as a navigation device for returning to a completed step.

Render a progress indicator as a small one-line or one-column map near an edge so it does not compete with content, give the current and already-visited steps distinct treatment, place it near the Back/Next controls, and label steps with numbers plus short page titles.

Use Breadcrumbs instead of a progress indicator when the navigation topology is large and hierarchical rather than linear; when there are many order-independent steps, it becomes a Two-Panel Selector.

Breadcrumbs show the path from the top of the hierarchy down to the current screen as parent-child links (a single linear slice of the site map) and are best for showing where the user is relative to the rest of the site (context), not merely how they got there.

Use breadcrumbs when the site has a hierarchy of two or more levels and users may arrive deep via browsing, filtering, search, or deep links, so global navigation alone cannot serve as a 'you are here' signpost.
condition: the site has a hierarchy of two or more levels and users can arrive deep out of context

statement: Render breadcrumbs near the top as parent page titles from the top level down to the current page, linked and separated by a character such as a right arrow or greater-than sign; if the current page is shown as the last item, make it visually distinct because it is not a link.

Turn the scroll bar into a map by adding position indicators or notifications for document- or data-centric apps where users scan for page numbers, section or chapter titles, or alerts, because fast scrolling makes the content unreadable and the scroll bar is where the user's attention already is.

Implement annotated scroll bars with static indicators (blocks of color in the track) or dynamic ones (tool tips that change as you scroll), showing what the user is most likely seeking, such as a function name for code, a row number for a spreadsheet, or the positions of search results.

Use an animated transition to smooth a startling or dislocating change (a zoom, rotate, relayout, section open/close, or page jump) into something visually continuous, which keeps users oriented by letting their eyes track a location as the view changes, and also confirms input and boosts perceived quality.

Keep transition animations quick and precise to avoid making users motion sick: minimal lag from the initiating gesture, limited to the affected part of the screen rather than the whole window, and short (around 300 milliseconds is a good target for smooth scrolling), tested with users.
When a user issues multiple actions in quick succession (such as pressing the down arrow repeatedly), combine them into a single animation rather than playing each one in turn.

Navigation and wayfinding have among the longest life cycles of any feature, so designing them from the user's point of view and fit for purpose yields evergreen value and helps onboarding, error recovery, task completion, and user confidence.

Layout is the arrangement of a screen's informational, functional, framing, and decorative elements, and thoughtful placement guides users about the relative importance of the information and functions.
Make a layout 'clean' by following visual information hierarchy, visual flow, alignment through a grid, and Gestalt principles.

Give a screen a clear visual hierarchy so the most important content stands out most and the least important least, letting a viewer deduce the informational structure from the layout and get instant clues about relative importance, relationships, and what to do next.

Size, position, and color are the primary levers of perceived importance: bigger, higher-contrast, or more prominently placed elements read as more important (a large headline versus a small quiet footer).

Density (the space between elements) affects reading: content spread far apart is slightly harder to read and makes it harder to see which elements are related, so use spacing to group related elements together.

Use a distinct background color, shading, or contrast to draw attention to a block and set it apart (contrast draws the eye), and use rhythm from lists, grids, whitespace, and alternating elements to draw the eye through content.

To make small items stand out, place them at the top, along the left, or in the upper-right, give them high contrast and visual weight, and set them off with whitespace, remembering that sought-after controls like search and sign-in fields stand out by meaning regardless of styling.

Base the design on a grid (composed of margins and gutters) for visual consistency and balance, to let multiple designers work on related layouts, to support responsive and dynamic content, and to reduce the viewer's cognitive load.
By the Gestalt principle of proximity, elements placed close together are perceived as related (the basis for grouping controls) while isolation implies distinction.

By the Gestalt principle of similarity, items alike in shape, size, or color are seen as related, so give peer alternatives an identical distinctive treatment and align a list precisely into a visual line, and make one item 'special' with a slightly different treatment (like a contrasting background) while keeping it otherwise consistent with its peers.
By the Gestalt principle of continuity, the eye naturally follows the lines and curves formed by the alignment of elements.

By the Gestalt principle of closure, the brain completes lines into simple closed shapes even when they are not drawn; combined with continuity it explains alignment, since aligned edges form a line users follow and assume a relationship, and coherent shapes (even from whitespace) invoke closure.

Visual flow is the track a reader's eyes follow across a page and is tied to visual hierarchy: a good hierarchy sets focal points and flow leads the eye from the most important elements to the less important.
Control visual flow so people follow the intended sequence, accounting for the Western top-to-bottom, left-to-right reading tendency that strong focal points can redirect.
Use only a few focal points on a page, because too many dilute each one's importance, and use them to pull the eye through the page in the correct order.

Create visual flow with implied lines (straight or curved) connecting elements, arrange a narrative's critical pieces along a continuous uninterrupted line, and on forms place the call to action after the text users read first (or isolate it with whitespace if reading order does not matter) rather than scattering controls.
Exploit the dynamic display's extra dimensions of time and interaction (which print lacks) to present more content than fits at once, since screens have less usable space than print.

Use scroll bars to show a small viewport onto a large thing but never horizontally scroll text; alternatively chunk content into sections with module tabs, accordions, collapsible panels, or movable panels to hand layout control to the user.

Use Responsive Enabling (enable functionality only after the user completes a prerequisite action) and Progressive Disclosure (reveal information only after a specific user action) to guide users and prevent confusion.

Plan the typical UI regions: a header or window title (topmost, for global branding and navigation, and constant so choose its contents carefully), a menu or navigation region (top or left), a main content area (most of the space, for information, forms, and tasks), footers (secondary, global, or redundant navigation plus contact info), and panels (top, side, or bottom, persistent or dismissible).

Consider the Visual Framework early in a project because it affects all major pages and windows, and choose a layout driven by the content: Grid of Equals for search results, Center Stage for task, productivity, or creation tools.
A Visual Framework makes all screen templates across an app or site share a consistent layout, margins, header and gutter sizes, colors, and style while leaving flexibility for varying content.

A consistent visual framework with signposts in the same place lets users know where they are and find things without relearning each screen, makes constant elements fade so changing content is noticed, and strengthens branding.

Define the visual framework in a single place (a CSS stylesheet, a class, or a design-system library) so style can change independently of content, sharing color, fonts, writing style, signposts, navigation devices, spacing, and overall layout across pages.

The Center Stage layout puts the most important part of the UI in the largest subsection with secondary tools and content clustered around it in smaller panels, suited to a screen whose primary job is one coherent unit of information, editing a document, or a single task.

Center Stage guides the user's eyes straight to the most important information or task, anchoring attention with an unambiguous central entity that establishes the UI's purpose, after which users assess the periphery relative to the center.

Make Center Stage content dominate: at least twice as wide as its side margins and twice as tall as its top and bottom margins, taking more above-the-fold space than anything else, with big headlines as focal points; its exact position matters little because a large enough center ends up central anyway.

A Grid of Equals arranges similar-importance content items into a grid where each follows a common template with similar visual weight, which announces equal importance and signals the items are similar, so a user who interacts with one grid item learns how all of them behave.

For a Grid of Equals, design a compact per-item template (thumbnail, headline, subhead, or summary), lay items in a responsive grid mindful of page width, and highlight items statically or on hover with color or style changes but never change their positions, sizes, or structure.

Titled Sections define content sections each with a visually strong title, separated visually, chunking content into digestible pieces understandable at a glance that make the information architecture obvious and guide the eye.

For Titled Sections, first get the information architecture right by splitting content into coherent chunks with short memorable names, then make titles stand out (bolder, larger, colored, or outdented, optionally reversed on a contrasting strip), separate sections with whitespace or contrasting backgrounds, and use boxes sparingly so they do not become visual noise.
Trouble giving a content chunk a reasonable title signals the grouping is not a natural fit, so reorganize it, and treat a 'Miscellaneous' category as a warning sign of not-quite-right organization.

Module Tabs put content modules into small tabbed areas showing one at a time, suited to heterogeneous content with no room for all, where users need see only one module at a time, the modules are of similar size, there are fewer than about ten, the set is fairly static, and the contents are related.
condition: modules are few, similar-sized, static, and only one need be seen at a time

statement: For module tabs, get the information architecture right with short titles and test the organization, because splitting content wrong forces users to switch back and forth to compare, and indicate the selected tab unambiguously since color alone is not enough (make it contiguous with the panel).

Module tabs need not be literal or on top (they can go in a left column, underneath, or sideways) and are distinct from navigational tabs; when there are too many to fit, shorten labels, scroll them, or move them to a left column, but never double-row tabs.

An Accordion stacks content modules in a collinear set of panels the user opens and closes independently, suited to heterogeneous content where users might want more than one module open at once, the modules vary in height but share a width, they belong to a tool palette or menu, and their linear order should be preserved.

For accordions, use concise but informative titles and a visual affordance (an arrow or triangle) signaling expandability, and allow more than one module open at a time to avoid the abrupt disappearance of an open module and to let users compare content.

When an accordion is used in an application or for a signed-in user, preserve its open/closed state between sessions (more important for tool palettes than navigation menus), and choose another solution if open modules would push bottom labels off the screen.

Collapsible Panels put secondary or optional content or functions into panels the user can open and close, suited to modules that support the main content, need not be open by default, vary in value across users and over time, and may be opened more than one at a time.

Use Collapsible Panels rather than module tabs or accordions when the modules have little to do with one another, because tabs and accordions imply the grouped modules are related while collapsible panels do not group them.

For collapsible panels, label the toggle with the module's name or 'More' plus a chevron or rotating triangle showing content is hidden, collapse the freed space back to the main content on close, and animate open/close so users build a spatial understanding of where things are.
If most users open a collapsible panel that is closed by default, switch it to open by default.

Movable Panels are content boxes the user can open, close, and freely arrange into a custom configuration, common in Center Stage creator tools, dashboards, and portals, and suited to a major, frequently used screen with many varied modules users will want to see several of at once.

Movable Panels let users choose and rearrange their environment to their working style (placing tools near their work, hiding what they do not need, using spatial memory), which improves long-term efficiency and comfort, increases engagement through personalization, and accommodates new or third-party modules over time.

Implement movable panels by giving each module a name, title bar, and default size in a reasonable default arrangement, allowing drag-and-drop repositioning and click-to-open/close, optionally using a slot grid and ghosting drop targets to keep alignment, and letting users remove modules and re-add them from a browsable, searchable list.
Visual design is more than skinning an interface: done well it makes a product stand out, conveys the brand's attitude, and can make or break usability and trust.

The Stanford Web Credibility Project (2002) found the single most important factor in whether users trust a website is its appearance: users distrust amateurish-looking sites, and a professional look gains trust even when users have few other reasons to trust the site.
Beauty in digital design is form and function in harmony, so every element must add usefulness, understanding, or delight rather than merely being pixel-perfect.
Give controls clear affordance so an element looks or behaves like what it does, for example a slightly three-dimensional button that cues it is clickable.
Keep the visual language consistent so the same icon or word always conveys the same functionality throughout the experience.
Keep elements aligned and in the same place from screen to screen, and do not let text alignment (left, right, or center) change randomly, because unexplained shifts jar users and hurt legibility.
Before anything else, rule out color choices that make text hard to read: put dark foregrounds on light backgrounds and vice versa, and test by desaturating the design to grayscale.
When red or green marks a critical distinction, reinforce it with a different shape or with text, because roughly 10% of men and 1% of women are colorblind.

Avoid eye-fatiguing color combinations such as bright complementary pairs (like bright blue text on a bright red background), and note that although black on white is least straining, a bright white background's glow can fatigue the eye, so consider a dark background for tablet screens with much blank space.

Color choices set mood: warm colors (red, orange, yellow) versus cool (blue, green, purple); high contrast evokes tension and boldness while low contrast is soothing; saturated colors evoke energy but tire the eyes, so use only one or two and build the palette mostly from muted tones and tints.
Never rely on color alone to convey important information; double it up with shape and text (like a US stop sign, which is red, octagonal, and reads STOP, giving three cognitive cues).

Choose a typeface class by role: serif (end-strokes that guide the eye) for dense body text, sans serif (which stays legible at small sizes) for user interfaces, display typefaces only for large headlines and logos and never for body or UI text, and monospace for numeric or simple electronic displays.
Keep on-screen type at least 10pt (12pt is the standard body size and 9pt is acceptable for footer fine print), and for reading-focused experiences default to about 12pt and let users increase it.
Set leading (line spacing) enough that the eye flows from line to line and ascenders and descenders do not overlap, but not so much that lines feel separated.
When pairing fonts, differentiate with weight or style within a single family and never combine two similar typefaces (pair a serif with a sans serif instead).

Left-align text as the safe, highly readable default for large amounts of text, use center alignment sparingly (it draws the eye but is harder to read), avoid right-aligned or justified text in UI design, and check that a typeface's numbers and letters are distinguishable (l versus 1, 0 versus O).

For small body text on screens prefer sans serif (pixels cannot render tiny serifs) and avoid italic, cursive, ornamental, or highly geometric fonts because they are unreadable or hard to differentiate at small sizes.
Do not set body text in all capitals (which is fine for headlines and short text) because capital letters look too similar to read comfortably at length.
Set body text in a medium-width column of about 10 to 12 words per line, and do not right-justify narrow columns; leave them ragged right.
Give screen elements room to breathe with margins and whitespace, because spaciousness feels calm and open while crowding and collisions between elements or against edges create visual tension.

Straight lines and right angles look calm and still, while diagonals, many varied angles, and swooping curves add apparent motion, and focal points form at sharp angles and where lines cross or converge, which can be used to direct the viewer's eye.
Keep background textures subtle and avoid placing any but the subtlest texture behind small text, because texture interferes with the readability of small text.
Photography sets mood and is a powerful branding and emotional tool, telling a story in a single glance more efficiently than words.
In functional GUIs where content and ease of use matter most, use purely decorative images sparingly because they distract, and prefer custom photography over clichéd stock imagery.
When an image shows a person's face, direct its gaze toward what you want noticed, because people look where other people (even pictured ones) look.

Use icons to express an idea or function at a glance, follow common icon conventions so users need not relearn meanings, keep all icons in one visual style (weight, filled or outlined), and never rely on icons alone: pair them with text labels for comprehension.

A cultural reference can hook viewers emotionally, but use it only when your audience is defined enough to know they will recognize it, make it work with the rest of the design, and note it is rarely appropriate in functional applications.

Build visual unity through repeated motifs (consistent angles or curvature, one main body-text font, one headline font) and apply these rhythms only to groups of comparable things, because users assume similarity in form means similarity in function.

For enterprise and desktop applications, optimize for workflow and long-session comfort, and since you often must use the platform's standard control look-and-feel, focus graphic-design effort elsewhere (backgrounds, color schemes, fonts, borders, and per-item images).

Ensure your design works with the high-contrast themes and large fonts that visually impaired users rely on, because it is the right thing to do and is sometimes legally required (for example US Section 508 and the ADA).
Avoid fatiguing users of full-size or long-use applications by toning down saturated colors, huge text, high contrast, and eye-catching textures; make the design quiet, not loud.
In high-stress applications such as a machinery control panel, strip out anything superfluous that could distract from the task, because cognitive concerns outweigh aesthetics.
condition: the application is used in high-stress situations

statement: Use a skeuomorphic style (mimicking real-life objects) to help users learn a new interaction from a familiar concept, or embed a skeuomorph within another style to boost usability (such as check imagery that shows where routing and account numbers are).
Use an illustrated style, when it fits the brand, to set a fun and approachable tone and, with custom illustrations, to build a memorable brand freed from real-world constraints.

Flat design (solid colors, simple icons, sans serif type) is culturally agnostic, easy to localize, and scales across viewports, and as a truly digital style it lets the UI recede so users focus on the content.
Use a minimalistic style, reducing screen elements to the barest minimum, for task-based apps with straightforward actions or for interfaces used mainly to view rather than manipulate data.

Because most users will interact with a product primarily on mobile, designing for mobile is common sense, and mobile's direct manipulation (touching the object to act on it) makes such interfaces easy and intuitive to learn.

Do not merely make a compact copy of the website; adopt a mobile-first approach (design the mobile experience before the fuller web one) or responsive design (one experience that gracefully scales to different screen sizes).
Know your users' needs, tasks, and contexts of use before choosing between mobile web and a native app, since building a native mobile app is a nontrivial investment.

On tiny mobile screens, strip the design to its essence: keep the most important functions on the front screen and discard or bury the rest, since there is no room for sidebars, long menus, or decorative images.
Make mobile touch targets large enough to hit easily (at minimum about 48 by 48 dp on Android or 44 by 44 pt on iOS, with space between them) while still serving keypad devices.

Design mobile interactions so typing is unnecessary or minimal, using autocompletion and prefilling fields when you can do so reliably, and preferring numeric entry which is easier than text in some contexts.

Design for challenging mobile environments: varying ambient light (gray-on-gray text fails in bright sun), ambient noise (some users cannot hear the device and sudden noises can be jarring), and motion, using large targets for 'fat fingers' and making mistakes easily corrected.
Leverage device location awareness to serve location-specific information and anticipate the user's situation and needs.

Design for distracted mobile users and social situations: make task sequences easy, quick, reentrant, and self-explanatory, and behave gracefully when a device is passed around, viewed over a shoulder, or its sound must be turned off.

Design mobile for real mobile-context needs (a fast fact now, a few minutes of entertainment, a social connection, a timely alert, or what is relevant to the user's current location) rather than the full range of desktop needs.

Strip the mobile site or app to its essence, removing extra content, sidebars, ads, and images, and place relevant content high on the first screen rather than stacking a 'layer cake' of logos, ads, tabs, and headers.

Provide an obvious link to the full non-mobile site (many users have only a phone), or, for a full parallel mobile design, reorganize into a somewhat narrower and deeper hierarchy so the home screen carries fewer options.
Use the mobile device's hardware where it helps: location, camera, voice, gestural input, haptic feedback, and background multitasking.
Linearize mobile content vertically because width is the binding constraint, and order the content so it reads well when stacked in a single column.

Optimize the most common mobile interaction sequences: eliminate or minimize typing, use as few and as light screen loads as possible (downloads can be slow), reduce scrolling and sideways dragging except where it saves screen loads or typing (prefer one long vertical screen to many small ones), and reduce the number of taps.

Order mobile content in a single scrolling vertical column with little or no side-by-side layout, letting text line-wrap, which is the right default for text and form content across devices of unknown width.

Prefer a vertical stack because device widths vary and cannot always be anticipated, fixed-width designs that scroll sideways or zoom are less usable than scroll-down, and a line-wrapped stack adjusts gracefully when font sizes change.
Put the most important items at the top of a vertical stack, with useful content in the first roughly 100 pixels, and do not waste that space on a layer cake of tall logos, ads, and toolbars.

Place form labels above their controls (not beside them) to save horizontal space, put buttons side by side only if their total width will always fit (beware localization and font enlargement), and make sure the design degrades well at the minimum realistic screen width.

The Filmstrip pattern lets users swipe through conceptually parallel full screens (like weather in different cities), giving each item the whole screen and encouraging browsing, but it does not scale to many screens and new users may not realize swiping navigates.
When using a filmstrip, show a dot indicator to hint that multiple swipeable screens exist, and avoid it when there are too many top-level screens to swipe through comfortably.

The Touch Tools pattern shows controls in a small dynamic overlay on touch or keypress atop full-screen immersive content (video, photos, games, maps, books), letting the content dominate while the user controls when tools appear.

Reveal touch tools only when the user touches a designated region (to avoid accidental invocation), show them in a small translucent floating area, and remove them after a few seconds of nonuse or immediately when the user taps outside them.

Place global navigation at the bottom of a mobile screen, reserving the precious top of the home screen for fresh, interesting content and putting only the two or three most important navigation links (if any) at the top.
Make bottom-navigation items easy to tap by arranging them across the full width of the screen with large, readable text, since users can easily scroll to the bottom to find navigation.

Use Collections (thumbnail lists) and Cards (thumbnails plus content and functionality) for lists of image-bearing items, because thumbnails make lists appealing, help identify items, set a generous row height, and improve scanning under poor mobile reading conditions.

Place the thumbnail beside the text (usually on the left), add visual markers like ratings or social presence, and do not fear bright, saturated colors on mobile, since small screens handle strong colors better than large ones.

An Infinite List appends more content as the user scrolls to the bottom of a long or bottomless list (email, search results, archives), giving fast initial and incremental loads under user control with no context shift to a new page, unlike pagination.

For an infinite list, truncate the initial list to a reasonable length and either offer a 'load more' button stating how many more will load, or silently lazy-load the next chunk when the user scrolls to the end (and skip fetching if they do not scroll).

Leave generous margin and whitespace around every tappable element on touch screens so the hit target is large enough (and tall enough) for fingers, which is especially hard for text-only buttons and links.
Make the whitespace immediately around a touch target tappable so the control looks its designed size while gaining a few pixels of sensitivity in each direction.

Always render as much of a partially loaded mobile screen as possible, and show a lightweight animated progress indicator where a slow part (a graphic or video) will appear, because indicators make loading feel faster and reassure users something is happening.
Show a progress indicator in place, where the user's gesture occurred, when an action reloads part of the screen or loads a new one.

Connect your app's data to the device's built-in apps (phone numbers to the dialer, addresses to maps or contacts, dates to the calendar, email addresses to the email app, hyperlinks to the browser, media to players) and capture images, sound, or video via the device.

Richly connecting apps matters because a mobile user sees one app at a time, switching by hand is annoying, and mobile platforms lack the desktop's easy copy-paste and filesystem for shuffling small amounts of data between apps.

Treat the mobile web or app as critical, not an afterthought, since it may be the primary way a user experiences the brand, so give special attention to small details, microinteractions, usability, and the mobile context of use.

Before designing a list, analyze its use cases: getting an overview, browsing item by item, searching for a specific item, sorting and filtering, and rearranging, adding, deleting, or recategorizing items.

Support the list use cases concretely: convey the whole-list impression (often with images or visual organization), make it easy to return to the list and move to the next item, let users find a specific item in minimal clicks, and offer sort and filter when users seek a characteristic or insight.
For lists the user owns, permit direct manipulation (drag to reorder or regroup) and multiple selection using platform standards (Shift-select or an edit mode) or checkboxes beside each item.
condition: the user owns the list and its items

statement: Before designing, analyze a list's nonvisual characteristics: its length (does it fit or is it bottomless), order (natural order, user-sortable, order versus grouping), grouping (natural categories, multilevel hierarchy, multiple or user-defined categorizations), item types (simple versus rich, homogeneous versus varied, images, sortable field structure), interaction (whole item or a representation, look/select/act, multi-select), and dynamic behavior (load time and live updates).

Choose between ordering and grouping a list by how users search for items: for example, grouping blog posts by month can make a specific post hard to find when users recall only its relative position, so a time-ordered flat list of titles may work better.

Choose where to show a selected item's details by space and use case: Two-Panel Selector (details beside the list) best supports overview and browsing with no context switch; One-Window Drilldown (details replace the list) fits small or mobile spaces but causes pogo-sticking; List Inlay (details expand within the list) supports browsing and comparison but a crowded overview if many are open.
The three list-detail patterns are analogous to familiar controls: Two-Panel Selector works like tabs, List Inlay like an accordion, and One-Window Drilldown like a menu screen.

Set how much detail to show per list item by the use case: for a focused lookup show just the name, for browsing show more (up to a point) to make items interesting, and show thumbnails when items have visuals.

For heavy-visual lists choose Cards (image, text, and actions in one element), a Thumbnail Grid (a 2D grid of similar pictures that dominates the screen), or a Carousel (a linear, space-saving alternative the user scrolls).

Use Pagination to load a long list in sections when the desired item is likely on the first screen (many users will not go further) or the full list would be too long or slow, and make the control show how many screens exist and let the user jump between them.

Use an Infinite List (or continuous scrolling) when a list's length is unknown or bottomless, loading the first section and appending the next by button or automatically on scroll so the user stays on one screen.

For a long alphabetized or date-ordered list provide an Alpha/Numeric Scroller (the alphabet along the scroll bar) to jump directly, and provide a Find field and filtering to locate specific items and shorten the list.

For categorized lists use Titled Sections for a single level (allowing sort within a section without breaking the categorization), an Accordion when there are only a few sections, and indented trees with open/close controls for two or more levels of hierarchy.

The Two-Panel Selector (Split View) shows a selectable list in one panel and the selected item's content in the other, suited to a list whose items have interesting content where you want the list always in view and only one item shown at a time, on a display large enough for two panels (tablets, not small phones).
condition: the display is large enough for two side-by-side panels

statement: A Two-Panel Selector reduces physical effort (a single click changes selection and eyes travel little), reduces visual cognitive load (only the small area changes, with no big context switch), reduces memory burden (the persistent list acts as a 'you are here' signpost), and is faster than loading a new screen per item.

Put the selectable list on the top or left and the details below or to the right to match left-to-right visual flow (reverse for right-to-left languages), select on a single click with arrow-key navigation for keyboard use, and make the selected item visually obvious with distinct color and brightness.

In One-Window Drilldown a list occupies the whole screen and selecting an item replaces the list with its details, suited to mobile or constrained space where each view needs the full space, with a shallow hierarchy that makes returning to the list easy.

On a drilldown item screen place a Back or Cancel control (unless the platform supplies one), allow drilling further or stepping to contained or previous/next items while always replacing the screen and enabling step-back, and mitigate pogo-sticking with Back/Next links plus enough per-item text to identify and triage items.

A List Inlay shows list items as rows and, on selection, opens the item's details in place within the columnar list (items opening and closing independently), which uniquely lets the user compare several items' details at once and see them in the context of surrounding items.

Open a list inlay downward, pushing later items down within a scrolled area, put a clear close control near the open control (and near the top if the panel is long), and animate the open and close to keep the user oriented.

Cards are self-contained, responsive components combining an image, text, and sometimes actions, suited to a list of heterogeneous items that share the same behaviors (image, text, favorite or share, link to detail) and may differ in size or aspect ratio.

Design cards for the extremes by mocking up both the item with the most content and the one with the least and tweaking until both read clearly, deciding which actions are icons versus text links, and using real photos to choose portrait or landscape orientation.

A Thumbnail Grid arranges similar-size visual items in a small-multiples grid (a specialized Grid of Equals) that presents items as peers, is dense and attractive, draws the eye, and whose roughly square thumbnails make easy touch targets, suited to items with small unique visuals and little metadata.
Scale thumbnails to the same size for a tidy grid and keep metadata small and close to the thumbnail so the picture stays prominent.

When source images vary in size or aspect, process them to a common size and aspect, cropping carefully to preserve the most relevant part, except when the image's size or proportion is itself useful information (keep personal photos' portrait or landscape orientation, but make product galleries uniform).
exception: the image's own size or proportion carries useful information for the viewer

statement: A Carousel arranges visually interesting items of similar size in a horizontal strip or arc the user scrolls or swipes, suited to a flat list where each item is potentially interesting, users browse casually rather than search, and there is not enough vertical space for a Thumbnail Grid.

A Carousel encourages browsing and serendipity (users cannot jump deep, so they scroll through everything), is vertically compact, and can deliver focus-plus-context by enlarging a central item to give it single-selection semantics.

In a carousel, provide large left/right paging arrows (each moving more than one item) so users know more content lies beyond the window, and if users end up scrubbing through it a lot, reconsider a conventional vertical list with a find capability.

Use Pagination to break a very long list into pages loaded one at a time when most users seek a specific item or browse the top and the technology cannot load the whole list quickly, and make the first screen enough since most users will not go past it (so put the most relevant items, and best search results, there).
Let users set the number of items per screen on paginated pages where they linger, such as product or video lists.

In a pagination control include Previous/Next links (disabled at the ends), an always-visible link to the first screen, numbered screen links with the current screen shown non-linked in a contrasting style as a 'you are here' cue, ellipses to elide when there are too many screens (keeping first, last, and adjacent), and optionally the total number of screens.

The Jump to Item pattern lets a user type an item's name to jump straight to the matching entry in a sorted scrolling list, table, drop-down, or tree, exploiting the computer's speed at scanning and keeping the user's hands on the keyboard.

Implement Jump to Item so the first typed character jumps to and selects the first match and further rapid characters refine to the typed string, and on no match stay at the nearest match rather than scrolling back to the top, optionally beeping.

The New-Item Row pattern uses the last or first row of a list or table to create a new item in place, suited to a vertical item list where users must add items but there is no room for extra creation UI.

For a new-item row, give an obvious way to start (click the empty row or a 'New X' button), make each column editable with good defaults, and establish a valid item from the start so an abandoned edit persists until the user deletes it.
When designing actions, make the appropriate actions available, label them well, make them easy to find, and support sequences of actions.

Follow platform style guides and established UI conventions for actions, menus, and buttons even when they seem unoriginal, because users depend on behaviors learned from other applications and want to work with methods they already know.

Treat established standards, UI toolkits, component libraries, and frameworks as a foundation so common features need not be coded from scratch, freeing time to design the unique features that set the product apart.
Make drag-and-drop work exactly as users intuitively expect (dropping an object onto a target zone or folder), or the illusion of direct manipulation breaks.

On mobile, finger gestures are the primary way to act: tap performs a context-dependent action, swipe navigates or reveals per-item actions (like archive or delete), and pinch zooms; rotating the device switches portrait and landscape, and shaking can undo or skip.

Buttons sit directly on the interface (grouped semantically) and are big, readable, obvious, and easy even for novices but space-hungry, which is why landing-page calls to action are single large eye-catching buttons.

Menu bars show an application's complete set of actions organized predictably (File, Edit, View) and are indispensable for accessibility because they duplicate toolbar and context-menu functionality reachable by screen readers and keyboard accelerators.
Keep pop-up (context) menus short, listing only context-specific common actions rather than everything possible.
Do not use drop-down controls for actions; they are for selecting choices on a form.

Use an iconic toolbar only when the actions have obvious visual renderings, and when actions need words use combo boxes or text-labeled buttons instead, because cryptic icons are a classic source of confusion.

Use clickable link text for actions where you do not need to draw attention or clutter the page (reinforcing clickability with a cursor and rendering change on hover), use an always-visible Action Panel when actions are better described verbally than visually, and use Hover Tools to show per-item actions only on hover (mouse-only, not touch).

Because invisible actions (double-click, keyboard commands, CLI) carry no labels and do not aid discovery, always also provide visible actions in buttons, links, and menus so users can inspect and learn the interface's capabilities.
In object-oriented desktops, single-clicking an object selects it so an action can be applied, while double-clicking opens, launches, or edits it depending on context.
Design keyboard shortcuts into desktop applications (following platform style-guide standards) for accessibility and expert speed, and support access keys for menus and controls.
Provide tab-order navigation so users can move keyboard focus through selectable components and operate the UI without a mouse, for accessibility and efficiency (voice browsers, limited mobility).

Give a UI object an affordance so it looks like what it lets you do (a raised button affords clicking, a scroll bar affords dragging, a blue underlined word affords clicking), designing so that every interesting visual feature does something.

On mobile, assume direct manipulation of screen components (tap to submit, swipe to delete or open a contextual menu, drag to move, pinch to zoom, tap an image for controls) rather than the desktop select-then-command approach, acting on objects one by one with simple gestures.

Because software gives users few sensory clues about what is manipulable, carry the clues with visuals and affordances (highlighting, movement), and show a selected object with a highlight outline so users know it is selectable.
When you reflexively reach to put actions on a menu bar or pop-up menu, consider instead Button Groups, Hover Tools, or an Action Panel, which can make the actions more visible and discoverable.

Sequence-of-action patterns (multilevel undo, command history, macros) suit complex apps whose users invest in learning them, but are hard to implement because they require modeling the user's actions as discrete, describable, and sometimes reversible operations, which is difficult to retrofit.

Button Groups cluster related actions as aligned buttons with similar graphic treatment, making an interface self-describing because visible clusters announce the available actions and Gestalt proximity and similarity signal that grouped buttons do related things.

Group two to five related actions of the same scope (never mixing different scopes), give every button in a group the same graphic treatment, and label each with a short, unambiguous verb in the users' vocabulary.

Give a primary action (like a form's Submit) a stronger graphic treatment to stand out, and place a button group that acts on an object to its left or right rather than below, where a user's blind spot at the bottom of lists and trees may hide it.

Hover Tools place per-item action buttons next to items but hidden until hover (or tap on mobile), keeping the UI clean while revealing tools exactly when and where needed, and are more discoverable than pop-up or pull-down menus because a rollover is simple and natural, though they do not work on touch screens without a hover state.
exception: the interface is used by touch, which has no hover state

statement: Make hover tools feel lightweight: show and hide them immediately with no animated transition, never enlarge the hover area or rearrange the page on hover, optionally highlight the hovered item, and on touch show the tools in a pop-up panel grouped with the tapped object.

An Action Panel is an always-visible grouping of commands on the main UI (not in a menu bar, drop-down, or pop-up), suited when a list has too many per-item actions for hover tools, when you want actions more discoverable than menus, or when the actions are too complex or grouped for a flat menu, though it consumes a lot of space and is poor for small devices.

An Action Panel wins on visibility (actions fully visible and discoverable without opening a menu), available space, and freedom of presentation, since a menu gives only a short flat list while a panel can organize verbs as freely as nouns.

Place an action panel near its target (proximity matters), make its contents dynamic with the application state or selection, structure the actions with a task-centered grouping presented linearly (so it reads sensibly aloud for blind users), and use longer descriptive labels for first-time users and terser ones for experts.

Use a visually prominent button for the final step of any transaction or to commit a group of settings, because an obvious, well-understood last step gives users closure and assurance their work took effect.

Make the done or submit control look like a real button (not a link) with bold color and clear borders, and place it at the end of the eye's travel (usually bottom or right) near the last field, since a button placed too far away leads users to hunt for what to do next and can cause them to abandon the page or purchase.
Prefer a specific text verb on the final button (like 'Send' or 'Buy') over an icon or a generic 'Done', because most users look for a labeled button and a specific verb communicates the outcome.

Use Smart Menu Items whose labels dynamically state exactly what they will do (like 'Undo Increase Clarity' or 'Add this person to Contacts'), which makes the UI self-explanatory, reduces accidental wrong actions, and encourages safe exploration.

Update a smart menu item's label to include specifics whenever the selected object, document, or last operation changes, disable it when there is no target object, and apply the same technique to buttons and links.
The Preview pattern renders a lightweight sample of a command's effect before the user commits, letting them choose an outcome instead of activating a command and waiting to see the result.

Use a preview before a heavyweight or costly-to-reverse action (opening a large file, printing, submitting a long form, committing a purchase) or a change with a hard-to-predict visual result (a photo filter), because previews prevent errors and teach the action better than documentation, exactly when and where needed.
condition: the action is heavyweight, costly to reverse, or has a hard-to-predict result

statement: Just before commit, show the clearest, most relevant picture of what will happen (a print layout, an image close-up, a transaction summary), no more and no less, and let the user both commit straight from the preview and back out, with 'Change' controls next to changeable information.

A spinner is a stateless animation showing the system is processing, while a loading indicator is a meter showing key data (percent complete, bytes processed, time remaining) for a long task; show one after a submitted action when the response is delayed so the waiting user knows the session is live.

By Nielsen/Norman response-time research, under 0.1 second feels instantaneous (the expectation for usable software), 0.1 to 1 second is a noticeable delay the user will wait through on task, and longer than 1 second makes users think something is wrong or abandon the task, so a spinner or loading indicator becomes mandatory.
Users are far more patient when an indicator shows something is happening, even if they end up waiting longer, because they know the system is thinking rather than hung.

In a loading indicator tell the user what is happening, what proportion is complete, how much time remains, and how to stop it; wrong time estimates are acceptable if they converge quickly, and if progress is unknowable show a stateless spinner.
Do not lock up the rest of the UI while a loading indicator is visible, and offer a cancel affordance on or near the indicator where users will look for it.

Let users instantly cancel a time-consuming operation (one running longer than about two seconds, or a modal that shuts out other interaction) with no side effects, because cancelability embodies 'user control and freedom', aids error recovery, and encourages safe exploration.

First try to make a slow operation feel instantaneous (preloading or sending data incrementally so users read it as it arrives); if you still need cancel, put a Cancel or Stop button near the loading indicator with a recognizable stop icon.

Cancel immediately when the user asks (waiting more than a second or two makes them doubt it worked) and confirm the cancel took effect, and for parallel operations state exactly what each Cancel stops or give each its own Cancel button.

Multilevel Undo, which reverses a series of actions step by step in reverse order, lets users of every skill level feel safe to explore and experiment without making irrevocable changes, spares stressful recovery, and lets experts try work paths quickly while maintaining flow.

To support undo, build a strong model of an action (its name, object, how to record it, and how to reverse it), then make reversible anything that could be permanent (text entry, database transactions, image edits, layout changes, file operations, cut/copy/paste) while leaving transient or view-only states (selection, navigation, cursor and scroll positions, uncommitted dialog changes) untracked.
Define and name reversible operations in the user's terms, not the computer's (undo typed text in chunks of words, not letter by letter).
Implement undo as an action-history stack (each operation pushed on top, undo reversing the most recent first and redo working back up) at least 10 to 12 items long.
Present undo and redo on the Edit menu hooked to Ctrl-Z, and use Smart Menu Items to state exactly which operation will be undone, since most users do not understand the underlying stack.

Command History keeps a visible, manipulable record of the user's actions (what was done and when), suited to long complex sequences where users want to recall or repeat earlier actions, replay a sequence on another object, keep a log for legal or security reasons, or convert a series into a macro.

Record actions at the right granularity (one mass action as one entry, not many), record what is undoable, keep the history across sessions when possible, and display it optionally, oldest to newest and optionally timestamped, as a supporting rather than starring role.

Macros are single actions composed of smaller ones, created by recording or assembling sequences and saved for reuse, suited to users who repeat long sequences or loop the same operations over lists of objects.
Macros let the computer do repetitive work (supporting streamlined repetition), work faster while reducing slips and oversights, and enhance flow by compressing a long sequence into a single command.

Let users record a sequence and play it back with a single command, name it, review the steps, let one macro refer to another, and save macros to a searchable, sortable list; support literal or parameterized playback that can act on many objects at once, and present macros alongside built-in actions rather than as second-class citizens.

Recognize that macro recording plus composition is effectively programming (do not call it that if users are not programmers), and for a truly scriptable application consider how macros could be abused and constrain what they can do.

Make the most important actions visible so they guide new and existing users to the preferred next step, and let users safely preview, initiate, cancel, and reverse actions, which builds positive feelings and speeds learning.
Information graphics present data visually to impart knowledge, showing rather than telling so users draw their own conclusions, and include plots, maps, tables, trees, timelines, and diagrams.

Add interactivity to static graphics, because interactive tools let users hide and show information, control how they view and explore it, and become participants in discovery who notice aspects they would miss on paper.

Understand what the user needs to learn: for finding a specific data point provide search, filter, and the ability to zero in, and for understanding structure and relationships provide overviews with zoom in and out and the ability to compare views.

Design an interactive graphic to answer how the data is organized, what is related to what, how the user can explore it, whether they can rearrange it, how they can see only what they need, and what the specific values are.

Choose the data's shape from its inherent structure, and when several models fit weigh which aspects each plays up, because showing data that is both geographic and tabular only as a table can hide its geographic relationships.

Certain visual features are preattentive (perceived before conscious attention), so finding a target by color or size takes roughly constant time regardless of how many items there are, whereas reading text values takes time that grows linearly with the number of items.
To make data points stand out, vary a preattentive variable such as color or size, and use these variables to encode classes or dimensions of data.

For multidimensional data, encode several dimensions with distinct visual variables in one display (position on the axes, color hue, marker shape), and use redundant encoding such as shape plus color to help users separate groups.

Layering exploits preattentive factors and similarity so classes of data pop as if on transparent overlays, segmenting a graphic into simpler layers the viewer can study in turn while preserving the relationships among them.
Follow the mantra of focus plus context: let the user focus on a point of interest while showing enough of the surroundings to place it in the big picture.

Provide navigation via scroll and pan (with an overview plus a viewport rectangle to stay oriented), zoom (which changes scale so you need not pack every detail into the full view, revealing features as space appears), and opening, closing, or drilling into points of interest.
Link search results to navigation, so searching for a place zooms or pans the graphic to it, giving the user context and spatial memory.

Letting users sort and rearrange a graphic reveals unexpected relationships, because placing different data points next to each other makes comparison easier (neighbors are far easier to compare than scattered points) and users naturally zero in on the extremes.

Offer sorting and rearranging (sortable and draggable table columns, reorderable tree nodes, repositionable diagram elements) across orderings like alphabetical, numeric, date, location, category, popularity, user-defined, and even random.
For a stacked bar chart, let users choose which variable sits at the baseline, because the segments nearest the baseline are the easiest to evaluate and compare.

Provide simple filtering and querying with one-click controls such as checkboxes that toggle parts of a graphic on and off, and consider highlighting a subset rather than hiding the rest so it is seen in context.

Make filtering and querying interfaces highly interactive (fast, but not reacting to every keystroke if that slows typing), iterative (refine and combine search and filter), contextual (show results within the surrounding data), and complex (supporting nuanced combinations of conditions so users can test hypotheses).
Show search results in context on the graphic (for example by scrolling or centering the found item), because seeing results among the surrounding data helps the user understand them.

Match labeling effort to the audience: if users need only a qualitative sense do not spend pixels labeling everything, but include some numbers or text, applying good text design (readable fonts, appropriate size, separation of unrelated items, alignment of related items, no heavy boxes, and no obscuring of data).

Use labels for precise values placed in or beside the data point (avoiding legend round-trips but risking clutter if overused), place legends on the same screen as the graphic, and use axes or scales for position-based data when precise values are not needed and labeling would clutter dense data.

Datatips show data values in a temporary tooltip-like window when the user hovers or taps a point of interest, suited to an overview that hides more data behind points (like street names or bar values) that the user can point at.
Datatips put small, targeted, context-dependent data right where the user's attention is (the pointer or fingertip), can substitute for labels, are quick and lightweight, and reward curiosity.

Render a datatip as a temporary window layered where the pointer is, formatted densely but positioned to obscure as little of the graphic as possible, optionally varying its format by situation and offering drill-down links; an alternative is a reserved static data panel that updates on rollover.

A Data Spotlight highlights the slice of data the user hovers over (a graph line or map layer) and dims the rest, showing that slice in context, and often works alongside Datatips (the spotlight shows the slice, the datatip the specific point).

Use a Data Spotlight when a graphic is so rich it obscures its own structure or the data is structurally complex (lines, areas, scattered sets), reserving Datatips for when the rolled-over data is just a point, to give focus plus context by highlighting one data slice while dimming but keeping the rest.

Design the graphic to be coherent without the spotlight (it may be printed), color the spotlighted slice light or saturated while the rest fades gray, react quickly on rollover, put hot spots on legends too, and consider a spotlight mode or a click/tap trigger for touch to avoid accidental activation.

Dynamic Queries use standard controls (sliders, checkboxes) to define which data slices or layers show, filtering the display immediately as the user adjusts the controls, suited to large multivariate data with a fixed, predictable set of attributes and to faceted search.

Dynamic Queries are easy to learn because familiar controls express common-sense Boolean conditions with no query language, their immediate feedback encourages open-ended exploration and flow through an incremental question-and-answer session, and labeled controls reveal what the queryable attributes and their ranges are.

Map each data attribute to an ordinary control beside the display, choosing by data type: a slider for a single number in a range, a double slider for a subrange, radio buttons or a drop-down (with an 'All' option) to pick one value, checkboxes for an arbitrary subset, and text fields for precise values (which are more error-prone).

Data Brushing lets a user select data in one view and see the same data highlighted simultaneously in other views of the same data set, an instance of coordinated or linked views where a manipulation in one view is reflected in the others.

For data brushing, let users select points directly on a graphic (easier than defining them numerically, like drawing a box around outliers), make the other views react immediately, and show brushed points with the same visual characteristics across views using color hue, which stays visible even when attention is elsewhere.

A Multi-Y Graph stacks multiple graph lines sharing one x-axis (often a timeline) but with different y-axis units or scales, suited to encouraging viewers to find vertical relationships like correlations and differences, because x-axis alignment signals the data sets are related and enables side-by-side comparison.

Build a Multi-Y Graph with one shared x-axis and separate y-axis spaces that do not visually interfere, drop the y-axes when exact values are not needed, label each graph unambiguously, and add vertical grid lines so viewers can follow an X value across data sets.

Small Multiples show many small, similar pictures (each with two or three data dimensions) tiled by one or two more dimensions as a strip or 2D matrix, suited to large multidimensional data on a large display and poor on mobile unless the pictures are tiny.

Small Multiples are data-rich yet comprehensible because side-by-side placement lets users glance freely without remembering a previous screen or decoding a 3D plot, visually enforcing comparisons of changes and differences.

For small multiples, label clearly which dimension varies, keep every image similar in size, shape, and axis scaling so meaningful differences stand out and meaningless ones are eliminated, and avoid too many by binning or shingling; sparklines are tiny label-free small multiples for running text or table cells.
Great data visualization can be both beautiful and informative, doing the work of several charts in one image, and adding interactivity to such pictures increases understanding.
Respect the user's time and attention: the cost of filling out a form is higher in their eyes than the designer thinks, so make the form as short and simple as possible.
Make the form's purpose clear through its headlines, context, and wording, confirming why the information is asked for, how it will be used, and what the user gets in return.

Minimize the number of form inputs by considering each question and deducing what you can instead of asking (city and state from a Zip code, card type from the first card digits, a username from an email address).
Minimize visual clutter on a form, keeping it simple, clean, and focused rather than distracting the user with other material.
Break a long or complicated form into descriptive titled sections with grouped, labeled elements.

For long or complicated forms consider dynamic show/hide sections, displaying only the first section by default and revealing the rest in sequence with optional parts hidden by default, to reduce intimidation and skipped steps.
Give a form a strong vertical flow by aligning the left edges of inputs and using consistent vertical separation, so the eye moves from label to input with minimum travel.
Indicate which fields are required and which optional (a courtesy and an error-prevention strategy), choosing one standard approach across all your forms.

Use descriptive labels (still a best practice for accessibility), input examples, and help text on form fields, and avoid lots of placeholder text inside fields because it can make users think a field is already filled.
Use the width of an input field, and the choice of control, to preview the expected input (a radio button implies one of many, a one-line field a word or phrase, a large multiline field a paragraph).
Accept variations in input formatting for dates, addresses, phone numbers, and card numbers (the Forgiving Format pattern), and when a specific format is required show the user an example.

Prevent errors and validate as quickly as possible: give instructions and examples upfront, show an error as soon as a mistake is clear (field-by-field before whole-form submission), and make validation messages actionable by saying which field is wrong, why, and how to fix it.
Use autocompletion to tell the user what input is valid, remind them of previous entries, and offer the most common entries to save time.
Consider top-aligned labels for mobile and responsive designs, because they stack vertically without a layout change and are less likely to become misaligned with their inputs.

Design forms for internationalization: allow the language to change without breaking the layout (accounting for text length and writing direction), switch number, date, measurement, and currency formats, and respect that different data-privacy laws affect what you may gather, transmit, and store.

Confirm a successful form submission and tell the user what happens next, and usability-test forms even when confident, because designers and users often make radically different assumptions about terminology, answers, and intrusiveness.

For marking form fields, the most usable approach is to mark all required fields (per Nielsen/Norman), or alternatively label only the smaller set, or mark optional fields with the word 'optional' as US and UK government design systems do.
Present a gatekeeper form (sign-up or purchase) in Center Stage with few distractions, or as a Modal Panel over the page.
Break a long, multi-topic form into titled sections or separate pages (tabs work poorly for form grouping), and for a sequence of pages use the Wizard and Progress Indicator patterns.
Give a form a Prominent 'Done' Button for submission and make secondary actions like reset or help less prominent.

The Forgiving Format pattern lets users enter input in varied formats and syntax that the software interprets intelligently, suited to input with unpredictable vocabulary or styling (whitespace, hyphens, abbreviations, capitalization) when you want a visually simple UI.

Forgiving Format serves users who just want to get something done rather than think about correct formats, simplifies the UI, and can remove the need for input hints, but it turns a UI problem into a programming problem.

Implement Forgiving Format by anticipating what users will type, ensuring the software's response matches their expectations, echoing the interpreted value back in the user's own format, and testing repeatedly with real users.

The Structured Format pattern uses a set of small text fields reflecting the data's structure (credit card, telephone, license), suited to a familiar, well-defined format that will not vary, because the structure clues the user to what is expected and short fields reduce errors, but it is a bad fit for data whose format varies by user or country, where Forgiving Format is better.
exception: the data's preferred format varies by user or country

statement: For structured format, keep the fields short as length clues, automatically advance focus to the next field when one is full, and use an Input Prompt (like 'dd/mm/yyyy') for extra clues.

The Fill-in-the-Blanks pattern arranges fields as a prose sentence with blanks, making the interface self-explanatory because people know how to finish a sentence, and is especially good for defining conditions such as search or filter criteria.

Build fill-in-the-blanks with same-form-factor controls (text fields, drop-downs, combos) whose baselines align and sized to just fit, but be aware it is hard to localize because comprehension depends on word order, so work with a translator or rearrange the UI.

An Input Hint places a short phrase or example beside or below an empty text field to explain what is required, leaving the control blank so the field will not be skipped as if pre-filled, suited to when the required input is not obvious and cannot fit in the label.

Keep an input hint short (a sentence or two, beyond which eyes glaze over) and small but readable (about two points smaller than the label), shown always or on focus, and do not depend on linked pages for critical information because users rarely follow links mid-form.

An Input Prompt places prompt text inside the control where the value goes (Select or Choose for drop-downs, Type or Enter plus a noun for text fields), which cannot be ignored the way an input hint can, but it disappears on focus, unlike a floating label that shrinks and moves up but stays visible.

With an input prompt, disable the finish button until the prompt is replaced (avoiding an error message), restore the prompt when the user erases input, never make the prompt a selectable drop-down value, and use Good Defaults and Smart Prefills instead when you can accurately guess the value.

Show a Password Strength Meter giving immediate feedback on a new password's validity and strength as it is typed (weak, medium, or strong with color: red for unacceptable, green or blue for good), rejecting weak passwords instantly rather than after form submission, because strong passwords protect both the user and the site.

With a password meter, give specific advice to improve a weak password (minimum length, numbers, capitals) and explain the rules beforehand with input hints, default to hiding the password while optionally offering a view toggle, and do not suggest alternative passwords.

Autocompletion anticipates a user's answer as they type, shows a selectable list, and completes the entry when appropriate, suited to predictable input (a URL, name, address, date, or filename) you can guess from history or a preexisting set.

Autocompletion saves time, energy, cognitive burden, and wrist strain, prevents typos on long or strange strings, is especially valuable on mobile, and can guide users to content by showing what others have typed.

Build completions from previous entries, common phrases, matches in the searched content, context artifacts like contact lists, or most-popular strings, either offering a list on demand or auto-filling the single reasonable completion with it selected so a keystroke clears it; always let the user reject it (defaulting to no), never interfere with ordinary typing, and stop offering a repeatedly rejected completion.

A Drop-down Chooser is a drop-down or pop-up panel holding a more complex or hierarchical selection UI (a tree, 2D grid, or calendar), suited to a choice from a set when you want rich selection tools without spending main-page space, and it encapsulates complexity in a small space, hiding it until needed.

Show a drop-down chooser's current value with a down arrow in its closed state, make the panel small and compact in a familiar format, and consider using it (offering common or recent items) instead of going straight to a modal dialog to reduce clicks.

A List Builder (two-column multiselector) shows a source and destination list in one widget so the user can move items between them by buttons or drag-and-drop, suited to building a subset from a source list too large for checkboxes, and it lets the user see what is selected without jumping to a modal.

Place the source and destination lists together with Add/Remove buttons or drag-and-drop, make both searchable, use multiple selection, and decide whether moved items leave the source or the source stays unchanged (a filesystem listing should not change).
Prefill form fields with Good Defaults and Smart Prefills drawn from session data, account information, current location, date, and time, and high-probability guesses, to reduce the user's work.
Do not prefill sensitive or politically charged fields (passwords, gender, citizenship) because it can make users uncomfortable, and never leave advertising-opt-in checkboxes selected by default.

Choose a default only when you are reasonably sure most users most of the time will not change it (not merely to avoid a blank control), inferring later defaults from earlier input (like deriving state, city, and country from a Zip code), and defaulting technical choices in occasional-use interfaces like installers that most users will not care about.

Good defaults save work and, even when not what the user wants, show what kind of answer is expected, but be aware a skipped field may not register mentally, so require the user to type or select when you want them to consciously address the question.
On a form input error, place an eye-catching explanatory message on the form itself, describing how to fix it, with indicators next to the originating controls.

Do not report form errors in a modal dialog (which must be dismissed to fix the error, losing the message) or on a separate post-submit error screen (which forces the user to go back and remember); keep messages and controls together on the same page next to the offending field.

First design a form to prevent errors (drop-downs for limited choices; input hints, prompts, forgiving format, autocompletion, and good defaults for text; few fields; clear required/optional marking) before relying on error messages.

For a long form show a summary error at the top (the first thing seen and read first by screen readers), mark each error field with color plus another cue (since many users are red-colorblind, add language, bold text, and graphics), and validate on the client as soon as focus leaves a field rather than after submission, without flagging an error while the user is still typing a valid entry.
Write error messages that are short but detailed enough to name the field and what went wrong, in ordinary language rather than computerese, and polite.
The modern standard for form errors is to keep the submit button inactive until all required steps are filled in successfully, so the user cannot skip a required step or submit an invalid entry.
Screen interfaces are built from a system of commonly used components, and a component-based approach delivers consistency, scalability, and better usability.

UI design systems standardize functionality and look-and-feel across operating systems and devices while staying aligned to each OS's standards and without dictating implementation technology; major examples are Microsoft Fluent, Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, and Google Material.

Take a bottom-up (atomic design) approach: break screens into their smallest still-functional pieces, set a brand-driven style guide first (color, typography, layout grid, icons) that everything inherits, then build up.
Reuse the same component everywhere as a whole component to avoid UX debt (the slow accumulation of diverging styles), so the software can grow while its UI stays consistent.
Build the UI from a system of modular, LEGO-like building blocks that can be assembled into tools and screens to meet specific needs.
Compose larger components from smaller ones and let styles inherit upward, so changing a base style declaration once (a palette color or a button's corner radius) propagates everywhere it is used.

The atomic design hierarchy runs from atoms (the smallest units like an input field, label, color, or typeface) to molecules (a few atoms, such as a labeled input with a hint, prompt, and button), to organisms (collections of molecules like a header with logo, navigation, search, and avatar), to templates (layout recipes for recurring screen types), to pages (templates filled with real content).
Stay focused on understanding users and designing usable experiences; atomic design, UI frameworks, and patterns are tools to that end, not constraints tied to any technology.

UI frameworks (also called frontend or CSS frameworks, UI kits, or toolkits) are libraries of prepared, configurable code components that generate a screen UI's HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, giving speed, consistency, masking of browser differences, and built-in responsive design.
Treat UI frameworks as a floor, not a ceiling: a customizable starting point that handles the standardized, repeated parts of a UI and frees time to solve the harder interaction-design problems.

Most user-visible systems share the same core (the user contributes information or transactions and an interface shows the results), so social, news, and ecommerce products follow similar underlying patterns.

Algorithms and machine learning increasingly power what is displayed to users, and ubiquitous computing (the Internet of Things) embeds internet-connected sensors in objects and spaces, often invisibly.

As interactions become more automated and invisible, users need less direct input and increasingly just confirm or approve actions a system takes on their behalf, across smart-system types like connected devices, anticipatory systems, assistive systems, and natural user interfaces (motion, gesture, touch, or voice).

The designer's role is to understand these patterns and apply them to their particular context, so imagining the scenarios and the rules that apply to them (storytelling and narrative) is a primary design responsibility.

Regardless of how an interface reaches a user, the foundational principles are evergreen: a sound information-architecture foundation, a clear visual information hierarchy following the Gestalt principles, and appropriate user help together bring clarity and understanding to an interface.
Because the experiences designers build touch people's lives, they should design with an ethical, human-centered mindset that makes life better for people and the planet.
Forms are often designed 'inside out'—starting from the set of database fields that define a valid record—rather than 'outside in' from the perspective of the people who must fill them in.
Design forms 'outside in': start from how the people outside the organization would describe the outcome they want, not from the organization's database field list.
The primary goal of form design should be to get people through the form quickly and easily—ideally making it feel invisible—while still capturing the information the organization needs.
Form redesign projects commonly produced completion-rate increases of roughly 10–40 percent.
Because forms broker high-value interactions such as checkout and registration, improving form design can produce substantial increases in revenue and new customers.
Treat a form as a deliberate conversation—asking who is filling it in and why—rather than as the inputs for a database; framing it as a conversation reveals natural breaks between topics.

When a form's topics are short enough to fit into a few sections, put them on a single web page; when sections begin to run long, split the conversation across multiple pages to keep topics meaningful.
condition: deciding whether to place a form on one page or several

statement: When a form spans several web pages, give users an overview of the number of pages (scope), an indication of the current page (position), and a way to save and return to progress (status).
condition: a form spans multiple web pages

statement: Use top-aligned labels when the goal is to reduce completion times or when flexible label lengths are needed for localization.
