condition: reducing completion time or needing flexible label lengths for localization

statement: Use right-aligned labels when completion-time and flexibility goals apply but vertical screen real estate is constrained.
condition: vertical screen space is constrained but faster completion is still wanted

statement: Use left-aligned labels when people must scan labels to learn what is required or to answer a few specific questions out of many.
condition: users need to scan labels to find specific questions

statement: Use smart defaults—default selections that serve the interests of most people—to reduce the number of choices users must make and expedite form completion.

Add help text when the form asks for unfamiliar data, when people question why data is requested, when they may worry about security or privacy, when there are recommended ways to provide data, or when specific fields are optional/required against the norm of the form.
condition: one of the listed help-triggering conditions is present

statement: If most inputs on a form are required, mark the few that are optional; if most are optional, mark the few that are required.
Indicate required-versus-optional status with text, which is clearest; the asterisk (*) is relatively well understood to mean required.
Primary actions (such as Submit, Save, or Continue) enable completion—the primary goal of anyone filling in a form—whereas secondary actions tend to be far less used.
Measure the impact of a form design using multiple data sources: usability testing, field testing, customer-support records, site tracking, eye tracking, and web-convention surveys.
Useful form measurement does not require expensive testing—observing a few people complete the form or monitoring server logs with off-the-shelf analytics yields useful information.

Forcing first-time customers to register before checkout drives them away; replacing a mandatory 'Register' step with a guest 'Continue' option (noting an account can be created later during checkout) removes a major barrier to purchase.
condition: an ecommerce checkout flow that currently requires account creation before purchase

statement: Forced pre-purchase registration carries large hidden costs: in one retailer 45 percent of customers had multiple registrations, roughly 160,000 password requests occurred per day, and about 75 percent of those requesters never completed the purchase.
Removing a forced-registration barrier at checkout increased the number of purchasing customers by 45 percent and produced roughly $300 million in additional revenue in the first year.
There is no single right form design; the correct solution depends on the business goals, user needs, and context of the form.
Move from the answer 'it depends' to actionable solutions by working from design considerations—a combination of design principles and design patterns.
Apply the principle 'Minimize the Pain': make completing the form as simple and easy as possible, because people want what lies on the other side of it.
Apply the principle 'Illuminate a Path to Completion': make it abundantly clear how people can complete the form.
Apply the principle 'Consider the Context': design the form for the broader context (audience, application, business) in which it will be used.
Apply the principle 'Ensure Consistent Communication': a form must speak with one voice even though many groups (marketing, legal, engineering, design) contribute questions to it.
Express form best practices as conditional design patterns: if your goals are X a good solution is Y, and if your constraints are A a worthwhile approach is B.

The most effective way to speed up form completion is to not ask a question at all; put every question to the test—do you truly need it, can you obtain it automatically, and is there a better time or place to ask it.
Challenge legacy questions carried over from paper forms, because outdated questions are often ported into digital forms even when they no longer apply.
condition: digitizing or updating a form that originated as a paper document

statement: Keep the questions that users are eager and able to answer, then move on to design details.
Cut any question you do not need right now—this means less design work, less user work, and no long-term data storage.
Postpone a question until the point in the interaction where asking it shifts from unnecessary or intrusive to harmonious.
condition: a question is valuable but feels intrusive if asked immediately

statement: For necessary but difficult questions, explain with a short, clear reason that offers a benefit to the user; if you cannot state a user benefit, reconsider whether the question is needed at all.
condition: a needed question requires personal data or extra effort
exception: you cannot articulate any user benefit for asking

statement: Users care about what they are asked, why they are asked it, and above all whether the request is appropriate to what they are trying to achieve.

Before deciding where to place questions on the page, think about the people and the relationship—why they are filling in the form and how they feel about the organization; if you do not know, observe or ask them.
Organize a form as a conversation rather than an interrogation to make new customers feel welcome.
Treat input fields as part of the question posed by their label, mirroring how people answer questions in the real world; this matters more as questions become complex or unfamiliar.
Phrase labels using the customer's own vocabulary rather than internal or organizational jargon, so people can provide an answer more quickly.
Do not reword every label as a full sentence—concise single-word labels often work better; reserve conversational natural language for cases where a question is potentially ambiguous.
exception: a concise single-word label is unambiguous

statement: Organize the questions on a form into meaningful, logical groups to aid scanning and completion.
When several sections with many questions must be answered in sequence and do not make sense out of context, one long web page may be the best organization.
condition: questions are interdependent and must be seen together

statement: Ask optional questions (such as 'How did you hear about us?') after the main form is completed; in one redesign this increased answers by almost 40 percent, likely because optional questions feel less invasive as follow-ups.

Use a web-conventions survey—comparing design solutions across several similar, top-performing sites—as a starting point for form structure, but do not directly copy a competitor's form because a direct replica rarely fits your situation.
exception: copying a competitor's structure verbatim

statement: Use the minimum amount of visual information necessary to distinguish content groups; excessive contrast between groups creates visual noise that impedes people's ability to scan the form.

Alternating background colors used to pair left-aligned labels with their inputs do not solve the label-input correlation problem—eye-tracking shows people correlate them fine, just more slowly—and they add visual noise.
Any visual element that does not help a layout ends up hurting it—information consists of differences that make a difference.
Use initial capital letters for content-group titles to make them easier to scan.
The primary goal of anyone encountering a form is to complete it, so illuminating a clear path to completion is crucial.
Match form titles to the calls-to-action people used to reach them, because users rely on the title—not detailed instructional text—to know what a form does.

Use a start page for forms that require substantial time or information the user must look up (e.g., online surveys), stating what will be needed and roughly how long it takes; do not use start pages before forms whose answers are readily available.
condition: a form demands significant time or hard-to-gather information
exception: the form only asks for answers people have immediately

statement: Provide a clear vertical scan line—a strong vertical axis of labels, input fields, and the primary action—so people follow a single downward path with minimal diversions, which helps increase completion rates.
Space adjacent label/input pairs at roughly 50–75 percent of an input field's height to set an even, comfortable pace through the form.

On mission-critical forms such as checkout or registration, remove interface elements not directly related to completion—navigation, headers, promotions, even an active site logo—to eliminate paths to abandonment.
condition: a mission-critical form like checkout or registration

statement: For multi-page forms with a known sequence, provide progress indicators that communicate scope (number of pages), position (current page), and status (whether saved or submitted).
condition: a form spans a known, fixed sequence of web pages

statement: For long forms, provide an explicit save-and-return option or auto-save to keep people on the path to completion.
condition: a long, multi-section form

statement: Do not use a progress indicator that misrepresents the true number of pages or steps; such indicators promise well-defined linear steps but rarely deliver them.

For forms without a clearly defined page sequence, either omit the progress indicator or use a high-level one that lists the types of information needed without setting explicit step-count expectations.
condition: a form's number of pages or steps is not fixed or predictable

statement: Design an accessible form by accounting for users with limited or no vision, hearing, or movement, or with cognitive impairments, and by getting the content and structure right first so assistive technology can convey it.
Accessibility solutions—closed captioning, keyboard-only access, alt text for images—benefit all users, not only those with disabilities.

Provide text alternatives for all non-decorative content: alt text for images, summaries for tables, a label for every input (even if visually hidden), and meaningful, unique titles for frames and pages.
Make links unique and give them labels that are meaningful out of context, avoiding the generic 'Click here'.
Never use color as the only means of conveying information, and ensure good contrast between text and background, since color-blind users cannot distinguish certain color pairs.
Make all functionality on a page operable with the keyboard alone, providing a non-mouse alternative to any drag-and-drop interaction.
Avoid gratuitous animation (which distracts users with attention disorders) and anything that flashes more than three times per second (which can trigger seizures).
Allow users to turn off, adjust, or extend any timing—such as a security timeout—without losing their work.
condition: the product imposes a time limit on the user

statement: Provide a way for keyboard-only users to skip repetitive content at the top of each page.
Refer to interface objects by their name or function, not their physical characteristics (avoid 'the button on the right' or 'the green-arrow button').
Above every specific accessibility guideline, test the page with your intended users, including those who have disabilities.
More than half of users move between input fields using the Tab key, so design the tabbing experience of a form deliberately.
Two-column form layouts can produce jarring tab jumps between columns and disorient users; consider the tab experience when choosing a layout.
condition: a multi-column form layout

statement: Use the HTML 'tabindex' attribute to specify the input tab order explicitly; without it, fields are tabbed through in the order they appear in the HTML markup.
Every web form has three basic elements: labels ask the questions, input fields capture the answers, and actions submit the answers.
The right label alignment depends on your goals and constraints—completion speed, whether you want to deliberately slow users, vertical or horizontal space limits, and localization needs.
Top-aligned labels tend to reduce form completion time the most, because label and field sit in close proximity and users move in a single downward direction.

Top-aligned labels give ample horizontal room to expand or contract label text—useful for long labels and localization, where languages like French, German, or Dutch can run up to twice as long as English—and for grouping related fields horizontally.
Top-aligned labels consume more vertical screen space, so reconsider them when vertical space is limited.
condition: vertical screen real estate is constrained

statement: In Matteo Penzo's eye-tracking study, moving from a top-aligned label to its input took about 50 milliseconds—roughly ten times faster than left-aligned labels (~500ms) and about twice as fast as right-aligned labels (~240ms).
Live-site testing across several geographies found top-aligned labels produced the fastest completion and over 10 percent higher completion rates than the left-aligned versions tested against.
The measured speed advantages of top-aligned labels were obtained only with familiar data (name, address, credit card, email); whether they hold for unfamiliar data remains unproven.
exception: the form collects unfamiliar data users must look up or learn

statement: Right-aligned labels are quick to complete because of close label-input proximity, but their ragged left edge reduces scannability and label wrapping can hurt readability; favor them when you need to minimize vertical space.
condition: vertical screen space must be minimized

statement: Left-aligned labels make scanning the required information easier via an uninterrupted left column and suit unfamiliar data or data that does not group easily, but they are the slowest to complete (Penzo measured a ~500ms saccade, indicating heavy cognitive load).
condition: data is unfamiliar or does not fall into easy-to-process groups

statement: Deliberately choose left-aligned labels when you want people to slow down and consider each input—for example, forms with many optional fields, preferences dialogs, or advanced settings.
condition: you intend for users to consider each input carefully

statement: Use labels-within-inputs only when screen space is at a premium, and only if the label reliably disappears when the field receives focus.
condition: screen real estate is severely limited

statement: Do not use labels-within-inputs for long or medium-length forms or for non-obvious questions, because the label vanishes on entry and users lose the context needed to answer or review; reserve them for single- or few-input forms and very familiar data.
condition: a single- or few-input form asking familiar data
exception: the form is long/medium or asks non-obvious questions requiring reference to the label

statement: Make an in-field label visually distinct from real data (e.g., gray text, an ellipsis, or surrounding dashes) so it is obviously a label at first glance.
Avoid changing label alignment within a single form, because inconsistent alignment clouds the clear path to completion people seek.

When considering different label alignments across forms in one application, weigh the context-versus-consistency trade-off; unless there is a strong reason to differ, a single layout mitigates perceived inconsistency.
condition: an application containing multiple distinct forms
exception: you have a very good reason to change alignment between forms

statement: Choose the input field type that matches the question being asked—yes/no, a single choice from mutually exclusive options, multiple choices, or free text.
Use radio buttons to select exactly one of two or more always-visible, mutually exclusive options; give them a sensible default selection and make both the button and its label clickable.
Use checkboxes to select any number of options from a list (a single checkbox represents a yes/no question); make both the checkbox and its label clickable.

Use drop-down menus for a single choice from mutually exclusive options when saving screen space matters, and prefer them over radio buttons for long lists—but avoid very long drop-down lists, especially for options people already know such as their home state.
exception: the list is very long or the options are highly familiar

statement: Avoid list boxes in web forms; their dual single-versus-multiple-selection nature confuses many people, so they are rarely used.

When selecting input controls, weigh the trade-offs—click-efficiency vs. error prevention, learnability vs. efficiency, majority case vs. corner case, and flexibility vs. clarity—optimizing for the specific audience and usage model.

Plain text boxes are obvious and intuitive but weak at preventing input errors, whereas drop-down menus prevent errors more aggressively yet are among the hardest, most-overlooked controls—so each control trades obviousness against error prevention.
Match an input field's length to the expected length of its answer (for example, a 5-digit zip-code box) as an affordance that signals how to answer and avoids the need for extra help text.

Avoid arbitrary or inconsistent field sizes, which make people wonder whether they misunderstood a question; for fields lacking a meaningful affordance, use a consistent length with enough room for the answer.
Try to avoid optional input fields in forms altogether.

Indicate the minority case: if most inputs are required, mark the few optional ones; if most are optional, mark the few required ones; indicate neither when all fields are uniformly required or uniformly optional, because it only adds noise.
exception: all fields on the form are uniformly required or uniformly optional

statement: Prefer explicit text (such as the word 'optional') over symbols to mark required or optional status; if you use an asterisk, always provide a legend explaining what it means.
condition: you choose a symbol like an asterisk to mark required fields

statement: The asterisk is only a de facto required-field convention with exceptions—some sites use it to mark optional fields—so it can be misread.
Place required/optional indicators next to the labels rather than aligned with the inputs, because varied input shapes make input-aligned indicators hard to scan.
Group inputs that share a meaningful natural structure—address parts, first and last name, phone number, date and time—to give people clues on how to answer.
When more than one format is a valid answer, use a flexible input that accepts multiple formats and normalizes them in code, shifting the formatting burden off the user.
condition: there is clearly more than one correct way to format the answer

statement: Ensure flexible inputs still make the simplest, most common answer easy to provide; flexibility gained at the expense of the common answer's ease does more harm than good.
exception: the flexibility makes the most common answer harder to give

statement: Actions—not labels or input fields—are what actually let people complete a form.

Primary actions (Submit, Save, Continue) enable completion, the primary goal of anyone filling in a form; secondary actions (Cancel, Reset, Go Back) are less used, run counter to that goal, and can have negative consequences.
Avoid secondary actions on forms whenever possible to give people a single path to completion, since destructive secondary actions like Reset can erase all of a user's entered data.

Some secondary actions are legitimate (Save for Later, Preview, Export); in multi-page wizards, make forward movement a primary 'Continue' action and 'Back' a secondary action rather than treating Previous and Next as equal.
condition: a multi-page form wizard with forward/backward navigation

statement: Reduce the visual prominence of secondary actions to minimize the risk of erroneous clicks and steer people toward completion.

In an Etre eye-tracking test of six primary/secondary action designs on 23 people, five designs achieved 100 percent task success; the design with visually identical primary and secondary buttons was fastest (about 2.1 seconds faster than distinguished designs) but made users fear clicking the wrong button, while designs that made Cancel stand out scored higher satisfaction.
When a secondary action cannot be removed, visually distinguish it from the primary action, because users report the distinction helps them avoid taking the wrong action.
Avoid using red to label primary or secondary actions; reserve red for errors, given its strong association with something going wrong on a form.

To prevent catastrophic data loss from a destructive secondary action, provide an automatic Undo—replace the Reset button with an Undo button after it is clicked—rather than relying on a confirmation dialog.
condition: a form includes a destructive action like Reset or Clear

statement: Place primary and secondary actions left-aligned directly below the last input field; in the Etre test, a centered layout was about six seconds slower and a separated layout caused 26 percent of users to mistakenly click Cancel, because people expect the buttons aligned with the inputs above them.

After a form is submitted, clearly communicate that processing is underway—replace the active primary action with a progress animation or message—to prevent people from re-clicking and causing duplicate submissions.
Do not rely on help text urging people not to press Submit twice; that is an 'inside out' solution that unfairly burdens the user—disable or replace the button instead.
You may disable the primary action until all questions have valid answers, but avoid this on any form that includes optional questions, because you cannot reliably determine when the user is done.
condition: every question on the form is required
exception: the form contains any optional questions

statement: Keep the primary action always visible—even when disabled—so people can always see the action that completes the form; do not hide it until the form is complete.

Fold a required terms-of-service agreement into the primary action (e.g., 'I agree and move forward' or preceding text 'by clicking register below, I agree') to remove a separate question that people may skip mistaking it for a marketing opt-in.
condition: a form legally requires explicit agreement to terms of service

statement: Prefer wording that keeps the primary call to action aligned with the user's goal ('Buy Now') over combining it with the agreement in the label itself ('Agree & Buy Now').

If excessive instructions are needed to explain how to complete a form, the questions are probably poorly phrased, too complex, or unnecessary; treat heavy help text as a signal to revisit the questions.
Do not rely on instructional text to explain a form, because people tend not to read on-screen instructions—eye-tracking shows many jump straight to the first input field.

Add concise help text only in specific circumstances—unfamiliar data, when people question why data is requested, security or privacy concerns, recommended ways of providing data, or fields optional/required against the form's norm—and use the minimum amount needed.
condition: one of the specific help-triggering circumstances applies

statement: For forms that would be overwhelmed by per-field help text, use a dynamic help system—either automatically triggered or user-activated.
condition: a form requires extensive help across many fields

statement: With automatic inline help, reveal help when the user engages a field or group (click/tab), display it adjacent to the field it applies to, and use a strong visual element to tie the help to its field(s).
Automatic inline help has a drawback: people cannot tell help exists until they start filling out the form, so those who feel they need help may get discouraged and not try.

Help text placed inside an input field is suitable only for outlining recommended ways of providing an answer—not for explaining what is asked, why, or whether it is optional—and it must disappear on entry and be visually distinguishable from real data.
exception: the help explains what/why or the field is complex and benefits from always-visible help

statement: Automatic inline help works best for forms asking questions people can answer but are unsure how to provide.
condition: questions are answerable but users are apprehensive about the format

statement: For user-activated help, use a consistent trigger (icon, link, or label) with an actionable visual cue—the question mark is the most recognizable help symbol—and place the trigger next to the label rather than the input field.

Prefer surfacing user-activated help on top of the form (an overlay adjacent to the label/input) rather than inserting it inline, because inserted help pushes content down and causes disorienting page jumping.
For rollover-triggered help, enlarge the activation hot spot and add about a 500-millisecond delay so help does not appear on accidental mouse-overs.
condition: help is triggered by a mouse rollover

statement: User-activated inline and section help suit forms that are reused by the same people and ask complex questions—first-timers can access all help while advanced users trigger only what they need; use a consistent section location (not a new browser window) for extensive help with graphics or charts.
condition: a complex form that the same people use repeatedly

statement: When asking for sensitive information (credit card, bank details), include actionable reassurance that lets people verify security—such as a trusted third-party seal (VeriSign, TRUSTe) they can click to confirm—rather than empty 'your data is safe' text.
condition: the form collects sensitive personal or financial data

statement: Minimize the potential for errors through good design first; when mistakes still happen, deal with them quickly and gracefully.

When present, an error message is arguably the most important element on the page because it blocks completion, so its visual presentation must match that importance—use strong contrast (typically red text plus a warning icon) and prominent placement.
Make an error immediately noticeable, since it is blocking the user's progress, using differences in size, shape, position, texture, or color—alone or combined.

Surface an error in context, next to the input responsible for it, with actionable instructions on how to fix it, rather than in a modal dialog that must be dismissed—dismissing the dialog removes the indication of what to correct.

Mark the input field responsible for an error with 'double visual emphasis' (for example a red label plus red instructions below it, or an icon plus text), because a color change alone may not be noticed by color-blind users.
Match the visual style of the flagged input(s) to the style of the top-level error message so people can connect the error message to its cause.
Keep the number of message types minimal: one or two types is ideal, three edges into user-harming complexity, and four or more means you should start over.
Avoid error messages where possible by using inputs with no error states (like drop-down menus), inputs with undo, and inputs with good default values; where unavoidable, use them sparingly.

Show an error message only for one of two reasons: the customer entered something the system cannot accept (say what happened, how to fix it, and move on) or a serious system failure occurred (apologize and offer an alternate way to make contact); never disguise marketing as an error message.
Keep success messages short and pleasant—a simple acknowledgment that thanks the customer for completing the form.

Avoid adding ambiguous 'in-between' message types (educational, marketing-disguised, maybe-bad); if you must add one, define precisely when it is used, make it visually distinct, and test it thoroughly with real users.
condition: you feel compelled to introduce an additional message type

statement: When a form has multiple errors or an error with no responsible field, use the same structure: a prominent top-level message, double visual emphasis on any responsible inputs, and clear resolution instructions in both places; the top-level message should list all the errors to be fixed.
On short forms, 'less is more'—you may omit either the top-level message or the per-input indicators—but do so thoughtfully, ensuring whatever remains has strong contrast from the rest of the form.
condition: a short form

statement: Do not use red text for labels or help text; reserve red for errors, because red has the clearest error association for most people and reusing it causes confusion.

Relying only on per-input double emphasis without a top-level message can fail on long forms when the responsible fields are below the fold; a top-level message that lists all errors gives the overview that jumping to the first error does not.
condition: a long form where errors may fall below the visible area

statement: Provide a noticeable success message that confirms the form was completed and states what happened as a result.
Success messages must never block further progress (unlike error messages, which must be addressed); show them in context so people can continue.
Choose the success message's context to match the completed task—the same form for a record update, or the list where the newly created item appears.
Consider dynamic, animated success messages (fades, dissolves, roll-ups) that auto-remove when only confirmation is needed, since people are instinctively drawn to motion.
condition: the only feedback required is that the action succeeded

statement: Avoid success-message dead ends: include useful, relevant follow-up actions or next steps so people are never left hanging after completing a form.
Use inline validation to give real-time feedback—confirmation, suggestions, or limit updates—as people begin, continue, or stop entering an answer.

Confirmation via inline validation is most useful when people are unlikely to get the answer right first try (e.g., choosing a unique username); it tells them immediately whether the answer is valid so they stop cycling ('pogo-sticking') through error states.
condition: an answer that users must guess and often get wrong, like a unique username

statement: For answers with degrees of correctness, such as password strength, use inline validation (e.g., a strength meter) to steer people toward better answers—the meter compels more thoughtful input.
condition: an answer that can be more or less 'right', like password security

statement: Do not inline-validate every field; validating answers people already know (like their name) is unnecessary and can raise doubts about what the site is checking—reserve validation for answers people are not guaranteed to know.
exception: the answer is something the user already knows for certain

statement: When using inline validation, get the timing right: provide feedback only once it is clear the person has finished answering, not on the first keystroke, to avoid premature error states.
When a valid answer set is too broad to fit a drop-down or radio buttons, use inline suggestions (autocomplete) that appear as people type to guide them to a valid answer (e.g., airport codes).
condition: the set of valid answers is large but finite

statement: Generate inline suggestions from data the user already provided (e.g., propose usernames derived from the full name entered earlier) to guide them to a valid answer.
condition: a valid answer can be derived from information already given

statement: If you must reformat a user's valid-but-wrongly-formatted answer into a required format, do so only after they finish entering it, never while they are typing.
condition: the system enforces one specific answer format

statement: For questions with clearly defined limits (such as a 1,000-character message), use inline validation with a real-time counter that updates immediately as people type; any significant delay undermines its usefulness.
condition: an input has a defined maximum length or bound

statement: The fewer questions you ask, the better the odds people complete the form quickly and easily, so remove questions that are not absolutely necessary, can be asked at a better time, or can be inferred automatically.

eBay removed optional questions that tripped up customers (annual income, gender, promotional codes, date of birth) from its registration form; far more people registered successfully, and significantly more answered those optional questions when they were asked after registration.

Infer answers you can derive rather than asking for them—for example, detect the credit-card type from the card number's leading digits (Amex 34/37, Mastercard 51–55, Visa 4) instead of asking users to select it.

Do not complicate a question for the sake of removing an input; breaking a familiar structure (like asking for zip code before city/state, out of order) or needing extra help text signals the simplification has backfired.
exception: removing an input makes the question harder to answer

statement: Some redundancy is a deliberate safeguard: the U.S. Postal Service keeps both zip code and city/state on mailing labels precisely because people often mistype one or the other.
Verify that an inference-based simplification actually covers your audience; for example, deriving city/state from a zip code fails for international addresses that do not use the U.S. zip system.
exception: part of the audience falls outside the inferred pattern, e.g. international users

statement: Defaults powerfully shape outcomes: organ-donor participation is about 25 percent in the U.S. (opt-in default) versus over 80 percent in several European countries (opt-out default), despite similar approval of donation.

Use smart defaults—preselected options that serve the interests of most people—to reduce the number of choices and expedite completion, but ensure they align with customers' interests, since defaulting people into unwanted options (like marketing opt-ins) casts suspicion and can cause abandonment.
exception: the default serves the business at the customer's expense

statement: Where appropriate, include a default selection in a set of radio buttons, choosing the option right for the majority; because people tend to keep defaults, choose that initial selection carefully.
condition: one option clearly suits most users

statement: Omit a default when no option applies to most people or when you want an explicit choice (e.g., gender, birth date); a presumptuous default such as a fixed default birth date is worse than simply asking, and explaining why you ask helps.
condition: no single option fits the majority or the answer is sensitive

statement: Derive smart defaults from implicit behavior or context—for example, default the Country field to United States when the user is accessing from the U.S. or when most customers are U.S.-based.
condition: context or aggregate data reliably indicates the likely answer

statement: Use personalized 'sticky' defaults based on a returning customer's prior choices to speed completion; many can be set after a single use, but apply them only where they make sense, not on every input of every form.
condition: a returning customer with a known prior choice

statement: When a few options cover most people's needs, serve the minority who need more with additional inputs—inline additions, overlays, or progressive engagement—without burdening the majority.

Implement inline additions that expose extra fields on demand via clearly worded triggers (e.g., 'Add another manager', 'Attach files to this message'), provide an easy way to remove them, and keep the always-needed primary field non-removable.
Minimize page jumping when revealing inline additions—avoid pushing large amounts of content down the page; expose large option sets to the side or in an overlay rather than below the trigger.
Use an overlay (such as a calendar date picker) to surface many options only when needed, keeping them off the form the rest of the time to avoid noise.

Give an overlay enough useful capacity for the task—Kayak shows two months of dates because trips span a week or more, whereas showing only one month forces month-by-month scrolling—so use the space to present the options people actually need.
Signal that an overlay will appear (e.g., a calendar icon inside the field) and ensure the overlay does not cover the input field it serves, so users can still type directly.
Auto-display an overlay only when the additional options are clearly useful to most people; otherwise keep additional options user-activated so people choose whether to see them.
exception: the extra options are not clearly useful to the majority

statement: Use a modal overlay when additional inputs must be considered in isolation (disabling the rest of the form); ensure the selections made in the overlay appear on the original form after it closes, and provide clear ways to dismiss it.
condition: additional inputs require focused, isolated attention

statement: For a complex field with multiple valid formats (e.g., a location as address, MGRS, or lat/lon), move entry into a dialog with a tab per method, auto-convert between formats, validate on entry, and show a simplified read-only readout on the main form—saving space while retaining flexibility.
condition: a single field accepts several distinct input formats

statement: On touch devices, provide input-specific pop-up keypads that accept only valid values with buttons large enough to target by finger; observed users preferred the keypads even when a physical keyboard was available.
condition: the form is used on a touch-screen device

statement: Map additional inputs to prioritized customer needs: keep primary use cases up front and visible, and place secondary use cases a click away.
Prefer additional inputs that are user-activated over ones that are automatically surfaced, since people generally find invoked options more welcome.
Maintain a consistent approach to additional inputs within a single form.

When engaging customers matters more than pure efficiency, use progressive engagement to step people through choices in a captivating way—accepting the trade-off of more clicks and not seeing all options at once.
condition: engagement is a higher priority than completion speed

statement: Selection-dependent inputs reveal follow-up questions based on an initial answer (usually without a new page) and add requirements, since the form cannot be submitted until the dependent fields are filled.
Across tested solutions, hiding irrelevant form controls until people need them produces forms that are easy on the eyes and completed quickly.
Across tested solutions, displaying initial options and their selection-dependent inputs in close proximity leads to higher satisfaction ratings.

In every selection-dependent design, maintain a clear association between the initial choice and its dependent inputs—don't let people lose sight of their top-level selection—and clearly tie the dependent inputs to their trigger (e.g., a yellow background or gray outline).
Avoid excessive page jumping that disassociates selection-dependent inputs from the initial set of options.

Use page-level (two-page) selection-dependent inputs when each initial choice has a large set of dependent options: it avoids mutual-exclusivity confusion and the dynamic hide/show never confuses people, though it is among the slowest to complete.
condition: each initial choice leads to many dependent fields and completion speed is not critical

statement: Prefer vertical tabs over horizontal tabs for selection-dependent inputs: both perform well on usability, satisfaction, and eye-tracking, but horizontal tabs break the vertical scan line and both share a mutual-exclusivity ambiguity that must be resolved by clear design.
exception: you can resolve the mutual-exclusivity ambiguity, in which case either performs well

statement: Horizontal tabs force the eye to scan left-to-right and deviate from a clear top-to-bottom scan line, whereas vertical tabs sit within the scan line.

When the list of initial options is long (more than four or five), use a drop-down list plus visual grouping for the dependent inputs, because it scales past what horizontal or vertical tabs support and tested as a safe, average performer.
condition: there are more than four or five initial options

statement: When each initial option has only a few (roughly 1–3) dependent inputs, use expose-within (or expose-below) radio buttons—expose-within was the fastest solution tested—but add clear visual associations and animated transitions to counter page-jumping and disassociation.
condition: there are only 1–3 dependent inputs per initial choice
exception: the number of dependent inputs is substantial, where these methods break down

statement: Avoid the 'exposed inactive' (all options shown, unused ones grayed) and 'exposed groups' (all options shown) solutions; they overwhelm people and were the worst performers, with exposed groups scoring lowest success, highest errors, and lowest satisfaction.
Graying out irrelevant options performs better than leaving them fully active, but hiding irrelevant options entirely performs best of all.
Where possible, eliminate the sign-up form: do not greet new users with a registration form before they can experience what the service does.

Use gradual engagement—let people start using the service first (make a movie, build a family tree, forward a confirmation email) and defer account creation until it is actually needed (to publish, share, or return).
Gradual engagement teaches people what a service does through use and can dramatically boost adoption—Geni gained five million profiles in five months using this approach.

When a service auto-creates an account without an explicit sign-up, provide an easy way for people to access their account information, because some users will be unsure whether they even have an account.
condition: the service creates accounts implicitly rather than via an explicit form

statement: Design gradual engagement as a series of interactions that show potential customers how to use the service and why they should care—not by simply distributing sign-up fields across separate pages, which reduces efficiency and delights no one.
exception: the 'gradual' flow is just a sign-up form split across pages

statement: Single sign-on solutions (such as OpenID or Microsoft Live ID) can eliminate a lot of duplicative sign-up and checkout forms, though none has yet become a clear standard.

Forms that adapt or change per user are prone to confusion when poorly designed: done well they give a few people a slightly better experience, done poorly they confuse many—so apply adaptive form behavior cautiously.
condition: you are considering interfaces that change based on who is using them

statement: Use the LABEL element to give context to an individual form control, and use a LEGEND within a FIELDSET to give context to a group of related fields (such as a multiple-choice question).
Build forms from rich, semantic HTML markup first, then apply CSS for layout—for example, block-level labels for a stacked layout or floated labels for a side-by-side layout.
Do not pursue pixel-perfection in form styling, because form controls render quite differently across browsers and operating systems.
Break complex form structures into simpler ones—a form is a list of questions, and a multiple-choice question is a legend plus a list of labelled responses—to produce consistent, repeatable markup.
To get a form up and running quickly, consider hosted form-building services (such as Wufoo or Form Assembly) that help design, build, and host many kinds of forms.
condition: you need to build and host a form quickly without custom development

statement: Separate what a form does from how it looks into distinct markup (as the W3C XForms standard does) to keep form behavior and presentation independent.
However you build a form, design it from the viewpoint of the people who will use it—the 'outside in' perspective.
Interaction design is centrally concerned with designing the behavior of interactive products, not only their form.
An interaction design specification acts as a blueprint that tells programmers what to build and lets managers measure development progress against it.
Design for people's goals, the reasons why they use a product, together with their expectations, attitudes, and aptitudes, to produce solutions users find powerful and pleasurable.
It is possible to learn what users want through qualitative research and analysis; the claim that user needs are unknowable is false.

Structure the product organization so that design is an equal partner with engineering, marketing, and business management, giving each group well-defined responsibilities balanced by equal authority.

The design team is responsible for users' satisfaction with the product and therefore must hold the authority to decide how the product looks, feels, and behaves, plus access to users, engineers, marketing, and management.
Engineering is responsible for building the product's form and behaviors as specified by design, on budget and schedule, and needs a clear description of that form and behavior from the design team.
Management is responsible for the product's profitability and decides what each group works on, so it needs clear information from design, marketing, and engineering to make those decisions.

Because people perceive a product as a unified whole in its context (Gestalt), an interactive product cannot be designed by decomposing it into atomic requirements and solving each separately; it must be considered in totality.
Effective interaction design integrates three kinds of tools together: design principles, design patterns, and design processes.
There is no objectively good user interface; quality depends on context, namely who the user is, what she is doing, and what her motivations are.
condition: quality is judged relative to a specific use context

statement: Applying one-size-fits-all principles makes interface creation easier but not necessarily better; understanding the actual users must come first.
Customers who buy a product and the users who operate it day to day are often different people with different needs.
Feature-loaded products rushed early to market are frequently beaten by later entrants whose behavior was better thought out.

Human-oriented design means understanding users' desires, needs, motivations, and contexts alongside business, technical, and domain constraints, then using that knowledge to plan a product whose form, content, and behavior are useful, usable, and desirable as well as viable and feasible.
The design process should precede coding and testing so the product truly meets user needs, rather than being applied as a surface-level patch after construction.
Few users can clearly articulate their own needs; when asked direct questions they tend to focus on low-level tasks or on workarounds to product flaws.
Reducing an interactive product to a long list of features does not produce the graceful orchestration needed to make complex technology useful, and adding 'easy to use' to that list does not help.

Separate the people who design a product from the people who build it, because a programmer judged on coding efficiency and deadlines faces a conflict of interest between ease of coding and ease of use.
A single programmer cannot simultaneously advocate effectively for the user, the business, and the technology, even with the best skills and intentions.

Integrating customers directly into development does not by itself solve interface design, because it confuses domain knowledge with design knowledge: customers can articulate problems but usually cannot visualize the solutions.
exception: designers should still seek user feedback on proposed solutions

statement: Design is a specialized skill like programming, so users should not be asked to design solutions any more than they would be asked to write code.

Poor interactive products stem from three root causes: ignorance about users, a conflict of interest between serving human needs and construction priorities, and the lack of a process for understanding human needs.
Alongside established engineering and marketing methods, teams need a repeatable, predictable, analytical process that transforms an understanding of users into products meeting their needs.
Successful products must satisfy three concerns in tandem, capability, viability, and desirability; if any one is significantly weak the product is unlikely to endure.
Interactivity so dominates a user's attention that the interactive behavior of a product deserves the largest share of design attention, yet it frequently receives none.
Designing behavior requires understanding context and the user's whole relationship with the product from before purchase to end of life, not just rules of visual composition and brand.

Complex digital products that interact directly with humans require significant upfront design effort by professional designers, just as complex physical structures require upfront effort by architects.

Because interaction design is grounded in an understanding of users and cognitive principles rather than mere aesthetic choice, the design of behavior is amenable to a repeatable process of analysis and synthesis, though it cannot be fully automated.
Users' real goals are often personal (such as not appearing incompetent or staying engaged) and differ both from what designers would guess and from the employer's business goals.
Products built to achieve business goals alone eventually fail; a design must also meet users' personal goals, and doing so achieves the business goals far more effectively.
Rules of form and aesthetics should not be discarded but must work in harmony with the larger goal of achieving user goals through appropriately designed behavior.
A goal is an expectation of an end condition, whereas activities and tasks are intermediate steps that help someone reach a goal; they are not the same thing.
Analyze user goals first; task and activity analysis is useful only at the detail level and only after the user's goals have been understood.
Goals change very slowly if at all because they are driven by human motivation, whereas activities and tasks are transient because they depend on whatever technology is at hand.
Designing solely from tasks or activities risks trapping the design in a model imposed by an outmoded technology or one that meets a corporation's goals but not its users' goals.
Asking 'What are the user's goals?' rather than only 'What are the tasks?' is what yields differentiating solutions; task-only design produces at best incremental improvement.
The design target depends on context, namely who the users are, what they are doing, and their goals; ease of learning is not automatically the primary target.
condition: the appropriate emphasis is set by the specific user context

statement: A general guideline that applies particularly well to productivity tools is that good design makes users more effective.
condition: applies particularly to productivity tools

statement: The designer's job is to look beyond the user's immediate tasks to identify who the most important users are and to determine what their goals are and why.
Quantitative market research and segmentation are useful for selling products but fall short of revealing how people actually use products, especially products with complex behavior.
Most traditional research methods provide no means of translating research results into design solutions, leaving a gap between user research and the final design.
Involve designers directly in user research, because isolating designers from users eliminates the empathic knowledge that is one of design's most powerful tools.
exception: if the team lacks time to fully train designers in research, a cross-disciplinary team of designers and dedicated user researchers is appropriate

statement: Use an explicit, systematic process to bridge research and design: build user models, establish design requirements, and translate them into a high-level interaction framework.
The Goal-Directed Design process has six phases: Research, Modeling, Requirements Definition, Framework Definition, Refinement, and Support.
Personas are detailed composite user archetypes that represent distinct groupings of behaviors, attitudes, aptitudes, goals, and motivations observed during research.
Choose design targets from the cast of personas by comparing goals and prioritizing each persona by how broadly its goals encompass the goals of the other personas.
Requirements-phase scenarios should focus first and foremost on meeting the goals and needs of specific personas, not on user tasks in the abstract.
Persona-driven scenarios reveal which tasks are truly important and why, leading to an interface that minimizes necessary tasks and effort while maximizing return.
The output of the Requirements Definition phase should be a requirements definition that balances the user, business, and technical requirements of the design.
Interaction design patterns encode general, context-dependent solutions to classes of previously analyzed problems and give designers proven leverage rather than stifling creativity.

When a product takes physical form, industrial designers must not develop form concepts independent of the product's behavior; they should collaborate early using scenarios to weigh input vectors and form factors.
condition: applies when the product takes physical form

statement: Keep the interaction design team available during development to produce scaled-down design solutions as trade-offs arise, or developers will make those compromises under time pressure and damage the product's design integrity.
Reducing a product's definition to a list of features and functions ignores the real opportunity, which is orchestrating technological capability to serve human needs and goals.
Maintain focus on users' goals throughout the pressures of the product-development cycle; goals are the bedrock on which interaction design should be practiced.

A goal-directed process supplies a clear rationale for design decisions, which eases collaboration with developers and businesspeople and ensures the design is not guesswork or a reflection of team members' personal preferences.

Three distinct models exist for a software product: the implementation model (how the program actually works in code), the user's mental model (the user's cognitive shorthand for it), and the represented model (how the designer chooses to represent the program's working to the user).
The represented model is the one aspect of software over which the designer has great control, unlike the implementation and mental models.
Make the represented model match the user's mental model as closely as possible, because the closer they are, the easier the program is to learn, use, and understand.
A represented model that follows the implementation model too closely significantly reduces the user's ability to learn and use the program.
condition: holds whenever the user's mental model of the task differs from the implementation model, which is almost always the case

statement: Because people form mental models that are simpler than reality, a represented model that is simpler than the actual implementation helps the user achieve a better understanding.
Base user interfaces on users' mental models rather than on the implementation model.
A user's mental model need not be technically true or accurate; it only needs to enable the user to work effectively.
Interfaces that expose the implementation model (a control for every function, a field for every input, a dialog for every code module) are easier to build but alienate and confuse users.
Interaction designers must shield users from the implementation model; a technique well suited to constructing software is not necessarily a good mental model for the user.

Do not surface programming or mathematical constructs such as Boolean AND and OR in the interface, because nonprogrammers interpret the English 'and' and 'or' as the opposite of the Boolean operators, so a Boolean interface is doomed to severe usability problems.
Do not replicate Mechanical-Age artifacts in user interfaces without adding Information-Age enhancements.
Replicating a mechanical representation without change combines the weaknesses of the old medium with those of the new and forfeits the capabilities the information medium could provide.
Relying on Mechanical-Age representations blinds designers to the far greater information-management potential of the computer and can act as a metaphor that artificially constrains the design.
A significant change to a familiar representation must be significantly better to justify departing from what users already know.
condition: applies when replacing an established, familiar representation

statement: People do not find it difficult to adapt to newer, more useful representations of familiar systems, so familiarity alone is a weak reason to keep an inferior representation.
Most users are neither beginners nor experts but perpetual intermediates; experience level follows a bell curve with intermediates forming the large majority.
Nobody wants to remain a beginner; beginners quickly become intermediates or drop out, and both beginners and experts tend over time to gravitate toward intermediacy.
Optimize the interface for perpetual intermediates: devote the bulk of design effort to them while still providing mechanisms so beginners and experts can each be effective.
exception: specialized expert tools and transient or accessibility-focused products are optimized for experts or beginners respectively

statement: The interface's threefold goal is to move beginners rapidly and painlessly into intermediacy, to avoid obstructing intermediates who want to become experts, and above all to keep perpetual intermediates happy in the middle of the skill spectrum.

Optimize the user experience for experts when a product is a specialized tool that technically minded people rely on professionally, such as development tools, scientific instrumentation, or medical devices.
condition: applies to specialized professional tools whose users bring technical knowledge and will invest time to master the product

statement: Optimize for beginners when a product is used transiently or by people with certain disabilities, such as public informational kiosks or assistive medical devices.
condition: applies to transient-use or accessibility-focused products

statement: Beginner assistance must not be fixed into the interface; whatever extra help gets a beginner to intermediacy must know how to go away once its services are no longer required.
Beginners need overview information such as scope, goals, and a guided tour rather than reference material, so standard online help is a poor tool for assisting beginners.

Ensure the product reflects the user's mental model of the tasks so beginners grasp its concepts and scope quickly; users remember the relationships between objects and actions even when they forget the exact command.
Imagine users, especially beginners, as simultaneously very intelligent and very busy: give brief, targeted instruction plus an understanding of cause and effect rather than lengthy tutorials.
Experts demand faster access and shortcuts to their regular working set of tools and appreciate new powerful features, which their mastery insulates them from finding overly complex.
Experts have a disproportionate influence on less experienced prospective buyers, who trust an expert's opinion even when that opinion reflects only expert needs.
Perpetual intermediates need ready access to tools and demand that their frequently used working set be placed front and center in the interface, easy to find and remember.
Perpetual intermediates are reassured by knowing that advanced features exist even when they never use them, which confirms they made the right choice in the product.

ToolTips are an ideal perpetual-intermediate idiom because they state only a control's function in the briefest form while consuming minimal screen space, and index-accessed online help serves intermediates who want to dig deeper.
Deep knowledge of users, context, and constraints needed for design success can only be achieved through qualitative research; quantitative studies alone cannot supply it.

Quantitative research can only answer questions of how much or how many along a few reductive axes, whereas qualitative research reveals what, how, and why in rich detail reflecting the real complexity of human situations.

Qualitative research identifies patterns of user behavior far faster and more easily than quantitative approaches and gives the design team credibility because decisions can be traced to research results.

Begin research for any new product by understanding its business and technical context through stakeholder interviews, conducted before user research because they inform how that user research is carried out.
Interview each stakeholder one-on-one rather than in a cross-departmental group, because a private setting promotes candor and prevents individual views from being lost in the crowd.
Gather from stakeholders the preliminary product vision, budget and schedule, technical constraints and opportunities, business drivers, and their perceptions of the user.

Treat subject-matter-expert input carefully because SMEs represent a skewed perspective: they are often expert users who favor expert controls, may no longer be current users, and are knowledgeable but not designers.
When an SME or user proposes a solution, probe for the underlying causative problem by asking how that solution would help them or the user, rather than adopting the proposed solution directly.

Engage SMEs when designing for complex or specialized domains such as medical, scientific, or financial services to learn best practices and regulations, and secure access to them throughout the design process.
condition: applies to technical or specialized domains

statement: Users and customers are often different people, especially in corporate and technical domains; interview both but factor each group's distinct perspective differently into the design.
Understand and satisfy customers' purchasing goals to make a product viable, while recognizing that customers seldom use the product themselves and use it differently when they do.
Users, the people personally using the product to accomplish a goal, should be the main focus of the design effort, not their managers or support teams.
When refining an existing product, interview both current and potential users to reveal how experience with the current version shapes how users behave and think.
condition: applies when redesigning or refining an existing product

statement: Most people cannot accurately assess their own behavior, especially away from the context of their activities, and may avoid mentioning problematic software behaviors out of fear of seeming incompetent.
Interviews conducted outside the context of the activity yield less complete and less accurate data; observe behavior first-hand rather than relying on what users say they do.

The most effective technique for gathering qualitative user data combines one-on-one interviewing with immersive observation in the user's own environment, letting designers ask clarifying questions about observed behavior in real time.

Keep recording technology unobtrusive during interviews, because obtrusive equipment distracts subjects into behaving differently; a notebook and a camera introduced only after rapport is established usually suffice.
Contextual inquiry uses a master-apprentice model and four principles for ethnographic interviews: context, partnership, interpretation, and focus.
Verify with users any assumptions drawn from interpreting observed facts, rather than acting on the designer's own interpretation of behaviors and statements.
Identify and prioritize user goals before determining the tasks related to those goals, rather than running a fundamentally task-focused research process.

Base the persona hypothesis on likely behavior patterns and the factors that differentiate them, not purely on demographics; when demographics are used to screen interviewees they should serve as a proxy for a hypothesized behavior pattern.

For business products, use roles, the common sets of tasks and information needs of distinct user classes, as an initial organizing principle for the persona hypothesis, since roles map roughly to job descriptions.
condition: applies to business and technical products

statement: For consumer products, roles are often not a meaningful organizing principle; the significant patterns instead emerge from users' attitudes and aptitudes as manifested in their behaviors.
condition: applies to consumer products

statement: Distinguish technical expertise from domain expertise; if domain-naive users are in the target market, provide domain support in the interface, because a naive user can otherwise use only a small subset of a domain-specific product.
condition: applies when domain-naive users are part of the target market

statement: Each hypothesized behavior pattern or variable requires roughly four to six interviews to verify or refute, but interviews can overlap by mapping several variables onto one interviewee-screening profile to keep the total manageable.

Prefer a team of two designers per interview, one driving and taking light notes and one taking detailed notes, about one hour per user, and limit interviews to roughly six per day to leave time for debriefing and avoid interviewer fatigue.

Interview subjects where they actually use the product and observe the environment closely for clues to tasks they did not mention, such as papers, adhesive notes, cheat sheets, and inbox/outbox contents.
Avoid a fixed questionnaire in ethnographic interviews because you do not yet know enough to presuppose the right questions; keep types of questions and a topic checklist in mind instead.

Guide interviewees toward examining their problems and away from proposing solutions, because user-proposed solutions tend to be shortsighted and idiosyncratic; when a user offers an idea, ask what problem it would solve.
exception: a proposed solution can still be a useful jumping-off point to discuss the user's goals and problems

statement: Steer interviews away from discussions of product-implementation technology, distinguishing domain technology from product technology, and redirect an insistent subject back to goals by asking how it would help them.
Encourage users to tell specific stories about their real experiences with a product, covering typical and exceptional cases, rather than asking them for design advice.
Avoid leading questions in interviews, such as asking whether feature X would help or whether the user likes X, because they bias the subject toward the suggested answer.
After each interview compare notes and revisit earlier notes to strategize the next interviews, and after the whole cycle make a pass marking trends and patterns to feed persona creation.

Qualitative ethnographic research answers product questions at both the big-picture and functional-detail level with relatively small effort and expense, which no other single research technique can claim.

Focus groups are useful for gauging reactions to a product's form and appearance but are weak at revealing what people actually do or why, and because they drive to consensus they stifle the diversity of behavior a designer must accommodate, making them inappropriate as a design tool.

Market segmentation accurately forecasts marketplace acceptance and quantifies a market opportunity, assessing viability, but is an ineffective tool for defining the product that will capitalize on that opportunity.

Market research and qualitative user research complement each other: market research identifies and quantifies the opportunity and helps select interviewees, while qualitative research defines the product and can reinterpret quantitative results.
Usability testing requires a fairly complete, coherent design artifact to test against, so its appropriate place is late in the design cycle to validate a candidate solution rather than at the start.
exception: usability testing at the start of a redesign can still find opportunities for improvement

statement: Usability testing is especially effective at assessing naming, organization, first-time use and discoverability, and task effectiveness, and its measurable results are well suited to comparing specific design variants.

Usability testing predominantly assesses first-time use, and measuring a solution's effectiveness on its fiftieth use, the perpetual intermediate case, is difficult; a diary study is one technique for capturing that longer-term interaction.

Before usability testing, ensure that what you test is actually measurable, that the test is administered correctly, that the results will help correct design issues, and that resources exist to fix the problems observed.

Card sorting reveals one aspect of a user's mental model but assumes the subject has organizational skill and that abstract sorting correlates with product use, which is not always true; debrief the subject and consider sequencing cards by task to strengthen it.

Task analysis develops a detailed understanding of how people currently perform tasks, including why, frequency, cues, dependencies, actions, decisions, and errors, and should be incorporated into ethnographic user interviews.

Because the way people currently perform tasks is often an artifact of obsolete systems and bears little resemblance to how they would be most effective, focus first and foremost on user goals rather than on documented current tasks.

Match each research technique to the appropriate point in the development cycle and do the qualitative heavy lifting up front, which then makes later usability testing a more efficient judge of the design choices made.

To accommodate a diverse audience, design for specific types of individuals with specific needs rather than broadening functionality for everyone, because arbitrarily broad functionality increases cognitive load and navigational overhead for all users and ends up pleasing nobody.

Choose the right individuals to design for, those whose needs best represent a larger set of key constituents, then prioritize them so the most important users' needs are met without compromising the ability to serve secondary users.
Personas are descriptive, composite user models synthesized from observed behavior that give a precise way to think and communicate about how users behave, what they want to accomplish, and why.

Personas help determine what a product should do and how it should behave, provide a common language that keeps the design user-centered, build consensus and commitment, allow the design to be reality-checked at the whiteboard, and inform related marketing and sales efforts.

The vague term 'user' becomes an elastic user that a team bends to justify whatever it wants to build; real users, and the personas representing them, are not elastic but have specific requirements based on their goals, capabilities, and contexts.
Even designing to broad user roles or job titles introduces unproductive elasticity, because a lack of precision about the user leads to a lack of clarity about how the product should behave.

Self-referential design occurs when designers or developers project their own goals, skills, and mental models onto a product, which is appropriate only for a narrow range of products aimed at people like the designer.
Edge cases must be designed and programmed for but should never be the design focus; personas let the team prioritize by asking whether the target persona will ever perform the operation.

Personas must be based on real-world observation, primarily in-context user interviews, so that almost every aspect of a well-developed persona traces back to a user statement or behavior; supplemental data cannot replace direct interviews.
Represent personas as specific individual people because this personification engages the empathy of designers and stakeholders toward the human target of the design.

Personas are context-specific and generally cannot be reused across products, even in a closely linked suite, because similar behavior toward one product does not imply similar behavior toward another; research and develop personas individually per product.
exception: a persona set can serve multiple products only if it is researched against the usage contexts of all of them

statement: Do not confuse persona archetypes with stereotypes; stereotypes reflect designer bias rather than data, and personas built on inadequate research degrade into stereotypical caricatures.

Choose persona demographic characteristics with care so they are typical and believable but not stereotypical, and when data is inconclusive err on the side of gender, ethnic, age, and geographic diversity.

Personas should express exemplary or definitive behaviors within identified ranges of behavior rather than describe an average user, and a product's persona set carves those ranges into discrete clusters of correlated behavior.

Personas must capture motivations in the form of goals, because understanding why a user performs tasks gives designers the power to improve or even eliminate those tasks while still accomplishing the same goal.
Create customer personas to represent buyers who are not users, and served personas to represent people affected by the product without operating its interface, such as patients of a medical device.

User roles are abstractions that do not convey human motivation or context and cannot easily engage empathy, whereas personas express the same behaviors and relationships in terms of goals and narrative so teams grasp design implications in human terms.

Focusing on user roles rather than behavior patterns oversimplifies distinctions, since one persona can cover several roles and one role can contain people who think and act differently; in consumer domains roles are nearly useless as a design tool.

A user profile is equivalent to a persona only if it is generated from ethnographic data; a name, photo, and brief demographic sketch is likely based on a stereotype and is not useful as a design tool.

Market segments are based on demographics and purchasing behavior while design personas are based on usage behavior and motivations; they serve different purposes and seldom map one-to-one, so use segments only as an initial filter to limit interview scope to target markets.

When time or resources prevent rigorous fieldwork, provisional personas built from existing data and designer best guesses are better than no user model, provided they are clearly labeled provisional, drawn as sketches rather than photos, documented, and kept free of stereotypes.
condition: applies only when detailed qualitative research is not feasible

statement: Goals are the drivers behind behaviors, so a persona without goals lacks utility as a design tool; the product's function and behavior must address goals through as few tasks as absolutely necessary, because tasks are only a means and goals are the end.

Infer user goals from qualitative data rather than asking directly, because people cannot articulate their goals accurately; reconstruct goals from observed behaviors, answers, nonverbal cues, and environmental clues, and express each goal as a single simple sentence.
Product design should address Donald Norman's three levels of cognitive and emotional processing: visceral, behavioral, and reflective.

Visceral design is about eliciting the appropriate affect for a context, not about beauty alone, since different products such as an MP3 player and an online banking system require very different emotional responses.

Users initially judge attractive interfaces to be more usable and that belief often persists, so when an interface makes a visceral promise of ease it must deliver on that promise at the behavioral level.

Because behavioral processing uniquely both influences and is influenced by the visceral and reflective levels, the day-to-day behavioral aspects of interaction design should be the primary design focus, with visceral and reflective considerations in supporting roles.

Three types of user goals correspond to Norman's levels: experience goals (visceral, how a user wants to feel), end goals (behavioral, what a user wants to do), and life goals (reflective, who a user wants to be).

Any product that egregiously violates users' experience goals will ultimately fail regardless of how well it achieves other goals, because making users feel stupid or uncomfortable lowers their self-esteem and effectiveness.
End goals must be met for users to think a product is worth their time and money, so interaction designers should use end goals as the foundation for a product's behaviors, tasks, look, and feel.

Addressing users' life goals in addition to their end goals is what turns a satisfied user into a fanatically loyal one, even though life goals rarely drive specific interface elements and instead inform overall design, strategy, and branding.
condition: assuming the user's other goals are also met

statement: Nonuser goals such as customer, business, and technical goals must be acknowledged and addressed but must not form the basis of the design direction, and must never be met at the expense of the user.

Technical goals such as running in various browsers, safeguarding data integrity, and cross-platform consistency ease software creation but are not meaningful to a product's success unless they are derived from the need to meet more human-oriented user and business goals.
Good design has meaning only for a person using a product for some purpose, because purposes are inseparable from people.

The most important goals to design for are those of the individuals who actually use the product, so treat a user's personal goals as more significant than those of the corporation that employs her or the IT manager who supports her.
A user's most important goal is always to retain human dignity and not feel stupid.

Do not make the user feel stupid, which is arguably the most important interaction design guideline; a design makes users feel stupid when it lets them make big mistakes, keeps them from getting adequate work done, or bores them.
The essence of good interaction design is devising interactions that achieve the goals of the manufacturer or service provider and their partners without violating the goals of users.

Construct a persona set to represent the diversity of observed motivations, behaviors, attitudes, aptitudes, mental models, workflows, environments, and frustrations, filling gaps in interview data with supplemental research from SMEs, stakeholders, and literature.

The persona construction process has seven steps: identify behavioral variables, map interview subjects to those variables, identify significant behavior patterns, synthesize characteristics and goals, check for redundancy and completeness, expand the descriptions, and designate persona types.

Identify user archetypes from behavioral variables, chiefly activities, attitudes, aptitudes, motivations, and skills, rather than from demographics, and expect roughly 15 to 30 such variables per enterprise role.
