Map each interview subject against each behavioral variable, focusing on where subjects cluster relative to one another rather than on any subject's precise absolute position on a scale.

A significant behavior pattern is a cluster of subjects across roughly six to eight variables, and it is valid only when there is a logical or causative connection between the clustered behaviors, not a spurious correlation.

Synthesize personas by sticking to observed behaviors, because too much fictional idiosyncratic biography distracts and makes personas less credible; you are creating a design tool, not a character sketch for a novel.

Synthesize each persona's goals by inferring them from the logical connections between its behaviors and from answers to goal-oriented questions, keeping only goals that relate to the product being designed.

Expect most personas to carry about three to five end goals, zero or one life goal, and zero to two experience goals, with general experience goals like not feeling stupid and not wasting time taken as implicit.
The precision of detail in a persona description must not exceed the depth of the underlying research, because a detailed description implies a corresponding level of observational accuracy.

Each persona must differ from all others in at least one significant behavior; eliminate or sharpen personas that vary only by demographics to keep the persona set complete yet as compact a design target as possible.

Expand each persona into a one-to-two-page third-person narrative synthesizing the most important research findings and a brief day in the life, so the persona becomes an effective communication tool that carries the research into design.

Remember that personas are design and decision-making tools rather than an end in themselves, because too much embellishment and theatre can make them seem a fluffy waste of time and reduce their usefulness as user models.
Focus the design for each interface on a single primary persona, whose needs and goals can be completely satisfied by that interface without disenfranchising the other personas.
There are six persona types, typically designated in order: primary, secondary, supplemental, customer, served, and negative.

Allow only one primary persona per interface; if no clear primary persona emerges, either the product needs multiple interfaces each with its own primary or the product is trying to accomplish too much.

Design first for the primary persona and then adjust to accommodate secondary personas without upsetting the primary; more than three or four secondary personas signals that the product's scope may be too large and unfocused.

Use negative personas to communicate the specific user types the product is deliberately not built to serve, such as technology-savvy early adopters for consumer products or IT specialists for business-user enterprise products.

Interaction design based primarily on workflow tends to yield a business implementation model that captures all the functionality but little of the humanity, just as implementation-model software mirrors internal technical structure; and translating paper artifacts directly to digital without goal analysis usually causes usability issues.

Narrative is a powerful creative design method: imagining a story about a person using the product leverages creativity more than imagining screen elements alone, and experiences structured around a story are more comprehensible and engaging for users.

In requirements definition, keep design solutions at the level of sketchy plot points, because putting too much detail into storyboards wastes resources and tends to tie the team to suboptimal ideas simply because they were expensive to draw.

Personas are the ingredient that makes scenarios work as a design tool: a persona is a tangible agent that models goals rather than only tasks, broadening scenarios to answer product-definition questions such as what the product should do and how it should behave.

Persona-based scenarios are concise narratives of personas using a product to achieve specific goals, letting design begin from an ideal experience described from the persona's perspective rather than from technology or business goals.

Goal-Directed Design employs three types of persona-based scenario with successively more interface-specific focus: context scenarios explore high-level needs before any design, key path scenarios describe the most significant interactions in the design's vocabulary, and validation scenarios test the solution with what-if questions.

Persona-based scenarios and use cases serve different functions: use cases exhaustively catalog functional requirements but treat all interactions as equally likely and say nothing about how tasks are presented or prioritized, so they should be deployed only in the later stages of design validation.

Define what the product will do before designing how it looks, behaves, and feels; conflating the what and the how is one of the biggest pitfalls, because proposing a solution before agreeing on the problem leaves no way to evaluate the design's fitness except taste and gut instinct.
Treat requirements as needs, the human and business needs the product must satisfy, rather than as synonyms for features or functions.

Defining the user need rather than jumping to a feature gives the designer extraordinary leverage to create a more compelling product, as when an executive's real need is to spot exceptional situations and trends rather than to read static reports.

Separating the problem from the solution provides maximum flexibility against changing technology, because a clearly defined user need lets designers work with technologists to find the best solution without putting the product definition at risk when implementation hits problems.

The Requirements Definition process has five iterative steps: create problem and vision statements, brainstorm, identify persona expectations, construct context scenarios, and identify requirements, cycling through the last three until the requirements stabilize.

Write a problem statement that reflects a situation needing change for both the personas and the business, and a vision statement that inverts it by leading with user needs and then showing how business goals are met; connecting business issues to usability issues drives stakeholder buy-in.

Brainstorm early mainly to get preconceptions out of your head so you can construct context scenarios open-mindedly; keep the session unconstrained, uncritical, and brief rather than expecting the ideas themselves to be the solution.

Formally record each primary and secondary persona's expectations, including how they think about the basic units of data, as an important source of requirements, so the represented model can be made to match the user's mental model.

Analyze research data for how subjects define and describe objects and actions, the action verbs they use, and which intermediate steps they do not mention, since unmentioned steps are likely unimportant to how they think.

Keep context scenarios broad, shallow, and textual, describing high-level actions from the user's perspective, and do not represent current system behaviors, so the big picture can be mapped before designing specific interactions.

In the early stages of design, pretend the interface is magic to look beyond current constraints, because products that meet goals with the minimum of hassle and intrusion seem almost magical to users, and it is the goal-directed behavior, not the technology alone, that provides that magic.

Extract requirements from context scenarios in the form of objects, actions, and contexts, such as call (action) a person (object) directly from an appointment (context), optionally separated into data, functional, and contextual requirements.

Functional requirements are the operations or actions that must be performed on the system's objects, typically translated into interface controls, and they also define the places or containers where objects and information must be displayed.
After imagining the ideal experience, ground the design in the realistic business, brand and experience, technical, and customer and partner requirements it must satisfy.

The Design Framework defines the overall structure of the user's experience and is composed of an interaction framework, a visual design framework, and sometimes an industrial design framework, with form and behavior designed in concert with each other.

Take a top-down approach to the framework, starting with the big picture and rendering solutions low-fidelity without specific detail, because focusing on pixels, widgets, and specific interactions too early prevents designing a comprehensive framework that all the product's behaviors can fit within.

Render a design solution only in enough detail to provoke engaged consideration; sketchlike storyboards with scenario narrative explore solutions without undue overhead, and research shows pencil-like sketches encourage discourse and signal work in progress.

Define the interaction framework in six iterative steps: define form factor, posture, and input methods; define functional and data elements; determine functional groups and hierarchy; sketch the framework; construct key path scenarios; and check designs with validation scenarios.

Define the product's form factor, posture, and input methods first, driven by usage context and the personas' attitudes and aptitudes, and where multiple input methods apply choose a single primary one; look to personas and scenarios when the right choice is not obvious.

Define each functional and data element as a concrete interface representation that responds to a specific earlier requirement, so that every aspect of the product traces back to a usage scenario or business goal.
Comprehensively catalog the data objects because the product's functionality is commonly defined in relation to them, and consider the containment and associative relationships between data elements.
A single requirement commonly necessitates multiple interface elements, so expect to generate several candidate functional elements for one need.

Pretend the system is a person to structure interaction-level details, because interactions with a digital system should be similar in tone and helpfulness to interactions with a polite, considerate human; keep asking what a helpful human would do.

Apply general interaction principles and specific interaction patterns when translating requirements into functional elements, because neglecting them wastes effort re-solving known problems and deviating from standard patterns forces users to learn every idiom from scratch.
Obey established design standards unless you have a very good reason not to.
exception: sometimes it is appropriate to invent new solutions to common problems

statement: Group functional and data elements into functional units and a hierarchy that best facilitates the persona's flow within and between related tasks, placing containers for objects that are compared or used together adjacent, and objects representing steps in a process adjacent and ordered sequentially.

Begin sketching the interaction framework extremely simply in a rectangles phase, subdividing each view into labeled rough rectangular containers with described relationships, and examine the whole top-level framework first without getting distracted by widget-level detail.

Keep early framework renderings low-fidelity because it is easier to discard and try another approach when little effort is invested, whereas spending too much on intricate detail early discourages designers from changing course to a superior solution.

A key path scenario describes the primary, highest-frequency pathways the persona takes through the interface using the framework's vocabulary, evolving from context scenarios with increasing detail while goals remain the constant measuring stick used to trim unnecessary tasks and streamline necessary ones.
Use validation scenarios to poke holes in the design by asking what-if questions, addressing them in order: key path variant scenarios, then necessary use scenarios, then edge case use scenarios.

Necessary-use interactions, which must be performed but only infrequently, demand pedagogy because users may forget them, yet they do not require parallel interaction idioms such as keyboard equivalents nor user customization.

Edge cases must be handled but should never be the focus of the design effort, with their interaction buried deep and low-priority, because the product succeeds or fails on its handling of daily and necessary use even though the code may succeed or fail on edge cases.

Explore a variety of visual treatments through visual language studies of color, type, widgets, and material shown abstractly and independently of the interaction design, so stakeholders assess overall tone without being distracted by highly rendered rough interactions.

Relate visual styles to persona experience goals and brand and experience keywords, and adapt them for environmental factors and persona aptitudes, using high contrast and saturated colors for bright or distant viewing and larger type for sight-impaired users.

Present about three to five visual approaches to stakeholders, unlike interaction design where there is usually one optimal behavioral framework, and include one or two intentionally extreme options to help stakeholders differentiate and decide on a direction.
Never show a design approach that you are not happy with, because stakeholders just might like it and choose it.

There is only one user experience, arising from the combination of physical form and interactive behavior, so form and behavior must be designed in concert, with the demands of interaction guiding industrial design while fabrication and cost concerns constrain it.

Involve the programming team intimately throughout the Refinement phase, because once the design has a solid conceptual and behavioral basis, programmer input is critical to producing a finished design that will actually be built while remaining true to concept.

Deliver a form and behavior specification with screen renderings and callouts detailed enough for a programmer to code from plus storyboards for behavior over time, because prototypes alone rarely communicate the underlying patterns, principles, and rationale that must reach programmers.

Continue to work closely with the construction team throughout implementation, because it requires vigilance to keep the design vision faithfully and accurately translated from the design document into the final product.

Usability testing is a means to evaluate, not to create; it is not an alternative to interaction design and will never be the source of the great idea that makes a product compelling, but rather assesses the effectiveness of ideas already had.

User research must occur before ideation and usability testing after it; when constraints force a choice, time spent on research and on design provides more leverage to create a compelling product than time spent testing.

Evaluate a design before coding begins or early enough to change the implementation, because summative evaluations used as end-of-process quality assurance usually come too late to make meaningful design changes.

Run formative usability tests late enough to have a concrete design yet early enough to adjust it, recruiting from the target population using personas, having participants think aloud on defined tasks with a low-tech prototype, using a neutral moderator, and involving designers throughout.

Design principles are guidelines for creating useful and desirable products and for practicing design ethically, whereas design patterns are exemplary, generalizable solutions to specific classes of design problems.
Interaction design principles operate at several levels of granularity: design values, conceptual principles, behavioral principles, and interface-level principles.

A primary purpose of behavioral and interface-level principles for productivity tools is to minimize the user's work across four kinds, cognitive, memory, visual, and physical, while providing greater feedback and contextually useful information.
condition: applies to productivity and other non-entertainment products; entertainment products may deliberately require the right amount of work

statement: Design solutions should embody four values: ethical (do no harm and improve human situations), purposeful (help users achieve goals and accommodate their contexts and capacities), pragmatic (help the commissioning organization and meet business and technical requirements), and elegant (the simplest complete solution with internal coherence that accommodates cognition and emotion).

Because interactive products actually do things rather than merely persuade, designers must ensure their results do good and minimize interpersonal, psychological, physical, environmental, and social harm.

Purposeful design requires understanding users' limitations as well as their goals, describing their strengths, weaknesses, and blind spots so the product supports users where they are weak and empowers them where they are strong.

Take business goals and technical requirements into account during design, because a design must be built and deployed to be of value, and hold an active dialog among business, engineering, and design about which boundaries are firm and which are flexible.

Do not take everything stakeholders and programmers say at face value, because a claim that a design is impossible often means only that it is impossible given the current schedule; design works best amid mutual trust and respect among design, business, and engineering.

Represent the simplest complete solution by economy of form: use only the screens, widgets, and behaviors necessary and consistent with the personas' mental models, since perfection is attained not when there is nothing left to add but when there is nothing left to take away.

Good design has internal coherence and feels like a unified whole in balance, whereas products built from the implementation model, with teams working on modules without communicating, feel cobbled together from disparate pieces.

Elegance means the user is stimulated and supported both cognitively and emotionally in whatever context she is in, which is broader and more appropriate than appealing to the single narrow emotion of desire, especially for enterprise or technical products.

Design patterns capture and generalize useful design solutions in order to reduce design time and effort on new projects, improve the quality of solutions, facilitate communication between designers and programmers, and educate designers.

Interaction design patterns differ from engineering code patterns by focusing on the human aspects and by concerning not only the structure of elements but their dynamic behaviors that change in response to both application state and user activity.

When capturing an interaction design pattern, record the context to which it applies, one or more concrete examples, the abstracted features common to those examples, and the rationale for why it is a good solution, then organize patterns into a library by applicable context.

Design patterns are not recipes or plug-and-play components; each implementation differs and context is of absolute importance in defining a pattern's manifest form, which is one reason a general style guide can never substitute for a context-specific design solution.

Interaction design patterns are hierarchically organized into postural patterns that set the product's overall stance, structural patterns that arrange information and functional elements on screen, and behavioral patterns that solve specific widget-level interaction problems.

Building a mental catalog of interaction design patterns is one of the most critical aspects of a designer's education, because leveraging existing solutions lets designers focus effort on new problems rather than reinventing the wheel.

Choosing the right platform, the combination of hardware and software defining form, display, input, connectivity, and data capabilities, is a balancing act that must support the personas' needs and context while fitting the business constraints and technological capabilities.

A product's posture is its behavioral stance, describing how much attention a user will devote and how the product responds; choose it for a specific goal-directed reason based on likely usage contexts, not from the designer's personal preference.

Look-and-feel is a behavioral choice rather than solely an aesthetic one: a product's appearance and behavior should reflect how it is used, and any aesthetic choices should harmonize with its posture.

Define the predominant posture for a product as a whole while also considering the posture of individual features and usage contexts, since a product such as a word processor can be sovereign overall yet contain transient tools like a table constructor.

Make technical platform decisions, particularly hardware, in concert with and after interaction design rather than well in advance, and inform management that platform choices will be much more effective when made after interaction designers complete their work.
Optimize sovereign applications, which monopolize the user's attention for long continuous full-screen periods, for perpetual intermediate users rather than for beginners or experts.
condition: applies to sovereign-posture applications

statement: Be generous with screen real estate for a sovereign application and default it to a maximized, full-screen presentation while keeping it fully resizable, because no other application competes for the user's attention.
condition: applies to sovereign-posture applications

statement: Use a conservative, minimal visual style for sovereign applications because users stare at them for hours, favoring a narrow color palette and small accents over big colorful controls that look appealing to newcomers but grow garish with daily use.
condition: applies to sovereign-posture applications

statement: Sovereign applications benefit from rich modeless visual feedback and rich input, making every frequently used function controllable several ways and revealing status information subtly so intermediates discover it over time without cluttering the interface.
condition: applies to sovereign-posture applications

statement: Map control placement to usage by putting the most frequently used controls front and center and segregating infrequent or visually dislocating controls to the screen edges, so novices do not trigger them accidentally while experienced users can discover them.
Maximize document views within sovereign applications by default unless the user explicitly instructs otherwise or needs to work in several documents at once to accomplish a task.
condition: applies to sovereign, document-centric applications

statement: A transient-posture application presents a single function briefly, so its interface must be simple, clear, and obvious, spelling out what it does with big clearly labeled buttons rather than artistic but ambiguous icons, because users never grow familiar with it.
condition: applies to transient-posture applications

statement: A transient application usually supports a sovereign one, so it must take no more screen space than absolutely necessary, though the controls on its surface can be proportionally larger and bolder because it is not onscreen long enough for bold graphics to tire the user.
condition: applies to transient-posture applications

statement: Build instructions into a transient application's surface using verb-object button captions such as set up user preferences, avoid abbreviations, and give direct explicit feedback, because a user may see the application only rarely and forget the meaning of its choices.
condition: applies to transient-posture applications

statement: Limit a transient application to a single window and view and never force the user into supporting subwindows or dialog boxes for its main function; needing to add a dialog or second view is a sign the design needs review.
condition: applies to transient-posture applications

statement: Give applications a memory: a transient application should relaunch to its previous size, position, and configuration, which is almost always more appropriate than any default setting.
Almost all dialog boxes are really transient applications, so the guidelines for transient applications apply equally to the design of dialog boxes.

Because any interaction with a daemonic background application is transient in nature, apply the transient-design imperatives, and take extra care that status messages from an otherwise invisible daemon are presented in context so they do not confuse or dislocate the user.
condition: applies to daemonic-posture applications

statement: Display a daemon's persistent icon only when it provides continuous useful status information, and hide daemonic icons that are not actively reporting status or offering functionality.

Provide a consistent place such as a control panel to configure daemonic applications, and give direct in-line access to a daemon whenever an issue with it blocks the user from accomplishing a goal, without interrupting the user unnecessarily.

The ability to deliver complex behavior in a browser demands application-quality interaction design, because a visual designer's focus on look-and-feel and an information architect's focus on content structure are not sufficient to create an effective, engaging experience.

Web offerings form a spectrum: informational sites mainly involve searching and clicking and rarely need interaction designers, transactional sites add functional elements with complex behaviors and need both information architecture and interaction design, and Web applications are heavily interactive like desktop applications.

Let an informational site's balance of sovereign and transient attributes be set by how frequently its target personas visit: give real-time, heavily revisited content a more sovereign full-screen stance and infrequently referenced content a more transient, navigation-clear stance.

Optimize Web screen designs for common display sizes, accommodating the lowest common denominator appropriate for the primary persona, and use quantitative research to decide which resolutions those personas actually have.

On e-commerce and transactional sites a user's perception of page load time correlates more closely with whether she is able to achieve her goal than with the actual load time, so avoid forcing users to navigate more than necessary.

Web applications are neither easier nor faster to build than desktop applications and are not inherently more usable, because designing a good user experience for any platform requires careful, hard work that delivery through a browser does not provide for free.

Design sovereign Web applications like desktop applications rather than collections of pages, using a full-screen, densely populated interface with grouped panes and minimized redrawing, so users feel they are in an environment rather than navigating from page to page.
condition: applies to sovereign-posture Web applications

statement: To capitalize on internet information and collaboration without the browser's constraints, build a non-browser Internet-enabled native application on a standard desktop platform that communicates over standard internet protocols and APIs, delivering a far superior user experience than a browser could.

When designing any embedded system, keep seven principles in mind: don't think of your product as a computer, integrate hardware and software design, let context drive the design, use modes judiciously, limit the scope, balance navigation with display density, and customize for your platform.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Do not think of an embedded product as a computer: avoid bringing desktop idioms and terminology to a simple device, because users expect quick direct access to domain data and controls, not to wade through a computer operating system or file system.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Design an embedded system's hardware and software interface and the interactions between them simultaneously from a goal-directed, ergonomic, and aesthetic perspective, rather than letting hardware teams hand off finished mechanical designs for software to accommodate.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Let environmental context drive embedded-system design so the interface matches how and where the device is actually used, since users are often mobile, distracted, or in public; for example, a car dashboard must not use context-changing soft-keys that force the driver to look away from the road.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Use modes judiciously or not at all in embedded systems, and when a mode is truly necessary make it clearly accessible with an immediately clear exit path, preferring mode switches that result naturally from situational changes in context such as an incoming call.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Limit the scope of an embedded system to a specific set of tasks done well rather than turning it into a general-purpose computer, because users are better served by a device that does a limited set of tasks more effectively than by one that addresses too many disparate tasks.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: Approach the design of a device that shares information with a desktop as a satellite or extension of that desktop, providing key information and functions in contexts where the desktop is unavailable, and use scenarios to determine which functions are truly useful on the satellite.

On display-constrained devices, balance navigation against display density by building an information hierarchy that makes the most important information most prominent, avoiding blinking between values, and showing the state of associated hardware controls.
condition: applies to display-constrained embedded systems

statement: Limit and simplify input on embedded systems because every embedded input mechanism is cumbersome compared to a full keyboard and mouse; on kiosks avoid complex text input and dragging, favoring large single-tap targets.
condition: applies to embedded systems

statement: For handheld devices, strive to integrate functionality to minimize navigation, guided by context scenarios, because convergence devices that attempt to do too much risk pleasing nobody.
condition: applies to handheld devices

statement: Use physical models reflecting a handheld's size, shape, articulation, and weight within context and key path scenarios to validate its form factor and to decide whether it supports one-handed or two-handed operation.
condition: applies to handheld devices

statement: Design most handheld data devices as satellites of a desktop system geared toward accessing and viewing information with lightweight input, while standalone devices such as cell phones succeed by focusing on a narrow set of functions with world-class behaviors.
condition: applies to handheld devices

statement: Avoid floating and pop-up windows on small low-resolution handheld screens; interfaces should resemble sovereign full-screen applications, and modeless dialogs should be avoided entirely.
condition: applies to handheld devices

statement: Cell phones and satellite handhelds take a transient interface posture, and because a phone user abandons the interface for the conversation, the best phone interface is arguably nonvisual, using voice activation to place a call and a flip lid to answer.
condition: applies to phones and satellite handheld devices

statement: Design kiosks for users who are at best infrequent or one-time users, usually in a public and distracting environment without a keyboard or pointing device, arriving with either one very specific goal or none at all.
condition: applies to kiosks

statement: Distinguish transactional kiosks, whose users have a specific goal to accomplish as quickly as possible, from explorational kiosks, whose users have open-ended expectations and must be engaged by an aesthetically and audibly interesting experience that encourages further exploration.
condition: applies to kiosks

statement: Plan kiosk placement and wayfinding jointly with interaction and industrial design: place transactional kiosks in visible, high-traffic, secure locations, and place explorational kiosks with room for groups to gather near but not obstructing the main attraction.
condition: applies to kiosks

statement: On touch-screen kiosks, make click targets large enough to hit with a finger, at least about 20mm when users are close and unhurried and larger at arm's length or in a rush, and keep them high-contrast and well-separated to avoid accidental selection.
condition: applies to touch-screen interfaces

statement: On touch screens use soft-keyboard input only for very small amounts of text, and avoid drag-and-drop and unnecessary scrolling, because casual kiosk users will never spend enough time to master demanding interaction idioms.
condition: applies to touch-screen kiosks

statement: When hardware buttons are mapped to onscreen functions, keep the mapping consistent by assigning similar functions to the same buttons from screen to screen and placing buttons close enough to the screen that the mapping stays clear.

Optimize kiosks for first-time use and bias them toward transient posture with simple navigation, large colorful engaging interfaces, and clear control affordances, integrating any information into a single full screen rather than using floating windows or dialogs.
condition: applies to kiosks

statement: For transactional kiosks, contextual orientation that shows users where they are in their process matters more than global navigation, and the kiosk should provide escape hatches to cancel a transaction and start over at any point.
condition: applies to transactional kiosks

statement: For television-based interfaces, use a layout and visual design readable from across the room with larger text, keep onscreen navigation simple and mappable to a five-way controller with visual wayfinding, and keep remote controls as simple as possible without dividing the user's attention between the TV and a remote's own display.
condition: applies to television-based interfaces

statement: Organize control of a home-entertainment or multi-device system around user activities such as watch a movie rather than around individual product functions or the device topology, translating the activity into the appropriate device-level command sequence.

For automotive interfaces, minimize time the driver's hands are off the wheel, enforce a consistent layout across screens, use direct labeled control mappings and knobs over button sets, keep mode switching to a single fixed-location press, and provide non-distracting audible feedback, because confusing interactions endanger everyone on the road.
condition: applies to automotive interfaces

statement: Treat appliance interfaces as transient posture, presenting the simplest interfaces possible for non-technical users who want a specific task done, preferring familiar hardware dials and buttons with tactile, audible, and visual feedback rather than cramming in unwanted features on a touch screen.
condition: applies to appliance interfaces

statement: For audible interfaces, organize and name functions by user mental models with the most common options first, and after every action signpost the currently available functions, offer a way back one step and to the top level, provide a way to reach a human, and give the user enough time to respond.
condition: applies to audible and voice interfaces

statement: Make the platform and posture among the first decisions in designing an interactive product, because many poorly designed products suffer from never consciously deciding what technical platform and behavioral posture best meet user and business needs.

Flow is a state of deep, nearly meditative concentration in which people are extremely productive, so design interactive products to promote and enhance flow and go to great pains to avoid any flow-disturbing behavior.

The ultimate user interface for most purposes is no interface at all, so no matter how appealing an interface is, less of it would be better, because directing attention to the interaction emphasizes the side effects of the tools over the user's goals.
condition: holds for pragmatic, goal-oriented software rather than games or creative or content-delivery tools

statement: Well-orchestrated user interfaces are transparent: when a product interacts well, the interaction mechanics disappear and leave the person face to face with their objectives, unaware of the intervening software, just as good prose makes the writer's craft invisible.

Harmonious interaction cannot be reduced to fixed numeric rules such as a maximum number of buttons; any judgment must take into account the problem being solved and what the person is doing and trying to accomplish at the time.

Fifteen strategies drive harmonious interaction: follow users' mental models; less is more; enable users to direct rather than discuss; keep tools close at hand; provide modeless feedback; design for the probable and provide for the possible; provide comparisons; provide direct manipulation and graphical input; reflect object and application status; avoid unnecessary reporting; avoid blank slates; differentiate command from configuration; provide choices; hide the ejector-seat levers; and optimize for responsiveness while accommodating latency.

Follow users' mental models by organizing and indexing information the way the target user thinks about it, such as sorting a clinician's view by patient name but a billing clerk's view by how overdue a bill is.
Less is more in interface design: constantly strive to reduce the number of interface elements without reducing the product's capabilities, doing more with less through careful orchestration.

Avoid interfaces that are complex but not powerful, which silo functionality so a user performs one task without access to related tasks; instead offer related functions in context so users are not forced to shuffle between separate windows to accomplish common work.

A minimalist product design is inextricably tied to a clear understanding of purpose, what the user is trying to accomplish, because without that sense of purpose an interactive product is just a disorganized jumble of technological capabilities.
The quest for simplicity can be taken too far, because reduction is a balancing act requiring understanding of users' mental models, and excessive visual simplicity can create cognitive complexity.

Enable users to direct rather than forcing them to discuss: the ideal interaction is like using a tool such as a car or hammer, where the user gives direction and receives direct feedback, not a dialogue in which the software interrogates the user.
The better, more flow-inducing interfaces are generally those with plentiful and sophisticated direct-manipulation idioms that let users point to what they want and move it directly.

Keep tools close at hand, on palettes or toolbars for beginner and intermediate users and via keyboard commands for experts, so a user selects a tool with a single click or keystroke without diverting attention, and never require the user to put tools away.

Provide modeless feedback by building status and effect information into the structure of the interface so it does not stop the normal flow of activity, rather than interrupting the user with a modal dialog box to convey information.

Design for the probable and provide for the possible: segregate the possible from the probable so that the readiness to handle improbable edge cases is not rendered directly into the interface, where rarely used controls would sit beside those used constantly.

Contextualize quantitative information so it answers the question compared to what and shows the data visually, for example a pie chart of disk usage rather than a raw byte count, relegating the exact numbers to supporting labels with reasonable, consistent precision.

Provide direct manipulation and graphical input, not just graphical output, letting users drag a marker or reorder list items directly, for instance setting an indent by dragging a ruler marker or ordering a list by personal preference that no algorithm could compute.

Reflect object and application status so that a busy application looks busy, a sleeping one looks asleep, and the state of interface objects such as unread mail is apparent, communicated best through rich modeless feedback.

Avoid unnecessary reporting: do not burden users with the internal details of what the program is doing, but do the work, issue reassuring clues that all is well, and reserve dialogs for events outside the normal course.

Do not stop the proceedings to report normalcy: never report an expected event with a dialog box, and do not interrupt the user with non-serious problems, instead building an unobtrusive status indicator for issues such as a failed server connection.
Take a goal-directed approach to orchestration by having the application take a good-enough first step the user can then adjust, rather than requiring the user to direct every action in advance.

Avoid blank slates: rather than asking users many questions up front, make a statistically reasonable assumption from past experience and let users adjust it, asking forgiveness rather than permission, since a blank slate is a difficult starting point and it is easier to fine-tune an approximation.

Differentiate command from configuration: invoking a function should simply perform it using previous or standard settings, while a separate configuration command exposes the detailed options, because users invoke a command roughly ten times for every one time they configure it.

Put immediate access to a function on a toolbar button and access to that function's configuration dialog on a menu item, because the configuration dialog is a better pedagogic tool while the button provides immediate action.

Provide choices rather than asking questions, because a question puts the software in a superior interrogating position that makes users feel badgered or inferior, whereas a toolbar quietly offers choices the user can take at will.
Interactive products that ask fewer questions appear smarter, more polite, and more considerate to users, and a question asked repeatedly and unnecessarily is especially irritating.

Because people treat and respond to computers and interactive products as if they were people, pay real attention to the personality your software projects, making it quietly competent and helpful rather than whining, nagging, or making excuses.

Hide the ejector-seat levers: an application's configuration facilities that cause major visual dislocation or irreversible action must be kept away from inexperienced users, and the design must ensure a user can never fire one accidentally while making a minor adjustment.

Optimize interfaces for responsiveness and accommodate latency, because nothing disturbs flow more than waiting; when latency is unavoidable, clearly communicate it, let the user cancel the operation, and ideally let them do other work while waiting.

User perception of response time falls into buckets: up to about 0.1 seconds feels instantaneous, up to about 1 second feels responsive, up to about 10 seconds is clearly slow and needs a progress bar, and beyond about 10 seconds loses attention so the work should run in the background with status, estimated time remaining, and a cancel mechanism.

Excise is the extra cognitive and physical work that satisfies the needs of the tools or outside agents rather than moving the user toward a goal, so eliminate excise wherever possible to make people more effective and productive.
When eliminating excise, do not remove it merely to suit power users, but also do not force power users to pay the full price of the help provided for new or infrequent users.

Facilities added to train beginners, such as step-by-step wizards, become excise once users become perpetual intermediates and therefore must be easily turned off; do not weld training wheels on permanently.

Pure excise, such as asking a user which hardware port to use, benefits nobody from power user to first-timer and should be struck from the interface and replaced with more intelligent behind-the-scenes behavior.

Visual excise is the work of decoding visual information, so over-reliance on visual metaphors and excessive ornamentation become pure excise, especially in sovereign applications, and visual style should primarily support the clear communication of information and interface behavior.
Determine whether a function is excise by comparing it to the personas' goals: work forced on a user rather than offered at his discretion, and not serving a significant persona's goal, is excise.
Do not stop the proceedings with idiocy: interrupting a user's flow for no good reason, such as a needless error or confirmation dialog, is one of the most disruptive forms of excise.

Error and confirmation message dialogs are high in excise and should be eliminated whenever possible, because the typical error box either tells the user something he does not care about or demands he fix a situation the application could fix itself.

Allow input wherever you have output: if a displayed value is user-modifiable, let the user change it right where it is shown rather than asking permission or navigating to a separate place, because the split between input and output is an implementation-model artifact that the user's mental model does not recognize.

Root out common excise traps: do not force users to switch windows for a function affecting the current one, to remember where they filed things, to resize or move windows, to reenter personal settings, to fill fields for arbitrary completeness, to ask permission, or to confirm actions, and do not let their actions result in an error.

Navigation is largely excise, since the work users do to get around software and web sites seldom aligns with their goals, and poorly designed navigation is one of the largest and most common usability problems and the place the implementation model shows most.
condition: except in games where navigating obstacles is itself the goal, and where navigation usefully instructs users about what is available

statement: Navigation among multiple windows, views, or pages is the most disorienting kind because it grossly shifts attention and disrupts flow, so sovereign applications should avoid navigational trauma by placing all main interactions in a single primary view that may contain multiple panes.

Adjacent panes reduce navigation by keeping supporting functions, links, and data within reach of the primary work area, and if objects can be dragged between panes those panes should be placed adjacent to each other.

Putting parts of a single facility onto separate tabbed panes increases excise and decreases users' understanding and orientation, because a tab label rarely describes its contents accurately, forcing users to click through each tab to find what they need.

Tabbed panes are appropriate for a main work area that holds multiple documents or independent views, and for multiple supporting panes that are mutually exclusive and used one at a time, each then a single click away.

Group frequently used tools that are used together spatially and make them immediately available in toolbars or palettes, and reserve menus for infrequently accessed commands, because menu contents are not visible until clicked and so require more navigational effort.

Minimize scrolling and understand the paging-versus-scrolling trade-off from users' mental models, provide orienting cues for the visually dislocating act of following links, and prefer an adjacent supporting pane over logical zoom, which is arcane to most users.

Improve navigation by reducing the number of places to go, providing signposts, providing overviews, providing appropriate mapping of controls to functions, inflecting the interface to match user needs, and avoiding hierarchies.

The most effective way to improve navigation is to reduce the number of places a user must go, keeping windows and views to a minimum such as one full-screen window with two or three views, limiting adjacent panes and controls to the minimum needed for user goals, and minimizing scrolling and zooming.

Provide signposts, the persistent objects such as the main window, menu bars, toolbars, status bars, and a top-level navigation bar that users navigate by, keeping them permanent and visible and making different sections look distinct rather than making every page identical.
Keep menus reliable and consistent, because unexpected changes to a program's menus deeply reduce users' trust in them.
Provide overviews, graphical such as a thumbnail navigator palette or textual such as a breadcrumb trail, to orient users within the content, keeping the overview area itself persistent.

Provide appropriate mapping of controls to functions, using natural spatial mapping and terms that match users' mental models, because poor mapping such as row-arranged knobs for square-arranged burners or Ascending and Descending for dates forces users to stop and think and breaks flow.

Inflect the interface for typical navigation by placing the most frequently used functions and controls in the most immediate and convenient locations while pushing less frequently used functions deeper, without removing them from the program.

By the principle of commensurate effort, users will willingly work harder for something more valuable to them, so an interface must not be complex to achieve simple results but may be complex to achieve complex results that are not needed often.

Organize controls and displays by three attributes: frequency of use, putting frequent items immediately in reach and rarer ones a click or two away; degree of dislocation, putting disruptive functions deeper; and degree of risk exposure, making irreversible or dangerous functions harder to stumble across.
Provide shortcuts for experienced users who will seek them, since commensurate-effort design does not remove the learning curve but makes it disappear from the user's mind.

Avoid presenting abstract hierarchies in the interface, because they are very difficult for users to navigate except when based on the user's mental model with truly mutually exclusive categories; monocline grouping, a single level of nesting, is the storage model most people actually bring to software.

Render a storage structure the way users imagine it, as monocline grouping, while providing the search and access tools that only a deep hierarchy offers, so that appropriate information is brought to users rather than forcing them to navigate deep tree structures.

Because people unconsciously treat sufficiently interactive software as sentient, design a product to behave like a likeable, supportive human colleague if you want users to like it and be productive with it.
The ideal division of labor in the computer age is that the computer does the work of information management while the person does the thinking and decision making.

Design software to be considerate, genuinely concerned with the user's goals and needs, rather than merely polite, because inconsiderate products that hoard information, hide their processes, and blame users irritate people regardless of how many features they have.

Building considerate products is not substantially harder than building rude ones, since it only requires envisioning interactions that emulate a sensitive, caring person, and behaving humanely can be the most pragmatic goal of all.

A considerate product takes an interest by remembering the user's habits and everything the user tells it, rather than gathering a piece of information, discarding it, and asking for it again whenever it is needed.

A considerate product is deferential and submits to the user: it may express an opinion that the user is making a mistake and explain the consequences, but it must not judge or limit the user's actions, which is why a Submit button reverses the proper relationship.

A considerate product is forthcoming, volunteering useful related information beyond the precise question asked, but does so without being obtrusive or interrupting when the user clearly does not want help.

A considerate product uses common sense: it does not place constantly used controls next to never-used irreversible ones, and it alerts a human when a nonsensical event occurs, such as repeatedly issuing a zero-dollar or absurdly large invoice.

A considerate product is conscientious, taking a larger perspective on the task's goal, for example detecting that two files share a name and disambiguating them rather than forcing the user to choose between overwriting and not saving.

A considerate product does not burden the user with its own internal problems, keeping quiet about them while having the intelligence, confidence, and authority to fix them, and keeps the user informed of what matters through rich modeless feedback.

A considerate product is perceptive, observing what users do and remembering their preferences without being asked, so that if a user always maximizes the window or places palettes a certain way, the product adopts that configuration on later launches.
A considerate product is self-confident, standing by its convictions rather than asking Are you sure, while anticipating that the user might change his mind by being prepared to undo the action.

A considerate product fails gracefully, preparing for failure without hurting the user, for example writing downloaded email to local disk before telling the server it succeeded, or preserving a user's valid form entries when one field is rejected.

A considerate product knows when to bend the rules by supporting intermediate suspense states, letting humans perform actions out of sequence or before prerequisites are met, because inflexible all-or-nothing rules cast human and software as adversaries and end up causing bigger mistakes.

A considerate product takes responsibility and shoulders its part of the burden rather than washing its hands after handing work to a hardware device, for example actually canceling a print job at the printer instead of merely claiming the operation was canceled.
A smart product is one that works hard even when conditions are difficult and even when users are not busy, which is a more useful and achievable notion than science-fiction machine intelligence.

Put idle CPU cycles to work proactively rather than letting the processor idle while the user works, because modern computers are powerful enough to make several assumptions in the background and discard the wrong ones once the user chooses.

For a product to be perceived as considerate and smart it must have a memory, a facility for tracking and responding to user actions across multiple sessions, so that the next time you find your application asking the user a question you make it ask itself one instead.

By the principle of task coherence, a user's goals and the tasks by which they achieve them are generally similar from day to day, so remembering what the user did the last several times reliably predicts future behavior and greatly reduces the questions the application must ask.
If it is worth the user entering, it is worth the application remembering: any information a user provides should be retained from run to run rather than discarded.
Use a user's previous setting as the default instead of a hard-wired default, remember any options the user sets until they are manually changed, and do not re-offer features the user has turned off.

Remember the last file location per file type, and remember window position and size, so the user never has to step through the directory tree to a location more than once and windows reappear as they were left.

Remember repeated patterns of user actions, such as two formatting steps done together without an intervening selection, and offer to turn them into a new style or control, since configuration of defaults is too onerous for all but power users.
Remember essentially everything the user does, because storage is cheap; a kilobyte of execution notes per run accumulates to only a couple of megabytes over a year of daily use.

Remember deduced information such as a file's typical changed-byte count and use it for silent reasonableness checks, keeping a milestone backup copy when an anomaly occurs rather than interrupting the user with a confirmation dialog.

Persist the undo stack across sessions by writing it to a file, so that reopening a document restores the actions the user could still undo from previous sessions, rather than discarding the undo history on close.
Reduce user errors by remembering and auto-filling past data entries and standard field values, because the fewer fields a user must retype, the fewer opportunities there are for typing mistakes.

By decision-set reduction, people reduce an infinite set of choices to a small repeating set, so remember more than one previous choice, because remembering only the single last choice is guaranteed to be wrong when the user alternates between exactly two options.

By preference thresholds, only a few of the many decisions in an activity are important, so do not ask users for successively detailed decisions but make reasonable assumptions and remember them, offering the options dialog only for the settings a user actually wants to control.

Because task coherence predicts behavior with reasonable but not absolute certainty, have the application do what it thinks is most appropriate and let users override or undo it, rather than offering a choice that would needlessly bother the majority for whom the prediction is correct.
condition: depends on providing a sufficiently easy-to-use undo facility

statement: Metaphors, especially physical and spatial ones, have an extremely limited place in software design, because there are not enough good metaphors, they do not scale, users' recognition of them is questionable across cultures, and strict adherence needlessly ties an interface to the limitations of the physical world.

Three paradigms dominate interface design: implementation-centric, based on understanding how the software works internally, metaphoric, based on intuiting how it works, and idiomatic, based on learning how to accomplish things, and the idiomatic paradigm is the most natural and human.
Avoid implementation-centric interfaces that force users to learn how the program works internally in order to use it, because most people would rather be successful than knowledgeable.

Avoid org-chart-centric products and web sites that organize information by how the company is structured rather than by how users think, because like implementation-centric interfaces they force users to understand internal structure to find what they want.
Metaphors do not scale well, because a metaphor that works for a simple process in a simple program often fails as that process grows in size or complexity.
Metaphors rely on associations shared by designer and user, so they fail when the user lacks the designer's cultural background and can be ambiguous even within a shared culture.

A metaphor offers a small learnability boost to first-time users but exacts a tremendous cost once they become intermediates, because reflecting the physical world of mechanisms permanently limits the power of the software.

Idiomatic design focuses not on technical knowledge or intuition of function but on the learning of simple, nonmetaphorical visual and behavioral idioms, which the human mind can pick up and remember quickly and easily.

Most elements of so-called intuitive graphical interfaces, such as windows, title bars, close boxes, screen-splitters, hyperlinks, drop-downs, and the mouse, are actually learned idiomatically rather than intuited metaphorically.
All idioms must be learned, but good idioms need to be learned only once, because the human mind picks up distinctive idioms from a single exposure.

Good metaphors are hard to find, since it is easy to find visual metaphors for physical objects but difficult or impossible to find them for the processes, relationships, services, and transformations that are software's most frequent uses.

Global metaphors, single overarching metaphors that frame all others, tie interfaces to Mechanical-Age artifacts and add navigation overhead, and the belief that lower-level metaphors gain cognitive benefit merely by being consistent with the global one is mistaken.

Extending a metaphor snares both parties: once the user depends on the metaphor for recognition he expects consistency with the real-world object, which tempts the designer to render the software in terms of its obsolete mechanical referent and usually makes it worse.

Never bend your interface to fit a metaphor: design idiomatically and use a metaphor only when a truly appropriate and powerful one falls in your lap, because there is an infinity of idioms to invent but only a limited set of metaphors to discover.

The Macintosh succeeded not because of its desktop metaphors but because of overall attention to design and detail: a tightly restricted mouse-based vocabulary, direct manipulation of rich visual objects, and high-resolution WYSIWYG output.

A properly formed interaction vocabulary is an inverted pyramid of primitives such as pointing, clicking, and dragging, compounds built by combining primitives, and idioms that structure compounds using domain knowledge, and any language that does not follow this form is very hard to learn.

The more atomic elements an interaction vocabulary has, the more time-consuming and difficult it is to learn, so restrict the number of primitives and build more complex interactions from them, the way letters combine into words and sentences.

Manual affordances, the instinctive understanding of how objects are manipulated by hand, underlie much visual interface design, and simulated-3D shading and shadows create virtual manual affordances that tell the tool-manipulating brain an element can be pushed.

A virtual manual affordance shows only that an element can be manipulated, not what it does, so controls must carry text or iconic labels, because software cannot be inspected like a mechanism and its function can only be learned.

Rendering a control makes a contract with the user that it will respond visually when actuated and perform reasonable work accurately described by its legend, so deliver on the expectations set by manual affordances and never offer bait-and-switch affordances.

Effort spent understanding users and crafting behaviors falls short unless significant work also goes into clearly communicating those behaviors to users, which for interactive products commonly happens visually through a display.

Visual interface design is a critical, unique discipline to be conducted in concert with interaction and industrial design, not an afterthought or mere skinning, because it strongly influences a product's effectiveness and appeal.

Unlike artists who pursue self-expression, visual designers create artifacts for other people and are concerned with clear communication, finding the representation best suited to conveying the specific behavior and information of the product.

Place aesthetic concerns within a functional framework and minimize questions of taste, using clear articulation of user experience goals and business objectives to guide even the brand and visceral aspects of the visual interface.

A visual interface designer must understand behavior more deeply than a graphic designer, matching the visual structure of the interface to the logical structure of the users' mental models and the program's behaviors, and communicating program states and visual hierarchy.

Meaning in a visual composition arises from similarity and contrast of properties: when two objects share properties users assume they are related, and the items with the greatest contrast demand attention.

Shape is the primary way we recognize what an object is, but distinguishing among shapes takes higher attention than properties like color or size, so shape is not the best property to contrast when the purpose is to capture attention.

Size is an ordered and quantitative variable that people automatically read as a hierarchy of importance, and sufficient size contrast draws attention quickly, making size useful for conveying information hierarchy.

Use hue judiciously with a limited number of colors to avoid a carnival effect that overwhelms users, and do not rely on hue as the sole communication vector, because hue is not intrinsically ordered and color-blindness is common.

Texture is seldom useful for conveying differences or calling attention because it demands attention and pixels, but it is an important affordance cue, since ridges or bumps suggest an element is draggable and a bevel or drop shadow makes a button seem clickable.

Visual interfaces should use visual properties to group elements and create clear hierarchy, provide visual structure and flow at each level of organization, use cohesive and consistent imagery, integrate style and function purposefully, and avoid visual noise and clutter.

Create visual hierarchy by ranking controls and data from scenarios into what users need instantly, what is secondary, and what is needed only by exception, then distinguishing levels with hue, saturation, value, size, and position so the most important elements are larger, higher-contrast, more saturated, and outdented.

Adjust hierarchy properties with restraint, since varying just one property often suffices, and prefer turning down the less important element rather than turning up the more important one to preserve headroom for emphasizing critical elements.

A good visual hierarchy is almost never noticed by users; it is only the lack of one and the accompanying confusion that jumps out, so establishing a clear hierarchy is one of the hardest and most important challenges in visual interface design.

Group elements that are used together spatially to minimize mouse movement and group elements with similar functions visually, using differences in proximity and whitespace rather than heavy-handed bounding boxes, while emphasizing differences between groups and minimizing differences within a group.

Use the squint test, closing one eye and squinting at the screen, to see which elements pop out, which are fuzzy, and which group together, revealing previously undetected issues in layout, hierarchy, and balance.

Align visual elements so that every element aligns with as many others as possible, aligning labels, controls within a set, and control groups across panes to a regular grid, and make any decision not to align a deliberate choice for a specific differentiating effect.

Use a modular grid system with an atomic grid unit so all spacing is in multiples of it and screen areas relate by consistent ratios, being decisive by making near-fractions exact, which improves usability, aesthetic appeal, and production efficiency.

Lay out the interface to structure an efficient logical path for the eye, taking into account that in Western languages the eye moves from top to bottom and left to right, and use symmetry or balanced visual weight so the display does not look lopsided.

Use cohesive, consistent, and contextually appropriate imagery grounded in the personas' mental models, and understand the visual language of the users' culture and domain, since colors, gestures, and symbols carry different meanings across cultures and specialized fields.

Make similar visual elements share visual attributes such as position, size, line weight, and style, contrasting only what is important to differentiate their meaning, so the elements integrate into a cohesive whole.

Design function-oriented icons to represent both the action and the object acted upon, since nouns and verbs are easier to comprehend together than verbs alone, and rely on idioms plus ToolTips or labels for abstract concepts while keeping icons simple and reusing elements.
Visually distinguish elements that behave differently, and use a consistent symbol wherever an object type appears, so that users can navigate to the object faster than text labels alone would allow.

Keep icons simple and schematic with few colors and a modest size, because photorealistic icons draw undue attention to themselves, render poorly at small sizes, and reduce the visual cohesion of the interface.

Visually communicate function and behavior by rendering an illustrative picture, diagram, or preview of the result in addition to text, as with Print Preview, because a visualization clearly conveys consequences that words alone cannot.

Control stylized visual elements carefully, especially in sovereign applications, letting the shape, behavior, and affordance of controls drive the visual style so that purely aesthetic considerations never interfere with the meaning of the interface or the user's ability to interact.
condition: stylistic experimentation is more acceptable in educational or entertainment applications provided basic affordances are preserved

statement: Because brand value is the sum of all interactions people have with a company, the verbal, visual, and behavioral brand messages must be consistent, and a stunning visual design counts for nothing if the user cannot get the answer she needs.

By the Aesthetic-Usability Effect, people perceive more aesthetically pleasing designs as easier to use regardless of actual functionality, so a strong first impression aids usability, but long-term brand equity is built only by delivering behavior consistent with that first impression.

Avoid visual noise and clutter such as over-dimensional elements, heavy separators, insufficient whitespace, and overuse of color, texture, and contrast, because visually baroque or overcrowded screens raise cognitive load and interfere with users' speed, comprehension, and success.

Keep interfaces simple by using simple geometric forms, a restricted palette of mostly neutral colors with a few high-contrast accents, one or two typefaces at a few sizes, and consistent rendering of related elements so understanding transfers between them by inheritance.

Treat unnecessary variation as the enemy of coherent, usable design: make nearly equal spacing or type sizes exactly equal, ensure every visual difference exists for a reason, and remove any element whose presence you cannot justify.

Make visual interfaces visually efficient by experimentally removing individual elements to test their contribution, taking things away until the design breaks and then putting that last thing back in.
Avoid setting interface text in all capital letters, because people recognize letters by their shape and the familiar pattern-matching cues are absent in all-caps text, which makes it harder to read.

Minimize the text a user must read to navigate by representing what an object is with a visual symbol and using text only to tell which particular object it is, following the rule of visually show what and textually tell which.

Use high-contrast text of roughly 80 percent against its background in a crisp sans-serif typeface at 10 pixels or larger, phrase it with the fewest words needed for clear meaning, and avoid nonstandard abbreviations.

Avoid the common color misuses: too many colors, since search performance degrades at about seven or more; saturated complementary colors that cause chromostereopsis; excessive saturation; inadequate contrast when objects and background differ only in hue; and inadequate attention to color-blindness, which affects roughly 10 percent of males.

Follow Tufte's information-design principles for data displays: enforce visual comparisons, show causality, show multiple variables, integrate text, graphics, and data in one display, ensure content quality, show things adjacent in space rather than stacked in time, and do not de-quantify quantifiable data.

Ensure the quality, relevance, and integrity of displayed content: do not show information merely because it is technically possible, because unreliable or poor-quality information damages the trust you must build with users.

When showing change over time, present the states adjacently in space rather than superimposed on one another, as a cartoon strip does, though in software animation can also show change over time effectively.
Do not de-quantify quantifiable data: use graphs and charts to make trends easy to grasp but continue to display the actual numbers alongside them.

Consistency and a single interface standard improve users' ability to learn interfaces and raise throughput while reducing errors, and also benefit vendors by cutting training, support, development, and maintenance costs, because users can predict behavior from past experience.

A product following an interface standard is only as good as that standard, and most standards address the syntax and visual look-and-feel of the interface but say little about its deeper behavior or higher-level logical structure, because a general standard incorporates no knowledge of context.

Treat interface standards as detailed guidelines or rules of thumb that must evolve as technology and understanding of users evolve, because following guidelines too rigidly force-fits an application into an inappropriate interaction model.

Obey standards unless there is a truly superior alternative, and consider the alternative justified only when an idiom is clearly seen to be significantly better by most of the target user audience who try it in real working conditions.

Consistency does not imply rigidity: bend the rules when needed to serve users' goals, making changes compatible with the standard and following the spirit rather than the letter of the law, and do not force completely consistent interfaces across products whose users and goals differ.
Start crafting a data-retrieval solution from a good understanding of users' mental models and usage contexts, then structure storage and retrieval systems that accommodate those specific purposes.

In the digital world, storage and retrieval need not be linked as they are physically, yet most systems only implement the storage system and hand it to the user as the retrieval system, placing the entire burden of finding files on the user's memory.

Folder and directory retrieval is limiting because it requires users to know where an item was stored in order to find it, which is a backward step given that digital systems can provide far better retrieval methods than physical ones.

There are three ways to find a document digitally: positional retrieval by where it was left, identity retrieval by its name, and associative or attribute-based retrieval by some inherent quality, and most digital systems ignore the associative method.

Provide an attribute-based retrieval system so users can find documents by their contents and meaningful properties expressed the way they think, such as the Word documents about a client modified yesterday and printed, rather than depending on memory of location and name.

A retrieval system can automatically remember many document attributes, such as the creating application, format, size, edit, print, fax, and email history, and usage frequency, relieving users of much of the burden of organizing files in advance.
The speed at which search results are returned, achieved by indexing content during idle time, is one of the most important factors in a retrieval feature's usefulness.

Also allow users to tag or manually assign attributes to documents, forming a folksonomy, so they can fill gaps the system cannot detect and define de facto organizational schemes and dynamically overlapping sets, which is especially valuable in social and collaborative contexts.

Relational database technology demands that users define the form of data in advance and then conform to it, but users rarely can express their needs in advance and often change their minds, so unstructured information like email and the Web fails this litmus and needs associative rather than rigidly defined retrieval.

Relational databases store every record as a single predefined type with instances grouped together, which imposes storage order but fails retrieval for unpredictable data such as an email that must be findable under many overlapping identities that can change after it is stored.

Separate the storage system from the retrieval system: keep records in a database-like digital soup that accepts any record and returns a token, and build the retrieval system as an unlimited number of attribute indices each keyed for its own concept.

Fill retrieval indices two ways: automatically extract and index information such as names, addresses, and phone numbers from content, and make it easy for users to add ad hoc pointers through picklists, drag-and-drop, or typing.

Offer users powerful information-management tools without demanding that they configure their information in advance or conform to that configuration later, because they rarely can express their needs ahead of time and often change their minds.

Prefer natural language output over natural language input for attribute-based queries: provide an array of bounded controls that read like an English sentence, letting the user assemble a valid query from a grammar of choices, because reliable natural language input is beyond typical commercial systems.

Use natural language output to spare users Boolean and SQL syntax, joining clauses with plain English phrases like all of the following apply, and design the cascading controls with grammars mapped in advance and with attention to localization for languages with different word order.
Because Undo exists exclusively for humans, who make mistakes, while computers do not need it, model Undo the least like its implementation and the most like the user's mental model.

Treat everything the user does as valid and reasonable rather than as a mistake, abandoning the idea that the user can err, because people do not like to admit mistakes and the software should not contradict that mindset.

The primary purpose of Undo is to support exploration, not merely to reverse errors, because it reassures users and supports their willingness to experiment with a tool the way a rope ladder makes it easier to explore a cave.
Undo supports the necessary condition of trustworthiness rather than directly advancing a user's goal, keeping negative occurrences from spoiling the effort.

Design an Undo facility to satisfy the several mental models users bring, such as a panic button, a deleted-data store, and a stack of reversible operations, to support typically used tools, and to avoid any hint, whether visual, audible, or textual, that Undo signals a user failure.

Undo works best as a global, program-wide function that undoes the last action regardless of how it was performed, so do not remove the ability to undo after a document is saved, and save the undo buffer with the document.

Incremental actions have a data component such as cutting, pasting, typing, and deleting, whereas procedural actions such as reformatting or rotating have only a procedure component, and most Undo functions fail to discriminate between them.
