Explanatory Undo, which labels the specific operation to be reversed such as Undo Typing design, is generally much more pleasant than blind Undo, and a ToolTip is a good compromise for conveying it on a toolbar control.

Single Undo is effective because it is simple, clear, and easy to remember, and its absence is sometimes enough for users to abandon a product, but it fails when a later trivial action short-circuits recovery of an earlier important one.

Multiple Undo built as a strict function-by-function last-in-first-out stack models code and data structures rather than user goals and does not scale to convoluted situations where a user wants to reverse a discontinuous subset of interlaced actions while keeping others.

Recognize that a paired Undo-Redo doubles as a comparison or what-if tool, and consider offering a single Compare control that follows the user's mental model of apply this change versus do not apply it, halving the excise of toggling two commands.

Category-specific incremental Undo, like the Backspace key undoing only typed characters at the cursor while ignoring intervening functions, works well because everything is visible and consistent with the user's mental model, and users would adapt to analogous format- or transformation-specific Undo tools.

Provide a deleted data buffer, an independent browsable repository of everything the user has deleted, in addition to the normal incremental multiple Undo, so a user can recover deleted content directly and randomly rather than reversing every intervening step.

Support versioning by letting users explicitly snapshot the whole document and later revert, and make the revert command list the available versions with metadata such as time, author, size, and notes, saving the current state as a new version when the user reverts.

Distinguish genuinely undo-proof operations, such as a sent email, from the many that only masquerade as undo-proof and are really reversible, such as renaming a file, and audit your application for functions that should be undoable but are not.

When business rules or institutional policy forbid undoing an action such as a financial transaction or a medical record entry, still support human goals by providing a way to reverse or adjust the action while leaving an audit trail.
condition: applies where regulation or policy forbids deletion

statement: Managing disks and files is not a user goal, so a Save Changes dialog that forces people to confront the internal mechanics of memory versus disk storage makes them think like computers and should be avoided.

A dialog box that is always answered the same way is a redundant dialog box that should be eliminated, as with the Save Changes dialog whose Yes button is clicked orders of magnitude more often than No.

The proper time to reject changes is when the changes are made, using Undo, not when the document is closed, because closing a document and discarding changes have no natural connection in the user's mental model.

The root problem with files and save is faithfully rendering the file system's excellent implementation model as the user interface; many applications need not concern users with files at all, as iTunes and iPhoto let users ignore that files even exist.

The Save As dialog conflates naming and placing a file, demanding file-system knowledge and foresight, yet does not let users rename or relocate the document they are currently editing, and using it to make an archival copy is a trap that can silently discard recent changes.

Users' mental model is that there is only one document and it belongs to them, whereas the file-system implementation model violates both facts by keeping two copies, in memory and on disk, both belonging to the application, so design file interactions to match the single-document mental model.

Hide the file system's existence from users by rendering storage according to their mental models, keeping the disk copy's advantages while freeing users from spending mental energy managing the computer's file system.

Use a unified file model that treats a document as a single thing rather than a copy on disk and a copy in memory, leaving the writing of data between disk and memory to the file system so users never confront the internal mechanisms of the computer.

Save documents and settings automatically: on Close write changes without a confirmation dialog, and also save at intervals during the session, ideally after each change or in the background when the user pauses, while keeping an optional manual save control.
Provide an explicit Create a Copy function that makes an independent copy with a sensible automatic name placed in the same directory, acting quietly without a confirming dialog.

Let users rename a document in place by clicking its name on the title bar, and put newly created files somewhere users can find them, such as the Desktop, rather than hiding them in the application's own corner of the file system.

Separate specifying a document's stored format from the act of saving, treating format as a property of the document accessed through Document Properties or Export, because overriding format is rare while saving is common and combining them adds needless complexity.

Do not use the file system as a surrogate for Undo; reverse inadvertent changes through the Undo function, and provide an explicit Abandon Changes or Revert to version function with clear warnings rather than forcing users to understand the file system.

Because a unified model presents storage as a single thing, the leftmost application menu need not be called File, which reflects the implementation model, and can instead be labeled by the document type or generically as Document.

Disks are a cost compromise and a hack rather than a design feature, so wherever disk technology has left its mark on the design of software it has done so for implementation purposes and not in the service of users or any goal-directed rationale.

Users are not interaction designers and cannot predict the effects of interaction paradigm shifts, so they reject unfamiliar change yet will gladly give up painful, poorly designed software for easier, better software once it exists.

Validating and rejecting bad data at the point of entry, in the name of data integrity, places the database's needs before the user's, subjecting the user to a shakedown and asserting that the user works for the application rather than the reverse.

Prefer data immunity over data integrity: build applications smart enough to handle all permutations of data by looking before they leap, seeking help elsewhere in the system, and annotating problems, rather than erecting barriers to keep imperfect data out.

Design applications to assume the user entered what he meant, and since incorrect input is often close to correct, provide as much correction assistance as possible and give visual feedback on suspect entries, because users generally act stupidly only when applications treat them stupidly.

Do not stop a user for missing data; allow him to enter the information he has now and return later, communicating any required but missing fields through rich modeless feedback rather than blocking his work like a car that locks the steering wheel over low washer fluid.

For data that must be valid, use type-ahead auto-completion or bounded controls such as drop-downs and smart parsing text fields rather than free text, and give unobtrusive modeless feedback so the user takes control and the application does less policing.

Treating all information workers as untrustworthy to guard against the few who are is counterproductive and self-fulfilling, lowering productivity and morale and increasing the error rate of the clerks who want to do well.

A system that is too rigid cannot model real-world behaviors, so build fudgeability into it by making the queue, document, and its position visible and manipulable and by allowing records to be held in suspense, resolving the conflict between serving the database and serving the business.
The best strategy to prevent abuse of a fudgeable system is to let users do what they want while keeping very detailed records of their actions so that full accountability is possible.

An application's duty to report errors extends to other applications, not to users: it should accept whatever the user tells it regardless of how incorrect it believes the input to be, treating the user as always right.

A user error may not be the application's fault, but it is the application's responsibility, so the application should accept the action, warn modelessly, and work to protect the user from harm rather than blocking or scolding.

Audit, don't edit: when a user does something the application thinks is wrong, make the possible problem clear unobtrusively and rely on the user's intelligence to resolve it, while remembering every action, ensuring clean reversibility, and maintaining a clear audit trail, rather than jumping in to fix it and subverting the user's intent.

Warn about suspect input clearly and modelessly, the way a speedometer silently reports speed, for example by highlighting a suspect data-entry field, rather than stopping the proceedings with an error dialog.

Automatic correction that silently changes a user's input should leave a visible mark or audit trail, and overly smart auto-formatting that guesses wrong and cannot be easily undone should leave the thinking to the human and be easy to turn off.
The technical goal of data integrity should not be the user's problem to solve, so design applications to accommodate the way humans think about partially or incorrectly filled-in documents.

Direct manipulation, as defined by Shneiderman, consists of a visual representation of the objects of concern, visible and gestural mechanisms for acting on them instead of text commands, and immediately visible results, and rich visual feedback is the key to making it succeed.
Users can directly manipulate only what is displayed, so render data, objects, controls, and cursors with enough rich graphic detail to be manipulable.

Direct-manipulation idioms usually must be taught but are easy to teach and seldom forgotten, yet they can demand motor coordination and skill, so consider what users should manipulate directly versus what the application should help with more indirectly given the personas' skills and contexts.

Fully support both mouse and keyboard for all navigation and selection tasks, providing at least one non-mouse alternative for each mouse idiom, because many users, especially touch-typists, find the mouse difficult and dislike leaving the keyboard.
exception: drawing and other inherently spatial interactions cannot reasonably be supported without a pointing device

statement: Design around the cost of transitioning between fine and gross motor skills, since clicking requires fine control and controls like the classic split scrollbar force repeated switches, so place things that are used together together and avoid idioms that demand continual motor-skill changes.

Use meta-keys such as Ctrl, Alt, Shift, and Command to extend and modify direct-manipulation idioms, and use cursor hinting so that while a meta-key is pressed the cursor changes to reflect the new function of the idiom.

Double-click means single-click plus action, selecting an object and then acting on it, so include double-click idioms but ensure each has an equivalent single-click idiom because double-clicking is difficult or impossible for some less dexterous users.

Provide an escape hatch during clicking and dragging, such as canceling a button press by moving off the control before release or resetting a scrollbar when the drag strays too far, so users can recover from a mistake or a change of mind.

Reserve expert-only mouse idioms such as chord-clicking and double-click-and-drag for large sovereign applications with many selection permutations, and stick to basic mouse actions for most products.
Make the interpretation of mouse-down and mouse-up events rigidly consistent within a product and ideally across a platform, since inconsistent handling of these two discrete events confuses users.
When the cursor is over selectable data, mouse-down should select the object or data, because the click may be the first step of a drag and you cannot drag something without first selecting it.

When the cursor is over a control, mouse-down should propose the action by tentatively showing the state transition and mouse-up should commit to it, which lets a user gracefully bow out of an inadvertent click by moving off the control before releasing.

Visually communicate pliancy so it is obvious which interface elements are manipulable, which are informational, and which are decor, using static object hinting, dynamic hinting on cursor fly-over, or cursor hinting.
condition: the exception is expert-only interfaces where the screen space for communicating pliancy is better used elsewhere, a decision not to be made lightly

statement: Prefer dynamic visual hinting, where a control gains its affordance as the cursor rolls over it, to reduce persistent visual clutter while still signaling that the control behaves like a button.

Provide pliant response hinting when the mouse is pressed but not released inside a control, such as a button indenting or a check box highlighting without yet checking, which both signals a forthcoming action and forms part of the cancel mechanism.

Use cursor hinting to indicate pliancy and often the possible action, generally offering static or dynamic hinting on controls but cursor hinting on manipulable data such as dense tables and small controls like column dividers and screen splitters that cannot easily hint at pliancy themselves.

Object-verb command ordering, selecting the object first and then choosing the verb, suits direct manipulation better than verb-object because it needs no termination, lets a user apply several verbs to one selection, and lets the application show only the commands appropriate to what is selected.
exception: verb-object order is more usable when the objects cannot reasonably be defined without the context of the command

statement: Mutual exclusion, where making a new selection unmakes the previous one, is the default for both discrete and contiguous selection; allow additive selection for discrete data through a meta-key but generally not for contiguous data, because scrolling makes off-screen selections uncontrollable.

Make the selection state visually evident and unambiguous, easy to spot on a crowded screen, without relying on color alone since many users are color-blind, and for visually rich objects add selection indicators such as handles or indicate selection by movement like a marching-ants marquee.

Understand drag-and-drop as clicking on an object and moving it to imply a transformation, spanning truly direct idioms that put the object somewhere and slightly more indirect idioms that drop an object on a target to perform a function.

Provide strong visual feedback once a drag begins, because although users easily remember that an object can be dragged they may forget the details of the action, and forgiving interactions and Undo encourage them to try direct manipulation without trepidation.

During a drag, each drop candidate must visually indicate its receptivity while the drag cursor identifies the source object, and these two functions must not be confused by using the cursor to represent drop candidacy.
Avoid negative feedback such as the Not Permitted symbol for drag cursor hinting, because it tells users what they cannot do and is easily misread as a warning against releasing the mouse.

Drag a transparent outline or thumbnail of the source object rather than an exact image, so the dragged object does not obscure a small target and the arrow cursor's hotspot remains visible to indicate the precise drop point.

Show an insertion target whenever an object can be dropped in the space between other objects, such as the vertical caret bar shown when dragging text in a word processor or reordering slides, to indicate precisely where the dropped object will land.

Give visual feedback at completion so it is clear the drop's operation occurred, for example the source object disappearing from its origin and reappearing at the target, or a function icon animating to show it received the drop.

Any scrollable drag-and-drop target must auto-scroll, beginning just inside the window border, ideally at a variable rate that increases toward the edge with a speed limit, and after a time delay of about half a second so a slow-moving user does not inadvertently trigger it.

When an object can be both selected and dragged, bias the mouse toward selection by debouncing the drag with a drag threshold of about three pixels, interpreting movement within the threshold as a selection, because users rarely intend to drag an object only one or two pixels.

Use an axially non-symmetric drag threshold biased toward the more frequent action to distinguish two drag directions, such as a spool-shaped uncommitted zone that makes a common horizontal drag easy while insulating users from a rare vertical drag.

Any program that demands precise alignment must offer a vernier or fine-scrolling mode, activated by a meta-key or arrow keys, and should desensitize the mouse on the first vernier keystroke so that releasing the mouse button does not disturb the precise placement.
condition: applies at minimum to drawing, painting, presentation, and image-manipulation programs

statement: Because the menu is the primary control for beginners yet is one of the hardest to operate physically, requiring click-and-drag, provide an alternative non-drag idiom such as a toolbar button for any function used more than rarely, and support single-click menu operation.

Modal palette tools introduce users to a program's features well but do not scale for intermediates as the tool count grows, because the excise of selecting and deselecting tools rises, so keep the working set of modal tools small.

A charged cursor loaded with one instance of an object must visually indicate its modal state and provide a good cancel idiom to discharge it, and allowing either a single click for a default-sized object or dragging a rectangle for a custom-sized one is the most flexible and discoverable approach.

Dedicate a specific physical area of an object to repositioning, such as a window's title bar, so the object's click-and-drag idiom stays available for other functions, and provide explicit visual hinting of that area's pliancy.

Use a meta-key such as Shift for a constrained drag that locks movement to a single axis, determined by the predominant motion of the first several pixels, which is especially helpful for drawing neatly organized diagrams.
Assist object positioning with guides and snapping, including dynamic smart guides that help users align objects to each other and create evenly spaced rows and columns.

Use resize handles for graphical objects, which are visually bold, do not obscure the object, and conveniently double as selection indicators, and use vertex handles for polyline shapes and Bezier handles, reserved for specialized applications, for curves.

Handles obscure the object they represent, so they make poor permanent controls and are best replaced by frame or corner resizers for windows, and offscreen handles on an object larger than the screen are useless for both manipulation and selection indication.
Provide both a bounding-box idiom for proportional scaling and a vertex-editing idiom for fine-tuning the shape of a freeform object, because each serves a distinct and necessary purpose.

For manipulating 3D objects on a 2D screen, rich visual modeless feedback such as baseline grids, depthcueing, shadows, poles, and color-coded guidelines is a necessity to convey position and movement, while multiple viewpoints aid alignment but force users to triangulate mentally.
condition: applies to 3D applications

statement: Address the 3D picking problem of selecting occluded overlapping objects with techniques such as a hover menu of candidates, per-facet pliancy hinting, and fluid navigation like mapping zoom and orbit to the mouse scroll wheel, supported by a thumbnail absolute view to keep users oriented.
condition: applies to 3D applications

statement: Implement the object-connection idiom, dragging a line or arrow from one object to another, with rubber-banding feedback, active visual hinting so valid targets highlight when a connection is dragged over them, and a convenient means of canceling the action.

Modes are not inherently evil in the object-verb world of a GUI, even though they are poisonous in a command line, because the benefit of an interface like MacPaint comes not from modelessness but from the ease of seeing which mode the program is in and changing that mode effortlessly.

The overlapping-sheets-of-paper window metaphor does not scale beyond about three applications and causes lost-window confusion, though overlapping within a single application, as with dialogs, menus, and floating palettes, is a natural and well-formed idiom.

Multiple windows sharing a small screen, whether overlapping or tiled, is not a good general solution for navigating between programs; prefer full-screen applications with a minimal switching mechanism such as a taskbar.

Multipaned windows bring the best of tiled windows inside a sovereign full-screen application by displaying independent but related information in one window with adjacent panes, reducing navigation and window-management excise to almost nil, so adjacent-pane designs are practically a requirement for any complex sovereign application.

Treat each window, pane, or dialog box as a separate room and do not add one unless it serves a purpose that cannot or should not be served by existing windows, judged from users' goals and mental models.

Provide functions in the window where they are used: a task integral to the application's purpose belongs in the main window rather than a dialog box, as shown by an image editor placing brightness and contrast controls beside the image, and this is one of the most frequently violated principles in user-interface design.

Provide a separate room such as a dialog box for functions performed outside the user's normal sequence of events, like purging a database or importing clip art, using goal-directed thinking to decide which functions belong inline, in an integral dialog, or removed from the program entirely.

Avoid windows pollution from putting a single function in each dialog box, because achieving a goal involves a series of functions and there is no way to show the connections between many windows, so do not create many windows, and remember that the utility of any interaction idiom is context-dependent.

The normal window state for a sovereign application is maximized to full screen, with little reason to pluralize it except to support switching or dragging data between programs, while some transient applications are appropriately shown in a pluralized window.

A multiple-document interface is reasonable when users need multiple related views of information together in one environment, but it is abused when it forces users to manage little windows inside a big window and when changing menus destroy the orientation permanency users rely on, so going cleanly between full windows is often better.

Controls come in four flavors according to user goals: imperative controls that initiate a function, selection controls that select options or data, entry controls that enter data, and display controls that directly manipulate the program visually.

A multitude of control-laden dialog boxes does not make a good user interface, because standard controls guarantee ease of implementation but not ease of use and must be used judiciously, whereas a direct-manipulation interface consistent with user mental models is harder to build but better.

Satisfy users' expectation that a button visually changes from raised to indented when clicked, because painted buttons that do not move are disconcerting and leave users wondering whether their click did anything.

Butcons suit intermediate users because they are always visible and memorable, but their icons are seldom clear to novices, so provide ToolTips and prefer menus with explicit wording as the command vector for first-time users.

Use links for navigation through content and buttons or butcons for actions and functions, because users have learned that a link is a navigational idiom and are confused when clicking one executes an action.

Let a selection control double as an imperative control only when users benefit from seeing the immediate and easily undone impact of their choice; otherwise require an explicit imperative control so users can make a series of selections before committing.
Keep check boxes square and radio buttons round, following the established standard shapes users have learned to recognize, rather than deviating for marketing or graphic-arts reasons.

Avoid flip-flop buttons whose single label switches between states, such as a combined play and pause control, because a control can serve either as a state indicator or as a state-switching selection control but not both; spell out the verb or use two separate buttons instead.

Radio buttons are mutually exclusive, always appear in groups of two or more with one always selected, and suit a teaching role by showing all choices in infrequently used dialogs, whereas a drop-down list is often a better choice on the surface of a sovereign application because it saves space.
Distinguish important text items in lists with graphic icons, because a graphical identifier next to key entries lets users find them faster than unrelieved lines of text.

For multiple selection in a scrollable list, use earmarking with a check box on each item rather than disabling the list's mutual exclusion, because a check box clearly signals non-mutual selection and avoids the trap of a user silently deselecting an item that has scrolled out of view.

Support drag-and-drop from and within list controls so users can gather items into a set or reorder them directly, and implement auto-scroll so a user can scroll the list while still holding a dragged item.

Never scroll text horizontally, except in large tables with locked row and column headers, because horizontal scrolling hides the first letters of every line and destroys readability; instead shorten or wrap the entries or widen the control.
exception: large tables such as spreadsheets with locked headers may scroll horizontally

statement: Make items that are editable elsewhere editable in place within a list control, and provide a discoverable way to add a new entry, such as a perpetual open row labeled Click to Add Entry, rather than forcing users to a separate button or menu.

The combo box, a list combined with an edit field, is a superb single-selection control that is fast replacing groups of radio buttons because it is space efficient, can add items dynamically, shows the current selection without any action, and can reside permanently on a toolbar or a sovereign application's main screen.

Use a tree or hierarchy control only when the data is naturally thought of as a hierarchy, such as a family tree, because forcing arbitrary data into a treeview on the rationale that it is intuitive harms usability by hiding the more interesting non-hierarchical relationships between objects.

Use bounded controls for bounded input, meaning a control that visually communicates the acceptable data boundaries and makes an invalid entry impossible, rather than an unbounded field that accepts any value only to reject it afterward with an error, which is merely a rude control.

Sliders let users enter quantitative information by analogy through relative position and telegraph the range of valid entries, making them good for relative or zoom values but poor for precise numbers, for which a spinner is better.

Do not use an unbounded text edit control when the acceptable values are finite: use a bounded numeric control such as a slider for numbers, or a list control for a set of text strings, so users are not forced to type.

The best solution to input validation is to use bounded controls that make invalid entries impossible, such as offering a drop-down list of months rather than requiring the user to spell February correctly.

When an unbounded validation control is unavoidable, give users generous rich feedback rather than merely refusing input, and visually distinguish validation controls from ordinary controls through typeface, border, or background color.

When an active validation control rejects a keystroke it must make clear that and why it did so, and passive validation that checks when the control loses focus can be made responsive with a countdown timer reset on each keystroke that validates about half a second after the user pauses.

Use a clue box, a ToolTip-like pop-up that explains the range of acceptable data for a validation control, to give modeless feedback near the offending entry instead of stopping the user with an error dialog.

Handle out-of-bounds data gracefully by having a numeric entry control convert a spelled value like nine into 9 rather than declaring it invalid, and by substituting the nearest allowable value while modelessly explaining the substitution in a clue box.

Make text edit controls smart enough to recognize appropriate units such as inches or millimeters, and let users choose named values like default or best fit from a combo box so that such knowledge lives in the program where it is visible rather than in the user's head.

Use noneditable display controls for output-only text rather than text edit controls, because the edit control's system font and white box encourage data entry and mislead users into thinking read-only output is editable.

Display a changeable value in an editable field so users can click and change it directly where it is shown, because separating the mechanism to input a value from the mechanism to output it, through a special edit mode, is almost always excise.

Make scrollbars informative by using a thumb proportionally sized to the visible portion and adding context such as total pages and the current page as the user scrolls, plus navigation tools like jump-to-start and bookmarks.

Because scrollbars demand high mouse precision and poorly represent open-ended dimensions like time, consider a document navigator that gives a thumbnail overview and direct navigation, appropriate when the document's big picture can be meaningfully represented in visual form.

Advertise a movable splitter's pliancy with cursor hinting, do not let a splitter be moved so far that a pane's contents become unusable, and use a drawer idiom when a pane needs to collapse entirely.

Use drawers, panes that open and close with a single action, to hold less-frequently-used controls that are most useful in the context of the main work area, since they do not cover the work area the way a dialog does.
Attend to the details of controls, because frustrating controls cause constant low-level annoyance that undermines even an excellent overall product concept.

Flattening a menu hierarchy into monocline grouping, aided by dialog boxes that gather subchoices, greatly improves the scanability of the interface, especially for novices, so the deeply hierarchical sequential menu should be avoided.
A good user interface lets users move ad hoc and piecemeal from beginner to expert, reading the menu to find unfamiliar functions while invoking familiar ones with memorized shortcuts.

Use menus as a pedagogic vector whose primary role is to teach new users, remind those who have forgotten, and provide access to infrequently used functions, rather than as the main way normal users perform everyday functions, which toolbars and direct manipulation serve better.

Because menus teach, make menu item text verbose rather than terse, explaining what a function does such as Open Report rather than Open, avoiding jargon, and keeping the menus complete so that a scan reveals the full scope of the program.

Do not blindly accept the standard File, Edit, and Help menu structure, which reflects implementation-model thinking and names that sound like tools rather than goals; organize menus by users' mental models and a goal-directed structure, naming the primary menu after the document type when appropriate.
condition: sticking to recognizable standards can be appropriate for computer-savvy productivity applications, while specialized applications may need a different structure

statement: Use cascading hierarchical menus only in sophisticated sovereign applications for rarely used functions or as a secondary command vector, because they make items hard to find and require well-coordinated two-dimensional mouse movement; when used, allow a wide movement threshold so the submenu does not disappear.

Avoid adaptive menus that hide infrequently used items, because they run contrary to the two primary roles of a menu, teaching breadth and depth and providing access to less-frequent functions, and studies show users complete tasks more slowly and overwhelmingly prefer static menus.

Avoid bang or immediate menus whose title executes a function on the menu bar, because they break the menu convention and are disorienting; immediate commands belong on toolbars, where butcons are known by convention to be imperative controls.

Disable menu items by graying them out when they are not applicable to the current state or selected object, which improves the menu's teaching value by helping users understand the context in which each command applies.

Use a checkmark menu item that is either checked or unchecked rather than a flip-flop menu item that shows the state not currently chosen, because the flip-flop cannot distinguish offering a choice from describing a state while the checkmark makes the meaning unambiguous.

Use consistent visual symbols on parallel command vectors, showing the same icon on a menu item as on its corresponding toolbar butcon, so users build a strong visual language and connect the two, probably without even thinking about it.

Create good keyboard accelerators by following platform standards, assigning them to the functions in everyone's daily use, and showing each accelerator to the right of its menu item so intermediates discover it, triaging functions into always, never, and maybe daily use to decide assignment.

Treat access keys or mnemonics as not optional, providing a complete, consistent, and thoroughly considered keyboard equivalent of every menu command, because the most experienced users rely heavily on the keyboard.

On mobile and small-screen devices where menus are often the primary command vector, avoid cascading menus entirely and map the most frequently used functions to the number keys or the top of the list.
condition: applies to mobile and small-screen devices

statement: Design toolbars to give experienced users fast, visible, immediate access to frequently used functions rather than duplicating the menu, since toolbars are concise but inscrutable to beginners while menus are the comprehensive, descriptive pedagogic vector.

Use images on toolbars and text on menus deliberately, because text is precise and clear but slow to read, suiting the teaching role of menus, whereas a pictograph is ambiguous until learned but then recognized very fast, suiting the quick-access role of toolbars.

A butcon's icon does not need to teach its purpose, which is a quixotic quest, but only needs to be easily recognizable once learned, with its purpose taught through other means such as ToolTips, and labeling butcons with both text and images costs too many pixels.

Use ToolTips with all toolbar and iconic controls, relying on their well-timed lag of about a second so users are not barraged with pop-ups while working yet can find a forgotten butcon in half a second.

Disable toolbar controls, offering no pliant response and graying them out, when they are not applicable to the current selection, but do not make them disappear, because users remember toolbar layouts by position and vanishing butcons disorient them.

Put primary interactions in the primary window and let dialog boxes play only a secondary, supporting role, because forcing users to bounce back and forth between the main window and its dialogs inevitably leads to fatigue and frustration.

Use dialog boxes for functions that are out of the main interaction flow, namely anything confusing, dangerous, dislocating, or rarely used, providing a big friendly Cancel button and room for protective and explanatory information.

Use dialog boxes to organize the controls and information about a single domain object or a single application function in one place, reducing the navigation excise of searching the interface for a given function.

Design dialog boxes with a strong visual hierarchy, subject-based groupings, and a conventional reading-order layout, have them appear on the topmost layer when instantiated, and always give them a clear title.
Use a verb in a function dialog's title bar, such as Insert Break rather than Break, and use the object's name in a property dialog's title bar, so the title matches what the user is actually doing.

Modal dialogs are the easiest for users to understand because they clearly say to stop and deal with the dialog now, and applications should almost never use a system-modal dialog that halts the entire system, reserving it for truly catastrophic occurrences.

Modeless dialogs are more difficult to design and use than modal dialogs because the selection can change during their lifetime and their scope of operation is unclear, so freezing application state is what makes modal dialogs simpler.

Visually differentiate modeless dialogs from modal dialogs consistently, for example with a different background, distinct controls, or a different title-bar color, because the standard facility renders them indistinguishable.

Give every modeless dialog a single consistently placed Close button that is never disabled and never has a dynamically changing label, relying on the application-wide Undo function rather than a Cancel for reversal, since a modeless dialog's controls are always live and it stays open for repetitive use.

Prefer toolbars, palettes, and sidebars over modeless dialogs, because they are modeless without the conundrums, are visually distinct, are omnipresent so they need no terminating control, are efficient in screen space, and do not cover up what they operate on.

Because repositioning windows is never a user's goal, free-floating modeless dialogs create window-management excise, so use docked palettes and sidebars that reduce screen-management excise while providing the same modeless interactivity.

Use sidebars, task panes, or a dedicated properties area below a workspace to provide modelessly the functions formerly delivered through dialog boxes, which retains the user's context and minimizes screen-management excise.

There are four goal-directed types of dialog box: property dialogs to view and change a selected object's attributes, function dialogs to initiate and configure a single function, process dialogs to report a busy internal function, and bulletin dialogs for unrequested application messages.

Separate configuring a function from invoking it, while linking them seamlessly, because a dialog that combines the two forces users to confront the full complexity of the options even when they want to perform a routine task simply.

When an application begins a perceptibly time-consuming process it must inform the user that it is busy but that everything is otherwise normal, or the user will interpret the silence as rudeness or assume the program has crashed.

A process dialog must satisfy four requirements: make clear a time-consuming process is happening, show through continual time-related movement that things are normal, indicate how much time remains as progress relative to total time rather than size, and provide a way to cancel and regain control.

Consider eliminating a process dialog by showing the status in the main window, as a browser shows page-load progress in its status bar, whenever the process is integral to the main window, since a dialog is another room for what is really a this-room function.

Make a Cancel button mean cancel, undoing everything so no trace of the operation remains, rather than merely stopping the operation partway through; if it only stops the operation, label it Stop instead.

Never use transitory dialogs that take themselves down as error messages or confirmations, because an error or confirmation must stop the program so the user definitely gets the message, which a fleeting bulletin cannot guarantee.

Property and function dialogs serve the user because they are requested, whereas bulletin dialogs such as errors, alerts, and confirmations serve the application at the user's expense and should be avoided in most circumstances.

Group the contents of a tabbed dialog with a meaningful rationale, organizing for breadth with parallel aspects or for depth on one aspect, and remember that all interaction idioms have practical limits, so replace stacked tabs with several separate dialogs having fewer tabs each.

Cascading dialogs, in which one dialog summons another with its own terminating buttons, are confusing because the scope of each Cancel and OK is unclear, and needing them for anything but truly obscure functions is a symptom of excessive complexity and structural flaws in the interaction framework.

Error message boxes stop the proceedings with idiocy and should be avoided, because most report the program's own inability to work flexibly rather than alerting the user to a genuinely serious problem.

Most error bulletins report when the computer gets confused, such as out-of-bounds or out-of-sequence input, rather than a substantive user mistake, so the software should assume the human input is correct and work harder to understand and reconcile it rather than rejecting it.

Rather than halting on missing or out-of-sequence data, accept the transaction with modeless feedback that something is not yet recognized and let the user supply the missing information before the end of the session, the way manual systems work.

Error messages do not prevent users from making errors; they only prevent the program from getting into trouble, standing guard where the program is sensitive rather than where the user is vulnerable.

Eliminate error messages by redesigning the software so it is immune to the problem and prevents error conditions from arising, treating an error message as an abnormal idiom of last resort rather than a normal solution.

Make errors impossible by using bounded controls such as drop-downs and lists so users cannot enter bad values, and make the application smart enough to avoid unnecessary demands by supplying known values itself, remembering prior files, and reading the date from the internal clock.

People learn better from positive feedback than from negative feedback, so acknowledge or reward success rather than slapping users on the wrist for failure, because negative feedback from a machine is humiliating and degrading and helps nothing inside the computer.

Treat the ad hoc appearance and disappearance of hardware and networks, such as printers, drives, and wireless connections, as normal behavior rather than an error, and have the application do something intelligent like saving locally and synchronizing later.

Some time-critical situations genuinely require notifying the user in an obtrusive, attention-demanding manner, such as warning that after-hours trades cannot execute until the market reopens, when the user may no longer want to make them.
condition: applies to genuinely time-critical situations

statement: When an error dialog is truly unavoidable as a last resort, make it polite, illuminating, and helpful: never hint that the user caused the problem, make clear its scope, alternatives, default, and any information lost, and directly offer at least one button that implements a solution.

Eliminate alerts in favor of more useful idioms, because an application should either have the courage of its convictions or not take action without direct instruction, and it can keep users informed through built-in visual feedback rather than stopping the proceedings to go into another room.

Confirmation dialogs reflect the implementation model and pass the buck to users; the proper solution is to make the action easily reversible and provide enough modeless feedback that users are not taken off guard.

Confirmations only work when unexpected, because routine confirmations get dismissed by rote like the boy who cried wolf, so a real danger warning is ignored; a confirmation should appear only when the user will almost certainly cancel, which reveals how pointless they are.
Do, don't ask: give software the courage of its convictions, backed by user research, rather than interrupting with confirmation dialogs, because users respect its brevity and confidence.

Make all actions reversible, even deleting or overwriting a file by moving it to a holding area before it is physically removed, and let the user issue Undo on the rare occasion an action was wrong rather than asking for confirmation in advance.

Provide modeless feedback to help users avoid mistakes by keeping them constantly informed the way a car dashboard does, building clear modeless warnings such as visible printable-region guides into the interface rather than reporting the problem too late in a dialog.

Use rich visual modeless feedback, information about the status or attributes of processes and objects that is rich, visual, and always displayed without a mode shift, to keep users constantly informed and all but eliminate dialogs, since constant feedback is what users need but on a different channel.

Rich visual modeless feedback is not for beginners because it requires work to discover and decode, so keep menus and dialogs as support, and make any modeless feedback used to warn of serious trouble extraordinarily clear and visually emphasized over merely informational feedback.

Use positive audible feedback, a sound that signals success so its absence becomes an effective silent indicator of a problem, rather than negative audible feedback that beeps to announce failure and acts as an insulting public alarm.

Provide multiple parallel command vectors so that critical functions can be invoked through menus, toolbars, keyboard accelerators, and direct manipulation alike, enabling users of different skill sets and inclinations to command the program in the way that suits them.

Provide immediate command vectors for the minimal working set, the frequently used functions identified from persona scenarios, along with a way to promote other commands to immediate vectors and pedagogic vectors for beginners, so that most functions have multiple command vectors.

As an exception to the rule of multiple command vectors, dangerous commands such as Erase All, Clear, and Abandon Changes should not have easy parallel vectors but should be protected within menus and dialogs, consistent with hiding the ejector-seat levers.

Information in the world, embodied in pedagogic world vectors like menus and dialogs, is dependable but slow, while information in the head, embodied in head vectors like keyboard accelerators, is fast but must be learned, so beginners rely on world vectors and intermediates and experts increasingly on head vectors.

Provide a memorization vector, a path by which users learn the head vector corresponding to each world vector, built right into the interface through accelerators shown beside menu items, underlined mnemonics, and a Shortcuts item on the Help menu, rather than burying it in documentation.

Show each function's identifying icon on every artifact of the interface that deals with it, including every menu, butcon, dialog, help text, and printed documentation, because a memorization vector formed of consistent visual symbols is the most effective yet underexploited technique.

Distinguish personalization, decorating persistent objects such as colors and non-structural elements, which aids navigation and makes software likable and familiar, from configuration, moving, adding, or deleting persistent objects, which hinders navigation but is desirable for experienced users and necessary for experts.
Make personalization tools simple and easy to use, giving users a visual preview of their selections, and above all easy to undo, including a function that returns everything to the factory settings.

Most end users will not mind being unable to configure a program as long as it does its job well, but configuration is critical when supporting a rapidly evolving workflow and is highly valued by corporate IT managers who base buying decisions on it.

When user testing shows a population splitting roughly evenly on two idioms, a case of idiosyncratically modal preferences, offer both idioms rather than choosing one, ideally so they coexist without requiring the user to set a preference.

Immediate, idiomatic, visual command vectors such as direct manipulation and butcons globalize with relative ease, so long as chosen colors and symbols carry no unintended cultural meaning, whereas pedagogic textual vectors such as menu items, labels, and ToolTips are language-dependent and require localization by translation.

When localizing an interface, account for varying text length, difficult alphabetical sorting, and differing date, time, decimal, and calendar formats, and translate items holistically so the interface remains coherent as a whole rather than only item by item.
condition: applies to interfaces localized for multiple languages and cultures

statement: Offer users a gallery of ready-to-use templates so they can pick a premade starting design and make small changes, because a blank slate intimidates most people and few want to build a document completely from scratch.

Treat online help as a reference tool for perpetual intermediates already using the product who want to expand their horizons, not as a crutch or a resource aimed at beginners, and let good design greatly reduce users' reliance on help.

Make the index the priority of any reference document by generating it from an examination of the program and all its features rather than only the help text, including as many synonyms as possible and thinking in the goal-directed terms a user would actually search for.

Include in online help a Shortcuts digest of tools and keyboard commands and an overview describing each feature's scope, effect, power, and trade-offs, because perpetual intermediates need access to features more than detailed instructions.

ToolTips are modeless online help and are incredibly effective, whereas a standard help system implemented as a separate program covers up the application it explains and cannot point at objects on screen the way a helpful person would.

Wizards violate the principle of providing choices rather than asking questions, treating users as peripheral devices through step-by-step interrogation that devolves into confirmation-clicking; prefer a simple automatic function that does the job with no questions and lets users adjust the result afterward with standard tools.

Avoid anthropomorphic animated help agents, because employing lifelike characters raises users' expectations of the agent's intelligence beyond what it can deliver, making it cloying and distracting when users simply want direct, trustworthy assistance.

Design all aspects of a product before they are built, letting informed planning of the user experience precede construction even in a highly iterative process where building some parts can begin while others are still being designed.

Process, patterns, and principles are necessary but not sufficient for successful interaction design, which still requires the designer's spark of inventiveness and the judgment to know whether a concept is good, and requires close collaboration with business decision makers, technologists, and other experience-affecting team members throughout the project rather than designing in a vacuum.
